title: The operating system is responsible for:
subject: Operating System
text: The operating system is responsible for:

options.html: Controlling peripheral devices such as monitor, printers, disk drives
Provide an interface that allows users to choose programs to run/manipulate files

solution:
Answer: All of the above is correct.

  • Controlling peripheral devices (monitor, printers, disk drives): the operating system manages device drivers and I/O services so applications can use hardware without dealing with low-level details.

  • Providing a user interface to run programs and manipulate files: the OS offers command-line or graphical interfaces and program-launching facilities to let users and applications interact with the system.

  • Managing user files on disk: the OS implements the file system, handling storage allocation, organization, access control, and file operations.

Why this matters: The operating system acts as an intermediary between hardware and users/applications, providing resource management, device control, file management, and user interfaces so software can run reliably and users can interact with the computer.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The operating system controls peripheral devices (monitor, printers, disk drives) by providing and managing device drivers and input/output services so applications can use hardware without handling low-level details. This alone is not the full role of the OS, but it is an essential part.

Correct. The operating system provides user interfaces (command-line or graphical) and other services that let users choose and launch programs and manipulate files. This describes the OS’s role in presenting and managing user interaction.
Correct. The operating system manages files on disk through the file system, handling storage allocation, organization, access control, and file operations for users and applications.

Correct. All of the listed responsibilities are functions of the operating system: it controls peripheral devices, provides interfaces for running programs and manipulating files, and manages user files on disk. In short, the OS acts as an intermediary that manages hardware and provides services to users and applications.

title: The primary purpose of an operating system is
subject: Operating System
text: The primary purpose of an operating system is

options.html: To make most efficient use of the computer hardware
To allow people to use the computer

solution:
Operating-system theory presents two goals side by side: the user view — convenience, making the computer easy to use — and the system view — efficient resource management, allocating the CPU, memory, and I/O devices fairly among competing processes.

When a single-answer question asks for the OS's ‘primary purpose’, it is testing which of these two views is treated as foundational. For this exact ISRO CS 2009 item, independently published answer keys converge on the system view: efficient use of the computer hardware. The reasoning is that resource management is the enabling layer — it is what lets any program run at all — while ease of use is a benefit built on top of that management rather than a replacement for it.

  • To make computers easier to use — a genuine OS benefit, but it names a user-facing outcome that rests on resource management rather than the foundational, system-level function itself.

  • To allow people to use the computer — too generic to name any actual OS mechanism (scheduling, memory allocation, device management).

  • To keep systems programmers employed — not a real system objective; it can be eliminated outright.

Because independently published answer keys for this specific PYQ converge on efficient hardware use, and the other two options fail to describe any real OS objective, efficient use of the computer hardware is the defensible answer here — with ease of use standing as the closely related, but secondary, benefit.

optionFeedback.html: Efficient hardware use names the operating system's core system-level function — scheduling the CPU, allocating memory, and coordinating I/O devices among competing processes so the hardware is used well. This resource-management role is the enabling layer that makes any use of the machine possible at all, which is why it is the OS's foundational, primary purpose.
This phrasing only states that people can use the computer — it doesn't name any specific mechanism or goal, so it is too vague to serve as a definition of the OS's purpose.

Employment for programmers is a side effect of an industry existing, not something any system is designed to preserve — an operating system's objectives are defined by what it does for the machine and its users, not by job security for the people who write it, so this option can be eliminated outright.

Ease of use names a benefit users experience, not a design objective — 'primary purpose' calls for the goal the system is built around, and this option only restates the pleasant side effect of that goal being met, so it can't stand alone as the answer.

Therefore, the required value is Compilation.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q8
subject: Operating System
text: On systems with multiple operating systems, the decision to load a particular one is made by
solution:
Concept

During startup, firmware hands control to boot software. A boot loader locates a bootable operating-system kernel, loads it into memory, and transfers execution to it.

On a multiboot system, the same boot stage can present configured operating-system entries so that one kernel is selected before it is loaded.

Application

The question asks which component makes the operating-system choice at boot time. The component with boot entries and responsibility for loading the chosen kernel is the boot loader.

Contrast

  • Bootstrap names the startup process or initial routine more generally; it is not the specific multiboot selection component named here.

  • A process control block records the execution context and management data of a process after the operating system is managing processes.

  • A file control block records file metadata for file-system operations.

  • A boot loader provides the startup-stage path from a selected boot entry to the corresponding operating-system kernel.

Cross-check and result

If the user selects an operating system from a GRUB-style startup menu, the boot loader loads or chain-loads that system. Therefore, the answer is boot loader.

optionFeedback.html: Bootstrap describes the overall startup procedure or initial routine that brings a computer from reset toward an executable system state.
A process control block stores one process state, register values, scheduling data, and resource references for operating-system process management.
A file control block stores file metadata used by a file system, such as permissions, size, ownership, and storage-location information.
A boot loader runs during startup and loads the selected operating-system kernel or transfers control to it.

title: On systems where there are multiple operating system, the decision
subject: Operating System
text: On a system where multiple operating systems are installed, the decision to load a particular one at startup is made by ______.
solution:
Concept

Between power-on and the operating system taking over, a small program called the boot loader (bootstrap loader) runs first. It is responsible for locating the installed operating system(s), presenting a choice when more than one is installed, and loading the selected kernel into memory before handing over control.

Application

On a multi-boot machine, right after the hardware self-test, the boot loader reads the boot configuration, offers the installed operating systems to choose from, and loads the selected OS's kernel into memory. This is exactly the "decision to load a particular one" the question describes — it happens through the boot loader, not through any component that only becomes active after an OS is already running.

Why the other options don't fit

  • Process control block — created for a process only after the OS has already started running it; tracks that process's state, not OS selection.

  • File control block — belongs to the file system, tracking a file's attributes and disk location; unrelated to booting.

  • "More than one of the above" — wrong because a single dedicated program does this job, not a combination of components.

  • "None of the above" — wrong because one of the listed components does perform exactly this task.

optionFeedback.html: A process control block stores per-process bookkeeping — its state, program counter, and register values — once a process is already running; it plays no part in choosing which installed OS to load when the machine powers on.

A file control block records a file's attributes and its location on disk so the file system can manage it; it has no role in deciding which operating system kernel starts running when the computer is switched on.

This is the small program that runs right after the hardware powers on: it locates the installed operating system(s), presents the choice when more than one is present, and hands control to the selected kernel.
This task is carried out by one specific mechanism, not by a combination of the components listed above — so no combination of them jointly performs this job.
One of the components listed above does perform exactly this task, so it is not true that none of them do — this option would only hold if no listed component performed the function described.

title: Which of the following statement is true?

text: Which of the following statement is true?

options.html: Hard real time OS has less jitter than soft real time OS

solution: Hard real-time operating systems are designed to guarantee strict deadline adherence, requiring highly deterministic behavior with minimal variation in response times. Soft real-time systems prioritize throughput and can tolerate occasional deadline misses, often resulting in higher variability or jitter. Consequently, hard real-time OSs typically exhibit less jitter compared to soft real-time OSs to ensure reliability.

title: Which of the following is an example of time-sharing operating
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following is an example of a time-sharing operating system?
solution:
Concept

A time-sharing (multi-user) operating system lets many users interact with one computer at the same time by giving each a very short CPU time slice in rapid rotation. The fast switching makes every user feel as if they have the machine to themselves. The defining trait is concurrent interactive access by multiple users from separate terminals - not merely the ability to store more than one user account.

Application

Test each option against that defining trait - concurrent multi-user terminal access with CPU time-slicing:

  • MS-DOS - single user, one task at a time; no concurrency or time-slicing.

  • Windows 10 - supports multiple accounts, but the design serves one interactive desktop session; account creation is multi-user storage, not concurrent terminal time-sharing.

  • macOS - same as above: multiple accounts are supported, yet the architecture targets a single interactive desktop user.

  • UNIX - designed so many users at separate terminals share the CPU through rapid time slices simultaneously.

Result

Only UNIX matches the time-sharing definition (concurrent interactive multi-user access via CPU time-slicing). Having multiple user accounts, as in Windows 10 or macOS, is not the same as time-sharing, so UNIX is the correct choice.

optionFeedback.html: MS-DOS is a single-user, single-tasking operating system: it runs one program for one user at a time and has no terminal-based concurrent-user scheduling, so it does not fit the time-sharing category.

Windows 10 supports several user accounts, but only one interactive desktop session is the design focus at a time; creating multiple accounts is multi-user account management, not the classic terminal-based time-sharing model where many users share CPU slices concurrently.

macOS also lets you create multiple accounts, yet its architecture centres on a single interactive desktop user; account support is not the same as the time-slicing, many-terminal concurrency that defines a time-sharing OS.

UNIX was built from the start so that many users at separate terminals receive rapid round-robin CPU time slices, giving each the feel of a dedicated machine - the defining behaviour of a time-sharing operating system.

title: Which of the following is an example of real-time operating
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following is an example of a real-time operating system?
solution:
A real-time operating system (RTOS) is built to process inputs and deliver outputs within a strict, deterministic time bound, or deadline, so that timing is guaranteed and not just fast on average. A general-purpose operating system instead optimizes for overall throughput and fair multitasking, where occasional delay is acceptable.

QNX is a microkernel-based RTOS engineered from the ground up for deterministic, low-latency task scheduling. This is why it is widely used in embedded, automotive, and industrial control systems, where missing a timing deadline can cause the system to fail.

  • Windows 10: a general-purpose desktop operating system optimized for interactive multitasking, not for deterministic timing guarantees.

  • UNIX: a general-purpose multi-user, multitasking operating system; standard UNIX does not provide the deterministic guarantees of a true RTOS (separate real-time UNIX variants exist but are not standard UNIX itself).

  • Linux: a general-purpose operating system; although real-time patches or variants (such as PREEMPT_RT) exist, the standard/vanilla Linux kernel does not guarantee hard real-time deadlines.

Among the given options, only QNX is built as a true real-time operating system, so QNX is the correct answer.

optionFeedback.html: Windows 10 is a general-purpose operating system designed for desktop and laptop computers. It does not guarantee strict timing constraints required by real-time applications.

UNIX is a general-purpose operating system designed for multitasking and multi-user environments. While real-time UNIX variants exist, standard UNIX lacks the deterministic timing guarantees required for true real-time operation.
QNX is a microkernel-based real-time operating system built for deterministic, low-latency scheduling, which is why it is used in embedded, automotive, and industrial control systems.
Linux is a general-purpose operating system that lacks hard real-time guarantees by default. Even where real-time patches exist, the standard Linux kernel does not meet strict timing constraints.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q20
subject: Operating System
text: Multiprogramming systems

options.html: Are easier to develop than single programming systems.
Execute more jobs in the same time period.
Are used in only large mainframe computers.

solution:
Concept

Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU can switch to a ready job whenever the current job waits for input/output. Its central performance aim is to reduce CPU idle time and raise system throughput, which is the number of jobs completed per unit time. Throughput is different from the turnaround time of one particular job.

Application

  1. With only one resident job, an input/output wait can leave the CPU idle even though the system still has useful work to finish.

  2. With several resident jobs, the operating system can schedule a ready job during that waiting interval, so CPU work and another job’s input/output wait overlap.

  3. Because a larger share of the same time interval is spent doing useful CPU work, the system can complete more jobs in that interval. Therefore the applicable statement is “Execute more jobs in the same time period.”

Contrast

  • “Are easier to develop than single programming systems” concerns implementation effort; coordinating several jobs requires additional scheduling, memory-management, and protection mechanisms.

  • “Execute each job faster” concerns individual turnaround time; multiprogramming improves aggregate resource use but does not guarantee that every job finishes sooner.

  • “Are used in only large mainframe computers” imposes a hardware-size restriction that is not part of the definition of multiprogramming.

Cross-check and result

Compare two equal time windows. If the only resident job waits for input/output, some CPU slots are idle; if another ready job uses those slots, more useful processing is completed before the window ends. This confirms the throughput interpretation and the result “Execute more jobs in the same time period.”

optionFeedback.html: This statement uses system-development effort as its comparison axis. That effort includes designing and implementing scheduling, memory-management, and protection mechanisms.
This statement uses individual-job completion time as its metric. Turnaround time is measured from submission to completion and includes both running and waiting intervals.
This statement uses system throughput as its metric. Throughput is measured as the number of jobs completed per unit time.
This statement uses hardware deployment scope as its comparison axis. That scope classifies where a technique is used by machine class, such as mainframes or smaller computers.

title: Which of the following options best describes key function of
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following options best describes a key function of a multimedia operating system?

options.html: Providing database management tools for metadata indexing
Ensuring real-time scheduling and synchronization of multimedia data streams

solution:
A Multimedia Operating System differs fundamentally from a standard general-purpose OS (like basic Linux or Windows) because it must handle continuous, time-dependent data media streams natively.

1. Real-Time Scheduling (Timing constraints)
In a standard OS, a slight delay in executing a background task or opening a file is acceptable. However, in a multimedia environment, a delay causes jitter or frame drops.

To prevent this, a multimedia OS employs Real-Time Scheduling Algorithms (like Rate Monotonic or Earliest Deadline First).

These algorithms ensure that the CPU processes incoming audio and video frames before their strict deadlines expire.

2. Stream Synchronization
A standard video clip contains separate tracks: one for audio data and one for video data. These independent data blocks are read from disk or network interfaces simultaneously.

The multimedia operating system is tasked with managing these distinct streams and synchronizing them relative to a shared master clock. It maps timestamps to individual packets so that a specific audio sample plays at the exact millisecond its corresponding video frame is rendered on screen.

3. Resource Management & Quality of Service (QoS)
To stream high-definition content flawlessly, the OS must reserve a guaranteed amount of hardware resources. It implements resource reservation protocols that lock down specific CPU cycles, memory bandwidth, and network throughput for media playbacks, preventing a heavy background download from disrupting your video playback experience.

optionFeedback.html: High-level animation scripting, physics calculations, and rendering engines are managed by game engines (like Unity or Unreal Engine) or application-level software, not by the underlying operating system kernel.

Media compression (such as converting raw video to MP4/H.264) is handled by specific codecs and application software (like FFmpeg or video editors). The operating system provides the file system to store these files but doesn't perform the compression algorithms itself.

Metadata indexing and asset management are tasks for Database Management Systems (DBMS) or media library software (like Plex or iTunes). A multimedia OS focuses on the physical delivery and timing of the data rather than structural database querying.

Multimedia data (like live video streaming or audio playback) is highly time-sensitive. If data packets arrive late or out of order, you get choppy audio or lagging video. A multimedia OS must guarantee Quality of Service (QoS) through real-time process scheduling and ensure that audio and video streams remain perfectly synchronized (lip-sync).

title: What is the primary purpose of system call in an
subject: Operating System
text: What is the primary purpose of a system call in an operating system ?

options.html: Run arbitrary user code with full system access
Request access to system resources and services in a controlled manner
Communicate directly with hardware devices without OS intervention
Manage other processes and control system behavior

solution: A system call serves as the fundamental interface between a user application and the operating system kernel. Its primary purpose is to allow programs to request access to protected system resources, such as files, memory, or network connections, in a controlled and secure manner. This mechanism ensures that user code cannot directly manipulate hardware or access critical data without permission, maintaining system stability and security. Option A is incorrect because user code runs in a restricted mode (user space) and cannot have full system access without transitioning to kernel mode via a system call. Option C is wrong because direct hardware communication bypasses the OS, which violates security and stability principles; the OS must mediate all hardware interactions. Option D describes process management functions, which are tasks performed by the OS itself rather than the specific purpose of a system call interface. Therefore, Option B accurately defines the core function of system calls as controlled resource requests.

optionFeedback.html: This would be a massive security disaster. The system call mechanism exists precisely to prevent user code from having full system access. User code is intentionally sandboxed in "User Mode."

This is the exact definition of a system call. It acts as a controlled gatekeeper. When an application asks for a resource (like opening a file via open() or allocating memory via brk()), the OS intercepts the request via a system call, verifies if the application has permission to do so, executes the task safely in Kernel Mode, and then returns the result to the application.

Applications are strictly forbidden from communicating directly with hardware without OS intervention in modern operating systems. If every app could talk directly to the hard drive or network card simultaneously, they would overwrite each other's data and crash the system. The OS must always intervene, and it does so via system calls.

While there are specific system calls used to manage processes (like fork() to create a process or kill() to send a signal), this is just one specific subset of what system calls do. The broader, primary purpose of the system call mechanism as a whole is to provide a secure interface for all hardware and software services, not just process management.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q166
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following is NOT a system call ?
solution:
A system call is the interface through which a running program asks the operating-system kernel for a service that user-space code is not permitted to perform on its own — creating or terminating a process, moving data to or from a file or device, or passing data between processes. Invoking one switches the processor from user mode into kernel mode and back. A library function, by contrast, is ordinary code that executes entirely in user space; it may request a kernel service internally, but the routine itself is not that kernel interface.

The classification used in standard operating-system courses, and in Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne's table of process-control examples, turns on one question about a named routine: does the kernel itself provide a service of that name, or is the name purely a user-space convenience layered on top of some other kernel service?

Applying that test to each option:

  • fork() names a kernel process-control service: the kernel allocates a new process control block and duplicates the caller's address-space mapping, producing a child process that starts with a copy of the parent's memory image. No user-space routine can do this by itself.

  • exit() names the kernel's process-termination service (exit / exit_group on Linux), which releases the process's resources and leaves an exit status for the parent to collect. The C library entry of the same name first runs the program's registered termination handlers and flushes its stdio buffers, and reaches that kernel service through the low-level _exit call. Standard operating-system texts list exit() among the process-control system calls on the strength of the kernel service it denotes.

  • read() names a kernel file- and device-management service: the kernel transfers up to a requested number of bytes from an open file descriptor into a buffer the program supplies, since only the kernel may safely touch the underlying file system or device.

  • printf() names no kernel service at all: formatting its arguments against a format string happens entirely in user space inside the C standard I/O library, and the resulting characters reach the terminal or file only afterwards, through a separate write() system call.

Cross-check by exclusivity: fork(), exit() and read() each name a service the kernel itself provides — their user-space wrappers exist only to enter the kernel — whereas printf() has no kernel counterpart of that name and is a formatting convenience built on top of write().

A note on precision: read strictly as C-library entries, exit() is documented in manual section 3 alongside printf(), and the raw termination call is _exit(); under the standard operating-system classification this question uses, however, exit() denotes the kernel's termination service, and printf() is the only one of the four with no kernel service behind its name. Hence printf() is the answer — it is the one library routine among four names that otherwise denote kernel services.

optionFeedback.html: fork() creates a new process by duplicating the calling process, so the new process (the child) gets its own process ID while starting with a copy of the parent's memory image.
exit() terminates the calling process and makes an exit status value available for the parent process to collect, ending the process without returning to the code that invoked it.
read() copies up to a requested number of bytes from an open file descriptor into a buffer supplied by the calling program.
printf() converts its arguments into formatted text according to a format string and sends the resulting character sequence to the standard output stream.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q24

text: Match the following Windows API calls with their functionally corresponding UNIX system calls for process control and file manipulation. List I (Windows): A. CreateProcess; B. This ordering assigns CreateProcess to wait, WaitForSingleObject to fork, CreateFile to close, and CloseHandle to open.

title: Which of the following need not necessarily be saved on

solution: During a context switch, the operating system saves essential CPU state information such as general-purpose registers, program counter, and stack pointer into the Process Control Block (PCB) to ensure accurate resumption. However, the Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) is a hardware cache used for virtual-to-physical address translation. When switching between processes with different address spaces, the TLB entries are typically flushed rather than saved and restored. Therefore, the TLB does not need to be explicitly saved during a context switch.

title: Consider the statements below and choose the correct combination of
subject: Operating System
text:
Consider the statements below and choose the correct combination of "Yes" or "No" for each:

S1: Can two processes that are not parent/child be concurrently executing the same program executable?

S2: Can two running processes share the complete process image in physical memory (not just parts of it)?
solution:
Answer: (S1) Yes; (S2) No

  • S1 — Yes: Multiple processes can execute the same program binary concurrently. For example, launching the same executable twice creates two separate processes, each with its own process control block, registers, and stacks.

  • S2 — No: Processes do not share the complete process image in physical memory. Each process has its own virtual address space (private heap, stack, and writable data).

  • Notes/Exceptions: The operating system can map the same read-only code pages or shared libraries into multiple processes, and after a fork the kernel may use copy-on-write so pages are shared until modified. These mechanisms do not mean the entire, writable process image is shared by default.

Therefore the correct combination is: the first statement is Yes and the second statement is No.

optionFeedback.html: The first statement is correct: two processes can run the same program concurrently (for example, by launching the same executable twice). However, the second statement is incorrect: processes do not share the complete process image in physical memory. While read-only code pages or shared libraries can be mapped into multiple processes, writable parts like each process's heap and stack are private (and copy-on-write may temporarily allow sharing after a fork).

Correct. Two processes can execute the same program concurrently (e.g., running the same executable twice). However, processes do not share the entire process image in physical memory: each has its own virtual address space including private heap, stack, and process-specific data. The OS may share read-only code pages, shared libraries, or use copy-on-write, but not the whole image by default.

This combination is incorrect. The first statement is false here, but in reality the first statement is true: two processes can run the same executable concurrently. The second statement is also wrong to claim that the complete process image is shared. Processes may share some read-only pages or mapped files, but writable portions and per-process state remain separate.

This combination is partly incorrect. The second statement (that the complete process image is not shared) is correct. But the first statement is incorrect here: it claims that two processes cannot execute the same program, whereas in fact two distinct processes can run the same executable concurrently. Explain that separate processes have separate address spaces despite possibly sharing some read-only pages.

title: Operating systems must provide mechanism for parent processes to create
subject: Operating System
text: Operating systems must provide a mechanism for parent processes to create new child processes. Which of the following statements is true when a parent process creates new process?

options.html: The parent continues to execute concurrently with its children
The parent waits until some or all of its children have terminated

title: Any attempt by process to access memory allocated to OS
subject: Operating System
text: Any attempt by a process to access memory allocated to the OS or to the process of another user results in
solution:
Concept

Memory protection is a hardware-enforced boundary: every process runs in its own address space, and the Memory Management Unit (MMU) checks each address against the access rights granted to the currently running process. Any access that violates these rights is illegal and cannot be allowed to proceed.

How an illegal access is handled

When a process tries to read or write memory belonging to the OS kernel or to another user's process, the MMU detects the rights violation and raises a hardware exception. This exception is a trap: the CPU immediately switches from user mode to kernel mode and transfers control to the operating system, which then handles the fault (typically by terminating the offending process).

Why the other behaviours do not apply

  • Page fault: in the standard OS-course sense, the demand-paging event for a page that is valid for the process but not currently resident in physical RAM, which the OS resolves by loading the page. It describes a residency miss rather than a rights denial, so it is not the general outcome this question asks for.

  • Context switching: the act of saving one process's state and restoring another's during scheduling. It is driven by the scheduler, not by an illegal memory reference.

  • Scheduler dispatch: the dispatcher hands the CPU to a process the scheduler has already chosen. An illegal access produces a hardware exception first; any later scheduling is a consequence of the OS handling the trap, not the immediate result.

Result

The immediate, direct outcome of accessing memory allocated to the OS or to another user's process is a hardware exception that traps to the operating system.

optionFeedback.html: An access that violates the MMU's protection rights cannot proceed, so the hardware raises an exception and control transfers to the kernel in privileged mode to deal with it.
Context switching saves and restores process state during scheduling; it is triggered by the scheduler, not by a process touching memory it is not permitted to access.

In OS-course terms, a page fault is the demand-paging event for a page that is valid for the process but not currently in physical RAM, which the OS resolves by loading it. That describes a residency miss, a different failure mode from being denied access to memory you have no rights to.
The dispatcher only hands the CPU to a process the scheduler already selected. An illegal memory reference is caught by hardware first; scheduling is not its immediate effect.

Incorrect. PID 3 is just a regular dynamic Process ID assigned by the operating system scheduler to any standard user application or background service running during or after boot.

title: Which processing technique involves executing multiple tasks simultaneously

solution:
Correct answer: Parallel processing.

Parallel processing executes multiple tasks at the same time, usually using separate processing resources such as multiple processors or cores. title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q30

solution:
Concept

A program is a passive set of instructions stored on secondary storage. When the operating system loads it and begins execution, the active instance—with its own address space, program counter, registers, and resources—is a process.

One program can therefore create multiple processes, each with a distinct execution state.

  • Procedure: a reusable sequence of instructions that can be invoked within a program.

  • Instruction: one operation executed by a processor.

  • Function: a callable program unit, often with parameters and a return value.

Cross-check

If execution is paused, the operating system saves the active instance’s context in its process control block and later restores it. That runtime state belongs to a process, not to the passive program file.

Therefore, a program in execution is called a process.

A process has an operating-system process control block and moves among states such as ready, running, and waiting.
An instruction is a single machine-level operation decoded and executed by a processor.
A function is a callable program unit characterized by parameters and, where defined, a return value.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q60
subject: Operating System
text: In an operating system, a process is:
solution:
Concept

An operating system distinguishes a passive program from an active execution context. A process is the dynamic context created while program instructions run; it carries current CPU state, memory references, and allocated resources.

Application

A program in execution has exactly this active context: the operating system tracks its program counter, registers, scheduling state, and resources while the instructions are being carried out.

Contrast

  • A program written in a high-level language is source code that may later be translated or interpreted.

  • The contents of main memory are a collection of stored instructions and data, potentially belonging to several execution contexts.

  • A job in secondary memory is submitted work awaiting admission or loading and does not yet carry an active CPU context.

Cross-check

The same program can be launched more than once, producing separate contexts with different program counters and resource states. This confirms that the dynamic entity, rather than the passive code alone, is the process.

Therefore, a process is a program in execution.

title: Which of the following statements are TRUE about Process Control

text:
Which of the following statements are TRUE about Process Control Block (PCB) ?

Why the incorrect statement is false:

  • The PCB does not contain the process's actual program code or data segments; those reside in the process address space in memory or on disk. The PCB may hold pointers or references to those regions but not the code/data themselves.

Typical contents of a PCB:

  • Process identifier and current process state (running, waiting, ready, terminated).

  • CPU registers and program counter values needed to resume execution.

  • Scheduling information (priority, pointers in scheduler queues, accounting data).

  • Memory-management information (base/limit or page table/segment table pointers).

title: The Unix Operating System Kernel maintains two key data structures
subject: Operating System
text:
The Unix Operating System Kernel maintains two key data structures related to processes, the process table and the user structure. Now, consider the following two statements :

I. The process table is resident all the time and contain information needed for all processes, even those that are not currently in memory.

II. The user structure is swapped or paged out when its associated process is not in memory, in order not to waste memory on information that is not needed.

Which of the following options is correct with reference to above statements ?
solution:
Answer: Both statements are correct.

  • Statement I — The process table is resident all the time: The kernel keeps a process-table (process table) in memory to maintain bookkeeping information (process state, scheduling information, pointers to address space, etc.) for every process. This table must be available even for processes that are not currently loaded into physical memory so the kernel can manage them.

  • Statement II — The user structure can be swapped or paged out: The user structure (often called the u-area in traditional Unix) holds per-process kernel-mode state such as the kernel stack and process-specific kernel data. To avoid wasting physical memory on processes that are not resident, this per-process data may be swapped or paged out when the process is not in memory.

Summary: The process table remains resident for system-wide process management, while the user structure can be moved out of memory when its process is swapped to conserve kernel memory.

optionFeedback.html: This choice is incorrect. Statement I is correct — the process table remains resident in kernel memory and contains bookkeeping entries for all processes, including those that are swapped out. However, Statement II is also correct: the user structure (u-area) may be swapped or paged out when its process is not in memory to avoid wasting kernel memory.

This choice is incorrect. Statement II is correct — the user structure can be swapped or paged out when the process is not in memory. But Statement I is also correct: the process table is kept resident and contains information for all processes, even those currently swapped out.

Correct. Both statements are true. The process table is a resident kernel data structure that holds bookkeeping entries for every process so the kernel can manage scheduling and resources even for swapped-out processes. The user structure (u-area), which holds per-process kernel-mode state, can be swapped or paged out when the process is not in memory to conserve kernel memory.

This choice is incorrect. Both statements are actually correct: the process table is resident and contains entries for all processes, and the user structure can be swapped or paged out when its process is not in memory.

title: Which is the correct definition of valid process transition in

solution:
A process's lifecycle is governed by a fixed state diagram (New, Ready, Running, Blocked/Waiting, Terminated) in which every edge is caused by exactly one uniquely-named scheduling event — no two events share the same transition, so identifying the event correctly identifies the transition.

Mapping each event named in the options to the transition it actually causes:

Event

Actual transition

Dispatch

Wake up

Block

Only Dispatch is defined as Ready → Running; Wake up, Block, and Timer runout are each mislabeled in the other options against their true transitions above, so Dispatch: ready → running is the only option whose event and transition genuinely match.

Dispatch is the scheduler action that moves a process from Ready to Running.

Answer: The process is placed in the device queue for the requested I/O device.

  • When the I/O completes, the process is moved to the ready queue so it can be scheduled on the CPU.

  • This behavior is different from the job queue (used for newly admitted jobs) and the suspended queue (used for swapped-out processes).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q164
subject: Operating System
text: A process in the "ready" state is
solution:
In the operating system's five-state process model, every process moves through the New, Ready, Running, Waiting (blocked), and Terminated states as it executes. A process enters the Ready state once it has been loaded into main memory and holds every resource it needs to run except the CPU itself; it then sits in the ready queue until the CPU scheduler dispatches it.

Since a process occupies exactly one of these five states at any instant, the stem's phrase "a process in the ready state" can be matched against the offered descriptions by checking which state each one names:

  1. A process that is holding the CPU and having its instructions carried out is in the Running state, not the Ready state, because a Ready process is waiting for the CPU rather than using it.

  2. A process that has issued an I/O request or is waiting on some event is in the Waiting (blocked) state, not the Ready state, because it cannot proceed until that event completes, regardless of CPU availability.

  3. A process that has completed execution (or been aborted) and had its resources released is in the Terminated state, not the Ready state, because a Ready process is still eligible for future execution.

  4. A process that has every resource it needs except the processor, sitting in the ready queue awaiting dispatch, matches the Ready state exactly.

This matches the scheduler's state-transition rule: the short-term scheduler moves a process from Ready to Running through a dispatch event, and only a process already in the Ready state can be dispatched next — confirming that "ready to run on CPU" is the description that defines the Ready state, distinct from Running, Waiting, and Terminated.

optionFeedback.html: A process that is executing currently holds the CPU and is having its instructions carried out by the processor at this moment, rather than waiting for the processor to become free or for any external event to occur.

A process waiting for I/O has issued a request to a device (or is waiting on some other event) and cannot make further progress until that request or event completes, regardless of whether the CPU happens to be free at the time.

A process that is ready to run on CPU has already obtained every resource it needs for execution except the processor itself, and it remains in main memory until the CPU scheduler selects it for dispatch.

A process that has terminated has finished running (or was aborted), and the operating system is releasing its process control block and any other resources allocated to it; no further execution will occur for it.

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE about Long term
subject: Operating System
text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are false about the long-term scheduler?

P: It controls the degree of multiprogramming.

Q: It maintains a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes.
solution:
The CPU-scheduling hierarchy has three levels — long-term (job), medium-term, and short-term (CPU) schedulers — each acting at a different queue boundary. The long-term scheduler sits between the job pool (jobs waiting on disk) and the ready queue: it decides which new processes are admitted into main memory to compete for the CPU.

Because it gatekeeps admission, the long-term scheduler has two defining responsibilities: it fixes the degree of multiprogramming (the number of processes resident in memory at once), and it selects new jobs so that the resident set stays a balanced mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes — avoiding a memory full of only one type, which would leave either the CPU or the I/O devices under-used.

Checking statements P and Q against this role:

  • P — controlling the degree of multiprogramming is exactly the admission-control function described above, so P is true.

  • Q — deliberately balancing I/O-bound and CPU-bound admissions is exactly the mix-maintenance function described above, so Q is true.

Both defining responsibilities match, so neither P nor Q is false — a useful cross-check is to see why the near-miss combinations don't fit:

  • "Only P" would require Q to be false, but the balanced-mix objective is textbook long-term-scheduler behaviour, not an exception.

  • "Only Q" would require P to be false, but admission-rate control over multiprogramming is the scheduler's core job, not an exception. (This role is easy to confuse with the medium-term scheduler, which adjusts multiprogramming dynamically by swapping already-admitted processes out — but that doesn't make the long-term scheduler's own admission-based control untrue.)

  • "Both P and Q" would require both to be false, which contradicts both checks above.

Since both P and Q hold, the false-statement set is empty — the correct choice is the option stating neither P nor Q is false.

optionFeedback.html: This choice treats the multiprogramming-control claim as something the long-term scheduler lacks. Before ruling it out, trace which scheduling layer actually gatekeeps how many new jobs get admitted into memory — that's the specific point this option misjudges, and it's a common mix-up with the medium-term scheduler's later, swap-based adjustment of multiprogramming.

This choice treats the balanced-mix claim as something the long-term scheduler doesn't need to worry about — as if process composition were purely a workload characteristic rather than something the admission policy enforces on purpose. Revisit why an OS would care about admitting a mix of CPU-bound and I/O-bound jobs rather than a lopsided batch — that's the specific point this option misjudges.

Both defining responsibilities of the long-term scheduler are intact here: admission control over which jobs enter the ready queue fixes the degree of multiprogramming, and deliberately admitting a balanced mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound jobs keeps neither the CPU nor the I/O devices under-used. Since both properties hold, neither statement is false.

This choice rules out BOTH claims for the long-term scheduler at once — a strong claim, since it requires every commonly cited admission-time responsibility of this scheduler (its role in admission count and its role in admission composition) to be wrong simultaneously. Check each claim separately against the CONCEPT section before concluding both fail; overreaching to 'both false' at once is the specific mistake here.

title: Which of the following need not necessarily be saved on
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following need not necessarily be saved on a context switch between processes?
solution: During a context switch, the operating system must preserve enough information to resume the previous process later. General-purpose registers (Option A) and the program counter (Option C) are critical parts of a process's CPU state. If these were not saved, the process would lose its current computation and execution point, leading to incorrect behavior. Therefore, they must be saved.\nThe Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) (Option B), however, caches virtual-to-physical address translations specific to a process's page tables. Since different processes have distinct memory mappings, the TLB contents become invalid when switching contexts. Instead of saving and restoring TLB entries, the system simply flushes (clears) the TLB. This makes it unnecessary to save the TLB state, making Option B the correct answer.

optionFeedback.html: General purpose registers hold the active state of a process. They must be saved to ensure correct resumption.
The TLB caches address translations specific to a process and is typically flushed during context switches.
The Program Counter must be saved to preserve the instruction address so execution can resume correctly.
This option is incorrect because not all listed components can be skipped; critical state like the Program Counter must be saved.

title: There are three processes in the ready queue. When the
subject: Operating System
text: There are three processes in the ready queue. When the currently running process requests for I/O how many process switches take place?
solution:
A process switch (also called a context switch) is the single operating-system action that changes which process is occupying the CPU. The OS saves the execution context — program counter, registers, and other state — of the process being removed from the CPU, then loads the saved context of the process being placed onto the CPU. This save-and-restore action is counted as exactly one process switch per change of CPU ownership, no matter how many arrows on a process-state diagram are involved in bringing it about.

  1. The currently running process issues an I/O request, so the operating system removes it from the CPU and moves it into the waiting (blocked) state, saving its execution context.

  2. The short-term scheduler picks one process out of the ready queue, which has three processes waiting, to run next.

  3. The chosen process's saved context is loaded and it starts executing on the CPU.

  4. Steps 1 through 3 together are a single hand-off of CPU ownership, since exactly one process took over the CPU as a direct result of this one I/O request.

The size of the ready queue only confirms that a process is available to be dispatched immediately; it does not multiply the switch count, because only one of those waiting processes actually takes the CPU. A further switch would occur only if CPU ownership changed hands again afterward — for instance when the blocked process itself is eventually rescheduled — which is a separate event, not part of this single I/O-blocking transition.

So this single I/O request produces exactly one process switch.

optionFeedback.html: A value of 1 here would mean one process took over CPU control as a result of this I/O request.
A value of 2 here would mean two different processes each took over CPU control as a result of this I/O request.
A value of 3 here would mean as many processes took over CPU control as were recorded waiting in the ready queue before the I/O request.
A value of 4 here would mean one more process took over CPU control than were recorded waiting in the ready queue before the I/O request.

title: In multi-programmed systems, it is advantageous if some programs such
subject: Operating System
text:
In multi-programmed systems, it is advantageous if some programs such as editors and compilers can be shared by several users. Which of the following must be true of multi-programmed systems in order that a single copy of a program can be shared by several users?

I. The program is a macro

II. The program is recursive

III. The program is reentrant
solution: In multi-programmed systems, sharing a single copy of a program among multiple users requires the code to be reentrant. A reentrant program can be interrupted and entered again without affecting its execution by another user, as it does not modify itself and uses local storage for variables. Macros are compile-time expansions unrelated to runtime sharing, while recursion risks stack conflicts when shared without proper isolation. Therefore, reentrancy (III) is the necessary condition for safe program sharing.

Recursion typically uses stack memory that can conflict when multiple users share a single program copy.

title: Consider the following statements: Short term scheduler selects which process
subject: Operating System
text:
Consider the following statements:

S1: The short-term scheduler selects which process moves from the ready state to the running state.

S2: The medium-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming.

Which of the following is true?

options.html: S1 is true and S2 is false
S1 is false and S2 is true

solution:
Concept

Operating-system schedulers make different kinds of process-selection decisions. The short-term scheduler chooses a ready process for the CPU, while the medium-term scheduler swaps processes between main memory and secondary storage.

The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes resident in main memory. Swapping a process out lowers that number, and swapping it back in raises it; therefore medium-term scheduling can control this degree.

Application

  1. For S1, the short-term scheduler selects a process from the ready queue and dispatches it to the CPU, causing the ready-to-running transition. Hence S1 is true.

  2. For S2, the medium-term scheduler changes how many processes remain in memory by swapping processes out or back in. Hence S2 is true.

Cross-check and contrast

The long-term scheduler also controls the degree of multiprogramming through admission of new jobs. That does not make S2 false: S2 neither says “only” nor limits control to admission, and medium-term swapping independently changes the resident-process count.

  • “S1 is true and S2 is false” overlooks the direct effect of swapping on the number of resident processes.

  • “S1 is false and S2 is true” overlooks the short-term scheduler’s ready-queue dispatch role.

  • “None of the above” does not apply because the offered pair “Both S1 and S2 are true” matches the two scheduler mechanisms.

Therefore, both S1 and S2 are true.

optionFeedback.html: This combination places the ready-to-running dispatch with short-term scheduling and the resident-process count with medium-term swapping. Selecting from the ready queue and swapping processes are distinct mechanisms.
This combination treats swap-based removal as having no bearing on multiprogramming. Because the degree counts memory-resident processes, swapping a process out changes the counted population.
This combination moves ready-to-running dispatch away from short-term scheduling. The short-term scheduler is the CPU scheduler that selects a process from the ready queue.

This set-level value depends on whether any listed pairing follows from the scheduler mechanisms. Short-term ready-queue selection and medium-term swapping that changes the resident count are the two mechanism-level facts that determine the pairing.

title: On which of the following parameters, context switch is independent

On which of the following parameters, context switch is independent of?

(a) hardware support

(b) memory speed

(c) existence of special instructions

(d) process size

(e) number of registers to be copied
solution:
A context switch occurs when the CPU switches from one process to another, involving saving and loading process states. The time required for a context switch depends on the following:

Hardware support (a): Affects efficiency, as some systems have hardware features to speed up the switch.Memory speed (b): Impacts the time taken to save/load context data.Special instructions (c): May reduce the overhead if supported by the CPU.Process size (d): Independent of context switch, as only process state (registers, program counter, etc.) is saved, not the entire process memory.Number of registers to be copied (e): Directly impacts the time needed for context switching. Thus, context switching is independent of the process size (d).

Process Scheduler Type

(iii)

(R)

with respect to Process Schedulers of an operating system mentioned above in the table, which of the following statements is correct?
solution:
Concept

An operating system uses three kinds of process schedulers, each defined by what it decides and how often it runs:

  • Long-Term Scheduler (job scheduler): admits jobs from the job pool into the ready queue, thereby fixing how many processes are in memory at once — i.e. it controls the degree of multiprogramming. It runs infrequently.

  • Medium-Term Scheduler: temporarily removes (swaps out) processes from memory to disk and later brings them back (swaps in), so it is the scheduler associated with swapping.

  • Short-Term Scheduler (CPU scheduler): picks the next ready process for the CPU; because it must run very often (milliseconds), it has to be fast so that CPU time is not wasted.

Applying it to the table

  1. (i) Long-Term Scheduler → controls degree of multiprogramming = (Q).

  2. (ii) Medium-Term Scheduler → is associated with swapping = (R).

  3. (iii) Short-Term Scheduler → executes much faster to reduce wastage of CPU time = (P).

Cross-check

The defining property of each scheduler maps to exactly one activity with no overlap: admission/multiprogramming is unique to the long-term scheduler, swapping is unique to the medium-term scheduler, and high-frequency fast dispatch is unique to the short-term scheduler. Hence the consistent matching is (i)–(Q), (ii)–(R), (iii)–(P).

optionFeedback.html: Pairing the long-term scheduler with swapping is the slip here: swapping processes between memory and disk is a memory-management action, not the infrequent job-admission step that scheduler performs. The same pairing then forces the short-term scheduler onto multiprogramming control, which conflicts with its role of frequent CPU dispatch.

The scheduler that admits jobs is the one whose decision sets how many processes run concurrently, i.e. the degree of multiprogramming. Moving a process out to disk and later back in is precisely a swap operation. Selecting a ready process for the CPU happens every few milliseconds, so that step must be fast to keep CPU time from being wasted.

The mistake is treating the long-term scheduler as the fast-executing one; it is the rarely-invoked admission step, so speed of dispatch does not belong to it. That choice also pins multiprogramming control onto the short-term scheduler, which only selects among already-admitted processes for the CPU.

Here the long-term scheduler is again mis-tied to swapping, an in/out memory action rather than an admission decision. It additionally hands multiprogramming control to the medium-term scheduler, whose job is moving processes in and out of memory, not deciding how many are admitted in the first place.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q41
subject: Operating System
text: Which module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
solution:
CONCEPT

Process selection and execution transfer are separate operating-system functions. A short-term scheduler chooses a ready process according to policy, while a dispatch mechanism applies that choice through a context switch and execution-state restoration.

APPLICATION

Here, the process has already been selected by the short-term scheduler. The remaining work is to switch the processor context, enter the required mode, and resume the selected process from its saved instruction address. Those duties belong to the dispatcher. Therefore, the required module is the dispatcher.

  • Interrupt: a signal that redirects execution to an interrupt-service routine so an event can be handled.

  • Dispatcher: the component that performs the context switch, mode transition, and restoration of the execution point.

  • Scheduler: the decision-making component that chooses which ready process should run next.

  • None of the above: a residual-set claim, not the name of an operating-system component.

The two-stage check is therefore: the scheduler selects; the dispatcher carries out the handoff. This confirms Dispatcher as the result.

title: Process waiting time is given with the probability There are

Solution: Derivation of CPU utilization when each process waits with probability p.

  • Step 1: The CPU is idle only if every one of the n processes is waiting simultaneously.

title: Consider set of tasks with known runtimes to be run

text: Consider a set of n tasks with known runtimes r₁, r₂, …, rₙ, all ready at time 0 on a uniprocessor machine. If throughput is compared by the number of tasks completed by each intermediate time before the full batch finishes, which processor scheduling algorithm maximizes it?
solution:
Concept — Throughput is the number of tasks completed per unit time. When all tasks are ready and their runtimes are known, arranging them in non-decreasing runtime order minimizes every prefix completion time. Consequently, the maximum possible number of tasks has finished by each intermediate instant; the same ordering also minimizes average waiting and turnaround time.

Application — Sort the runtimes and execute each task to completion, from the smallest runtime to the largest.

  1. For a concrete check, take runtimes 8, 5, and 2 time units.

  2. Shortest-runtime order is 2, 5, 8, giving completion times 2, 7, and 15.

title: Which of the following option is use of Queue?
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following option is a use of Queue?
solution:
In operating systems, when multiple processes or tasks are waiting to be executed by the CPU, they are placed in a scheduling queue (like a Ready Queue). For instance, in First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) CPU scheduling, processes are dispatched to the CPU in the exact order of their arrival. This orderly, first-come handling inherently requires a Queue data structure.

  • Correct Answer: C (CPU scheduling)

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Recursive function execution relies on the Stack data structure (specifically the System Call Stack). Each recursive call pushes an activation record onto the stack, following the LIFO principle.

Incorrect. Similar to recursive functions, regular function calls and returns are managed by the operating system using a Stack. When a function finishes execution, the control returns to the last called function (LIFO).
Correct. CPU scheduling algorithms use a Queue (Ready Queue) to store incoming processes in a FIFO manner, ensuring that tasks are handled fairly according to their arrival sequence.
Incorrect. The evaluation or conversion of mathematical expressions (such as Infix, Postfix, or Prefix notations) is a classic application of a Stack, not a queue.

title: The time dispatcher takes and for the dispatcher to stop
subject: Operating System
text: The time dispatcher takes and for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running is known as _____.
solution:
In an operating system, the dispatcher is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.

When switching from one process to another, the dispatcher needs to:

  1. Save the state (context) of the currently running process.

  2. Load the saved state (context) of the newly selected process.

  3. Jump to the proper location in the user program to restart that process.

The total time spent by the dispatcher in stopping one process and starting another running is explicitly defined as Dispatch Latency. Since this overhead occurs during every context switch, operating systems aim to keep this duration as low as possible.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect: While dispatch latency is effectively an overhead (time where no useful user work is being done), "dispatch wasting time" is not a standard technical term used in operating systems.
Correct: This is the standard textbook definition for the time required by the dispatcher to halt one process and kickstart another.

Incorrect: Turnaround time is the total interval from the time of submission of a process to the time of its completion. It is a process scheduling metric, not a property of the dispatcher module itself.

Incorrect: Response time is the time taken from the submission of a request until the first response is produced. It measures user interactivity and is unrelated to internal dispatcher state-switching overhead.

title: Which of the following scheduling algorithms selects the process that
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following scheduling algorithms selects the process that has been waiting the longest?
solution:
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) is a non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm whose only selection rule is queue position: at every scheduling decision, the CPU is handed to whichever ready process has been sitting in the ready queue the longest -- that is, the process that entered the queue earliest among those still waiting -- regardless of its burst time, priority, or any other attribute.

Apply this to a concrete arrival sequence: P1 arrives at time 0 with burst time 99, P2 arrives at time 1 with burst time 1, and P3 arrives at time 2 with burst time 1.

  1. At time 0, P1 is the only process in the ready queue, so the scheduler dispatches P1.

  2. P2 and P3 arrive at t = 1 and t = 2, but must wait, because FCFS is non-preemptive and never interrupts a running process.

  3. When P1 finishes at t = 99, the scheduler looks at who has been waiting in the queue the longest -- P2, waiting since t = 1 -- and dispatches P2 next, then P3.

  4. The execution order is P1 -> P2 -> P3, decided purely by queue-entry (arrival) order -- even though P1 has the longest burst time, it is P1's arrival order, not its burst time, that gets it scheduled first.

Contrast this with the other listed algorithms, each of which uses a different selection rule:

  • Shortest Job First dispatches by the process's own predicted burst time -- the process needing the least CPU time next runs first -- so how long a process has already waited plays no role.

  • Round Robin cycles every ready process through a fixed time quantum in rotation; the next process to run is whichever is next in the rotation, not whichever has accumulated the most waiting time.

  • Priority Scheduling dispatches by an assigned priority level, so a process can be chosen purely because of its priority value even if other processes have waited far longer.

Only First-Come, First-Served defines its dispatch rule purely in terms of time already spent waiting in the ready queue, which is exactly the criterion the question describes.

optionFeedback.html: Shortest Job First dispatches by the process's own predicted burst (execution) time -- the process needing the least CPU time next runs first -- so how long a process has already sat in the ready queue plays no role in this rule at all.

Round Robin cycles every ready process through a fixed time quantum in a rotating order; the next process to run is whichever is next in the rotation, not whichever has accumulated the most total waiting time.

This rule dispatches strictly by queue-entry order: whichever ready process has been sitting in the queue the longest -- that is, arrived earliest among those still waiting -- is the one selected next, with no other factor considered.
Priority Scheduling dispatches by an assigned priority level, so a process can be selected purely because of its priority value even if other processes have been waiting far longer.

title: On system using non-preemptive scheduling, processes with expected run times
subject: Operating System
text: On a system using non-preemptive scheduling, processes with expected run times of 5, 18, 9 and 12 are in the ready queue. In what order should they be run to minimize wait time?
solution:
Concept. Under non-preemptive scheduling a process, once dispatched, keeps the CPU until it finishes, so the whole schedule is fixed the moment the serving order is chosen. Each process therefore waits exactly as long as the total burst time of everything placed ahead of it, which means a job sitting in position i adds its own burst time to the waiting time of every job behind it. Writing the total waiting time as the sum of (n − i) × bi shows that the biggest multiplier falls on the job served earliest, so the smallest burst time must go first and the queue must be served in non-decreasing order of burst time — the Shortest Job First (SJF) rule. An exchange argument settles it: whenever two adjacent jobs are out of order, swapping them strictly lowers the total waiting time, so no permutation can beat the fully sorted one.

Note on the wording. The stem names no scheduling algorithm on purpose. It asks which serving order makes the waiting time smallest, and the argument above derives that order from first principles; the name Shortest Job First is the conclusion of the reasoning, not an assumption handed to you.

Application — schedule the four given run times.

  1. Sort the four expected run times into non-decreasing order: 5, 9, 12, 18.

  2. The 5-unit process starts at t = 0, so its waiting time is 0.

  3. The 9-unit process starts at t = 0 + 5 = 5, so its waiting time is 5.

  4. The 12-unit process starts at t = 5 + 9 = 14, so its waiting time is 14.

  5. The 18-unit process starts at t = 14 + 12 = 26, so its waiting time is 26.

  6. Total waiting time = 0 + 5 + 14 + 26 = 45 time units, so the average waiting time = 45 ÷ 4 = 11.25 time units.

solution:
To solve this Preemptive Shortest Job First (SRTF) problem, we track the execution step-by-step using a Gantt chart based on the processes' remaining burst times:

  • At t = 0: Only P0 arrives (Remaining Burst Time, RBT = 9). It executes.

  • At t = 1: P1 arrives (RBT = 4). Since P1's burst time (4) is shorter than P0's remaining time (8), P0 is preempted. P1 runs until completion at t = 5 (since no other shorter job arrives at t=2, where P2 arrives with RBT = 9).

  • At t = 5: Ready processes are P0 (RBT = 8) and P2 (RBT = 9). P0 executes next from t = 5 to t = 13.

  • At t = 13: Finally, P2 executes from t = 13 to t = 22.

Waiting Time (WT = Turnaround Time - Burst Time):

  • P1: (5 - 1) - 4 = 0 seconds

  • P2: (22 - 2) - 9 = 11 seconds

Average Waiting Time ={4 + 0 + 11}/3 = 15/3 = 5 seconds

solution:
Concept

In Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling, whenever the CPU is free it picks the ready process with the smallest CPU burst and runs it to completion without interruption. A process's waiting time is the total time it spends in the ready queue before it starts executing; for processes that all arrive at time 0, that equals the sum of the burst times of every process scheduled ahead of it. Average waiting time (AWT) is the mean of the individual waiting times.

Application

All four processes arrive at time 0, so SJF simply orders them by increasing burst time and runs them one after another:

Order of execution

Building up the waiting time step by step:

  1. The 3 ms process runs first: it starts immediately, so its waiting time is 0.

  2. The 6 ms process runs next: it waited while the 3 ms process ran, so its waiting time is 3.

  3. The 7 ms process runs next: it waited for 3 + 6, so its waiting time is 9.

  4. The 8 ms process runs last: it waited for 3 + 6 + 7, so its waiting time is 16.

AWT = (0 + 3 + 9 + 16) / 4 = 28 / 4 = 7.0 ms.

Cross-check

Independent check using turnaround time: the completion times are 3, 9, 16, 24, so the turnaround times are 3, 9, 16, 24. Subtracting each burst (3, 6, 7, 8) gives waiting times 0, 3, 9, 16, whose mean is again 7.0 ms. SJF is also optimal here: it gives the smallest possible average waiting time for this set, which any other order (for example first-come-first-served) would only increase.

subject: Operating System
text: Let there be four processes P1, P2, P3, P4 whose CPU burst times are 6, 8, 7, 3 ms, respectively, and they arrive at time 0. Which of the following is the average waiting time and order of the process scheduling under the shortest-job-first scheduling?

options.html: Average Waiting time = 7.75 ms; Process order: P1, P4, P3, P2

solution:
In shortest-job-first (SJF) scheduling with non-preemptive execution, whenever every process is already available (arrives at time 0), the scheduler always picks the process with the smallest burst time next; because the order is decided just once at the start, the waiting time of each process equals the sum of the burst times of every process that runs before it, and the average waiting time is the mean of these four waiting times.

  1. The given burst times are P1 = 6 ms, P2 = 8 ms, P3 = 7 ms, P4 = 3 ms; sorting them in ascending order of burst time gives the execution sequence P4 (3 ms) -> P1 (6 ms) -> P3 (7 ms) -> P2 (8 ms).

  2. P4 runs first, so it waits 0 ms.

  3. P1 runs second, so it waits for P4's entire burst time: 3 ms.

  4. P3 runs third, so it waits for P4 and P1's combined burst time: 3 + 6 = 9 ms.

  5. P2 runs last, so it waits for P4, P1 and P3's combined burst time: 3 + 6 + 7 = 16 ms.

  6. The average waiting time is (0 + 3 + 9 + 16) / 4 = 28 / 4 = 7 ms, with the execution order P4, P1, P3, P2.

As an independent check, the sum of the four waiting times (28 ms) must equal the sum of each process's burst time multiplied by the number of processes still waiting behind it in the queue: (3 x 3) + (6 x 2) + (7 x 1) + (8 x 0) = 9 + 12 + 7 + 0 = 28 ms, which matches, confirming the average of 7 ms.

title: Which of the following best distinguishes Shortest Job First (SJF)
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following best distinguishes Shortest Job First (SJF) from Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling?

options.html: SJF is non-preemptive, while SRTF supports preemption when a shorter process arrives.
SJF allows preemption, while SRTF does not.
SJF is used in real-time systems, whereas SRTF is used in batch systems.
Both SJF and SRTF operate identically in all CPU scheduling environments.

solution:
Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) are both CPU scheduling algorithms designed to minimize average waiting time by prioritizing processes with the shortest burst times. The fundamental distinction lies in how they handle process execution once started.

SJF is inherently non-preemptive, meaning that once a process begins executing on the CPU, it runs to completion without interruption. Even if a new process arrives with a shorter burst time, the currently running process continues until it finishes.

In contrast, SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF. It continuously monitors the ready queue and allows a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining burst time to preempt (interrupt) the currently running process. This ensures that the CPU is always working on the task expected to finish soonest.

optionFeedback.html: Correct! Shortest Job First (SJF) is the standard non-preemptive version of the algorithm, meaning once a process gets the CPU, it holds it until it completes. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) is the preemptive variant of SJF; if a new process arrives with a shorter remaining burst time than the currently running process, the running process is preempted (halted) and the CPU is given to the new process.
Incorrect. This statement swaps the definitions. SJF does not allow preemption once execution starts, whereas SRTF is explicitly designed to handle preemption based on remaining burst times.

Incorrect. Neither SJF nor SRTF is ideal for real-time systems because both require knowing the future CPU burst time of a process in advance, which is practically impossible. Real-time systems use algorithms like Earliest Deadline First (EDF) or Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS). Both SJF and SRTF are theoretically discussed for batch systems or long-term scheduling approximations.

Incorrect. They do not operate identically. They will only produce identical results (Gantt charts) if all processes arrive at the exact same time (Arrival Time = 0). If processes arrive at different times, their execution orders and waiting times differ significantly due to preemption.

solution:
Answer: 2 context switches.

Explanation:

  • Processes: P1 requires 10 time units (arrives at 0), P2 requires 20 (arrives at 2), P3 requires 30 (arrives at 6).

  • Count context switches (excluding the initial start at time 0 and the final completion): switch at t=10 from P1 to P2 (1), switch at t=30 from P2 to P3 (1). Total = 2.

Therefore, the operating system performs 2 context switches under SRTF for these processes.

Under shortest remaining time first (SRTF), no preemptions occur when the shorter-running process still has the smallest remaining time at each arrival. Here P1 runs from 0 to 10 without being preempted, then P2 and P3 run in order. Only two switches occur (at t=10 and t=30), not four.

Correct. Under SRTF there are 2 context switches. P1 runs from time 0 to 10 (it is not preempted at t=2 or t=6 because its remaining time is shorter than arrivals). At t=10 P1 finishes and the CPU switches to P2 (one switch). At t=30 P2 finishes and the CPU switches to P3 (second switch). Do not count the start at time 0 or the final completion.

The choice "3" is incorrect. There are only two actual process-to-process switches here: from P1 to P2 at t=10 and from P2 to P3 at t=30. No preemption happens when P2 and P3 arrive because P1's remaining time is always less, so you should not count an extra switch.
The choice "1" is incorrect. There are two switches between processes: at t=10 (P1 -> P2) and at t=30 (P2 -> P3). Not counting the start or final completion gives a total of two, not one.
