title: Which scheduling algorithm can cause starvation
subject: Operating System
text: Which CPU scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of low-priority processes?
solution:
Concept — starvation (indefinite blocking). A ready process is starved when the scheduling rule lets it be overtaken without any limit, so it may never reach the CPU. Whether a rule permits this turns on one test: is the set of processes that may be dispatched ahead of a waiting process closed at the moment that process joins the ready queue, or can later arrivals keep entering that set forever? A closed set means the wait is bounded; an open-ended set means starvation is possible.

Application. Priority Scheduling always dispatches the ready process holding the best priority value. A process carrying a low assigned priority is passed over by every higher-priority process that becomes ready, and fresh higher-priority processes may keep arriving, so the set ahead of it never closes and its waiting time has no upper bound. That is precisely starvation of low-priority processes, so the answer is Priority Scheduling.

Cross-check — apply the same test to all four dispatch rules.

Algorithm

Dispatch rule

Can later arrivals keep overtaking a waiting process?

First Come First Serve

Earliest arrival time

No — the queue ahead of a process is fixed the moment it arrives, so its wait is bounded.

Round Robin

Cyclic order, fixed quantum q

No — with n ready processes a process waits at most (n − 1)q before its next turn.

Priority Scheduling

Best assigned priority value

Yes — every later higher-priority arrival jumps ahead, with no upper bound on the wait.

Shortest Job First

Smallest predicted next CPU burst

Yes — every later shorter job jumps ahead, so a long job can be postponed.

Why not Shortest Job First? SJF does starve processes, but its victims are long CPU bursts, not low-priority ones — SJF attaches no priority attribute to a process at all. Standard texts do note that SJF can be modelled as priority scheduling with priority equal to the inverse of the predicted burst, which is why the two feel close; this stem, however, is anchored to an explicitly assigned low priority, and Priority Scheduling is itself offered, so the directly named mechanism is the intended answer.

Standard remedy. Aging — steadily improving the priority of a process the longer it has waited — puts an upper bound on the wait and removes starvation from a priority scheduler.

optionFeedback.html: First Come First Serve dispatches by arrival timestamp, holding the ready processes in a plain FIFO queue, and is used in its non-preemptive form. The only information the scheduler needs about a process is the moment it entered the ready queue.

Round Robin dispatches in cyclic order with a fixed time quantum q, preempting a process on a timer interrupt when its quantum expires and returning it to the tail of the ready queue. The only information the scheduler needs about a process is its position in that cycle, together with the chosen value of q.

Priority Scheduling dispatches by an explicit priority value carried by each process, always taking the ready process that holds the best value, and exists in both preemptive and non-preemptive forms. The information the scheduler needs about a process is that priority number, set internally from measured quantities such as time limits or memory needs, or externally from administrative importance.

Shortest Job First dispatches by the length of the next CPU burst, taking the ready process whose predicted burst is smallest, and exists in both non-preemptive and preemptive (shortest-remaining-time-first) forms. The information the scheduler needs about a process is that burst length, which is not known in advance and is typically estimated by exponential averaging of its previous bursts.

title: Scheduling algorithm assigns priority proportional to the waiting time of
subject: Operating System
text: A scheduling algorithm assigns priority proportional to the waiting time of a process. Every process starts with priority zero (the lowest priority). The scheduler re-evaluates the process priorities every T time units and decides the next process to schedule. Which one of the following is TRUE if the processes have no I/O operations and all arrive at time 0?

options.html: This algorithm is equivalent to the first-come-first-serve algorithm.
This algorithm is equivalent to the round-robin algorithm.
This algorithm is equivalent to the shortest-job-first algorithm.
This algorithm is equivalent to the shortest-remaining-time-first algorithm.

solution:
Concept

Two structural properties of a scheduler fully decide which classical policy it mimics: (1) whether it is preemptive (can interrupt a running process at fixed intervals) or non-preemptive, and (2) what quantity it ranks processes by - elapsed waiting time, total burst length, or remaining burst length. A policy that periodically interrupts the CPU and always favours the process that has waited longest is, by definition, time-sliced fair rotation.

Application

  1. The scheduler re-evaluates priorities every T time units and may switch the running process at each boundary, so it is PREEMPTIVE with a fixed time quantum equal to T.

  2. Priority is proportional to WAITING time, not to burst length or remaining burst, so the ranking key is time spent waiting - never the size of the job.

  3. All processes arrive at t = 0 and start with equal (zero) waiting time. During its slice a running process accumulates zero additional waiting time, while every other ready process accumulates exactly T more - so the just-run process ends the slice with the SMALLEST accumulated waiting time of all.

  4. Because priority is proportional to (accumulated) waiting time, having the smallest waiting time means the just-run process now has the LOWEST priority, so it is placed behind everyone else; the process that has waited longest is dispatched next.

  5. After every process has had one slice they have all accumulated the same waiting time and are tied again, so the next cycle repeats the same rotation. Ties are broken consistently - whichever ready process has waited longest without a turn goes next - so no process is skipped or repeated out of turn. This produces exactly round-robin's rotation with quantum T: each still-ready process gets one turn of up to T time units (a full quantum, or less if its remaining burst finishes first), after which control passes to the next-longest-waiting ready process - regardless of individual burst lengths.

Cross-check / contrast

  • First-come-first-serve is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to completion. The described scheduler preempts every T units, so it is not FCFS.

  • Shortest-job-first ranks by total burst length and is non-preemptive; this scheduler never looks at burst length and does preempt, so it is not SJF.

  • Shortest-remaining-time-first ranks by remaining burst length; this scheduler ranks by waiting time and ignores burst entirely, so it is not SRTF.

  • Only round-robin matches both signatures: preemptive, fixed quantum T, and rotation driven by who has waited longest.

optionFeedback.html: First-come-first-serve is non-preemptive - a process, once dispatched, keeps the CPU until it finishes. The scheduler here re-evaluates and can switch processes every T units, so equating it to a run-to-completion policy ignores that periodic preemption.

Re-evaluating every T units makes the quantum exactly T. During a slice the running process gains no waiting time while every other ready process gains T, so the just-run process ends with the smallest accumulated waiting time and therefore the lowest priority - it is rotated to the back while the longest-waiting process runs next. This fixed-quantum rotation through all ready processes is precisely round-robin with quantum T.

Shortest-job-first orders processes by total burst length and is non-preemptive. This scheduler never inspects burst length - it ranks purely by accumulated waiting time - and it preempts at every T boundary, so the job-length basis does not apply.

Shortest-remaining-time-first preempts based on the remaining burst length of jobs. The metric here is waiting time, not remaining work, so the deciding quantity is unrelated to how much execution a process still needs.

text: Consider the following preemptive priority scheduling algorithms based on dynamically changing priorities. Large priority numbers imply higher priority. When the process is waiting for the CPU in ready queue, its priority changes at a rate 'α'; when it's running, its priority changes at a rate 'β'. All processes are given same priority, when they enter the ready queue. Which one of the CPU scheduling algorithm results from α > β > 0 ?
solution:
All processes start with the same priority. While waiting in the ready queue, their priority increases at rate α, and while executing, it increases at a slower rate β, with α > β > 0.

A running process therefore gains priority slowly, whereas waiting processes gain priority faster. Very soon, a waiting process attains a higher priority than the currently running one, causing preemption.

As a result, the CPU keeps switching between processes, and each process gets to run only for a short duration before being preempted. This creates a time-sharing type of system.

Hence, this behavior closely resembles Round Robin scheduling, where each process gets CPU for a small time and is then preempted.

optionFeedback.html: Because waiting processes increase their priority faster than the running one (α > β), a process in the ready queue quickly gains higher priority and preempts the currently running process. This leads to each process getting the CPU for short intervals in turn, creating a time-sharing behavior that closely resembles Round Robin scheduling.

Shortest Job First selects the process with the smallest CPU burst (or remaining time), not the one that has waited the longest. The given rates make waiting duration determine priority, so scheduling favors older arrivals rather than shortest jobs.

Last-In-First-Out always favors the most recently arrived process. With waiting priority growing faster than running priority, the longest-waiting processes gain the highest priority, which is the opposite of LIFO behavior.

Because priorities are dynamically increasing and waiting processes gain priority faster than the running one (α > β), the CPU does not follow a strict arrival order. Instead, processes can preempt each other frequently, which violates the non-preemptive nature of FCFS. Hence, this scheduling behavior does not match First Come First Serve.

Concept

Assumption on arrival time: when a problem gives no arrival times, the standard convention is that all processes arrive together at time 0 and enter the ready queue in the listed order (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5). title: Consider the following set of processes, with arrival times and
subject: Operating System
text:
Consider the following set of processes, with arrival times and the required CPU-burst times given in milliseconds. 

Process  Arrival Time  Burst Time
   P1        0             4
   P2        2             2
   P3        3             1

What is the sequence in which the processes are completed? Assume round robin scheduling with a time quantum of 2 milliseconds
solution:
Concept

Round Robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time quantum, then preempts it and sends it to the BACK of a FIFO ready queue. The completion order therefore depends entirely on the ready-queue ordering. The one rule that decides this problem: when a running process's quantum EXPIRES at the SAME instant a new process ARRIVES, the standard convention places the NEWLY ARRIVED process into the ready queue FIRST, and the just-preempted process is enqueued AFTER it. This single tie-break determines who runs next.

Application (q = 2 ms)

Given: P1(arrival 0, burst 4), P2(arrival 2, burst 2), P3(arrival 3, burst 1). Simulate step by step:

  1. t = 0–2: Only P1 is present, so P1 runs one quantum. Remaining burst of P1 = 4 − 2 = 2.

  2. t = 2 (tie): P1's quantum expires exactly as P2 arrives. By the convention, the arriving P2 is enqueued first, then preempted P1 behind it. Ready queue → [P2, P1].

  3. t = 2–4: P2 runs (burst 2) and finishes at t = 4. Meanwhile P3 arrives at t = 3 and joins the queue behind P1. Ready queue → [P1, P3].

  4. t = 4–6: P1 runs its remaining 2 ms and finishes at t = 6.

  5. t = 6–7: P3 runs its 1 ms and finishes at t = 7.

Cross-check

Read the finish times in order: P2 at t = 4, then P1 at t = 6, then P3 at t = 7. Completion sequence = P2, P1, P3. The total CPU time also checks out: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 ms with no idle gap, so the schedule ends exactly at t = 7.

Why the common wrong answer appears

If instead you enqueue the preempted P1 BEFORE the arriving P2 at the t = 2 tie, P1 finishes first and you get P1, P2, P3. That ordering uses the opposite tie-break and is not the convention used by this exam; the accepted answer is P2, P1, P3.

optionFeedback.html: This ordering assumes that when a quantum expires at the exact instant a new process arrives (here at t = 2), the just-preempted process is put back on the CPU before the newly arrived one. That tie-break assumption is what produces this sequence, but it is not the convention this exam uses, so the resulting order is incorrect.

This follows from applying the exam's tie-break at t = 2 and then running the queue in FIFO order to completion. Tracing each finish time as shown in the solution yields exactly this sequence, which is why it is the accepted answer.

This ordering would require a process that arrives last and carries the smallest burst to finish first. That behaviour belongs to a shortest-job-first style policy, not Round Robin, which serves the ready queue strictly in arrival/enqueue order regardless of burst length. Hence this sequence cannot arise here.

This ordering assumes a process that joins the ready queue later can be served before a process that was enqueued earlier. Round Robin uses a FIFO ready queue, so a later entrant never overtakes an earlier one; the relative order assumed here violates that rule, so the sequence is incorrect.

title: Which of the following condition is/are false:
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following conditions are false?

options.html: Round Robin has the minimum average response time.
If all jobs have identical run lengths, Round Robin provides a better average turnaround time.

solution:
A: Round Robin has the minimum average response time — True.

B: All jobs having identical run lengths is the worst case for Round Robin in terms of turnaround time, because all jobs finish at nearly the same time.

C & D: FCFS does not suffer from starvation, but SJF does.

optionFeedback.html: This statement is considered true in the usual OS context: round robin gives good (typically low) average response time because every ready process gets the CPU within one time-slice cycle. However, saying it has the absolute minimum average response time is imprecise — other preemptive policies can yield lower response time for some workloads. The key idea: round robin improves response time compared with FCFS by giving each process early CPU service.

This statement is false. If all jobs have identical run length, round robin does not necessarily provide better average turnaround time. When bursts are identical, non-preemptive scheduling like FCFS (or SJF when jobs are equal) can achieve similar or better turnaround; with a small time quantum, round robin can increase overall turnaround because of repeated context switches. So the claim that round robin provides better average turnaround time in that specific scenario is incorrect.

This statement is false. First-Come First-Served (FCFS) does not suffer from starvation: every process eventually gets the CPU in arrival order. Starvation refers to a process never getting service; FCFS is fair in that sense, though it can suffer from convoy effect and long average waiting times.

This statement is true. Shortest Job First (SJF) can cause starvation: if short jobs keep arriving, longer jobs may be continually postponed and experience indefinite delay. That risk is why pure SJF is often modified or implemented with aging in practice.

title: Which of the following scheduling algorithms could result in starvation?
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following scheduling algorithms could result in starvation?
solution:
Answer: Priority scheduling can cause starvation.

Starvation (indefinite blocking) occurs when a process waits forever because other processes are continually favored.

  • Why this happens: In priority scheduling, lower-priority processes can be repeatedly bypassed if higher-priority processes keep arriving, preventing them from ever running.

  • Example: A low-priority background job may never execute if the system continuously receives higher-priority interactive jobs.

  • Prevention: Apply aging, which gradually increases the priority of waiting processes so they eventually obtain CPU time.

Contrast with other algorithms: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) serves in arrival order so starvation does not occur, and Round Robin gives each process regular time slices, making starvation unlikely.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Priority scheduling can cause starvation: low-priority processes may be repeatedly postponed if higher-priority processes keep arriving, so they may wait indefinitely. A common mitigation is aging, which gradually increases the priority of waiting processes so they eventually run.

Incorrect. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) serves processes in arrival order, so every process will eventually get the CPU and starvation does not occur. FCFS can, however, produce long waiting times for processes behind a long job (convoy effect).

Incorrect. Round Robin schedules processes in a cyclic order using time slices, ensuring each process receives CPU time regularly. Because each process gets turns, starvation is unlikely under standard Round Robin.

Incorrect. The statement 'none of the above' is wrong because priority scheduling can lead to starvation. Therefore at least one of the listed algorithms (priority scheduling) can result in starvation.

title: Which scheduling algorithm gives minimum average waiting time?
subject: Operating System
text: Which scheduling algorithm gives a minimum average waiting time?
solution:
Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling algorithm is provably optimal because it minimizes the average waiting time for a given set of processes. By scheduling the process with the shortest CPU burst time first, the waiting times of subsequent longer processes are reduced, moving the overall mathematical average to its minimum possible value.

Thus, the correct option is C.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Round Robin (RR) gives good average turnaround times for interactive systems but results in higher average waiting times due to frequent context switching and time-quantum overhead.
Incorrect. Priority scheduling executes processes based on external criteria; it does not structurally guarantee a minimum average waiting time and can cause starvation.
Correct. SJF (specifically its preemptive version, SRTF) is mathematically proven to generate the lowest possible average waiting time among all scheduling policies.
Incorrect. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) suffers heavily from the Convoy Effect, where short processes wait a long time behind a long process, maximizing average waiting time.

title: In round-robin scheduling algorithm with time quantum of milliseconds, process
subject: Operating System
text: Three processes P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 with CPU burst times of 12 ms, 8 ms, and 3 ms respectively. Using the Round Robin scheduling algorithm with a time quantum of 5 ms, what is the total waiting time experienced by process P3 (the process with the 3 ms burst)?
solution:
Concept: Round Robin scheduling gives every process one time-quantum turn in cyclic queue order. A process's waiting time before its own first turn equals the sum of the quantum slices used by the processes ahead of it in the initial queue, and once its completion time is known, waiting time = turnaround time − burst time (turnaround = completion − arrival).

Application: Time quantum = 5 ms. Initial queue order: P1 (12 ms), P2 (8 ms), P3 (3 ms), all arriving at t = 0.

  1. t = 0 to 5 ms: P1 takes its first quantum, using 5 of its 12 ms; 7 ms remain and P1 rejoins the back of the queue.

  2. t = 5 to 10 ms: P2 takes its first quantum, using 5 of its 8 ms; 3 ms remain and P2 rejoins the back of the queue.

  3. t = 10 to 13 ms: P3 gets its turn. Its entire 3 ms burst fits inside one quantum, so it finishes completely at t = 13 ms.

  4. P3 needs no further turn: completion = 13 ms, arrival = 0, so turnaround = 13 ms, and waiting time = turnaround − burst = 13 − 3 = 10 ms.

Cross-check: By queue position alone, P3 is third in the initial queue, so before its own first turn it must wait out one full quantum from each of the two processes ahead of it — 5 ms + 5 ms = 10 ms — matching the turnaround-based calculation above.

By queue position: two full 5 ms quanta run ahead of this process's turn — one for each of the two longer processes queued before it — so it waits 5 + 5 = 10 ms in total, then completes entirely within its own very first turn on the CPU.

title: What is the goal of round-robin CPU scheduling algorithm
subject: Operating System
text: What is the goal of a round-robin CPU scheduling algorithm ?

options.html: Minimize the average waiting time for all processes

solution:
Concept

CPU scheduling algorithms are each designed around a primary objective. Round-robin (RR) is a preemptive, time-sharing algorithm: every ready process is given a fixed time quantum in cyclic order, and a process that does not finish within its quantum is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. Its governing design goal is fair CPU sharing among all processes and good response time for interactive jobs.

Application

Because every process is served in turn for an equal slice, no process waits indefinitely and short interactive tasks get the CPU quickly, which keeps response time low. RR deliberately treats all processes uniformly rather than optimizing any single throughput or completion metric.

Contrast

  • Minimizing the average waiting time is the defining strength of Shortest Job First (SJF/SRTF), which is provably optimal for that metric; round-robin generally produces a higher average waiting time than SJF because of frequent preemption and context switches.

  • Prioritizing long-running processes or favouring I/O-bound versus CPU-bound jobs are properties of priority or specialized schedulers; round-robin gives every process the same quantum regardless of length or I/O behaviour.

  • Maximizing CPU utilization and throughput is a general scheduling concern, but RR can lower throughput because each context switch adds overhead; raw utilization/throughput is not RR's distinguishing goal.

Note

None of the four options above states round-robin's actual objective — fair time-sharing with a good response time. The option that sounds closest, minimizing the average waiting time, is in fact Shortest Job First's defining goal, not round-robin's.

optionFeedback.html: This describes priority-based or longest-job-favouring scheduling, where a process's length or priority determines how soon it gets served. Round-robin does not single out or favour any process on the basis of its length -- length simply is not a factor in how the CPU gets allocated under round-robin -- so this cannot be its stated aim.

Minimizing the average waiting time is the hallmark of Shortest Job First, which is optimal for that metric. Round-robin's frequent preemption typically yields a higher average waiting time than SJF, so this objective does not capture round-robin's purpose.

Maximizing CPU utilization and throughput is a general scheduling concern rather than round-robin's distinguishing aim. The repeated context switches caused by time slicing add overhead and can reduce throughput, so this is not what round-robin is designed to achieve.

None of these is the correct choice: round-robin's actual objective -- sharing the CPU fairly among all ready processes while keeping response time low for interactive jobs -- is not expressed by any of the other three statements. Minimizing the average waiting time names Shortest Job First's defining strength, not round-robin's; prioritizing long-running processes describes priority scheduling; and maximizing CPU utilization and throughput is a general concern that round-robin's frequent context switching can actually work against.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q29
subject: Operating System
text: Which scheduling policy is best suited to a time-sharing operating system?
solution:
Concept

A time-sharing operating system divides CPU time into short quanta so that multiple interactive processes receive recurring access. A suitable scheduler must therefore be preemptive and rotate runnable processes fairly enough to keep response time short.

Application

Suppose processes P1, P2, and P3 are ready and the time quantum is 20 ms.

  1. The scheduler runs P1 for at most 20 ms.

  2. If P1 is unfinished, it is placed at the end of the ready queue, and P2 receives the next quantum.

  3. The same rule then gives P3 a turn and continues cyclically, so no ready process waits for one long job to finish before receiving CPU time.

Contrast

  • Shortest Job First orders work by predicted CPU-burst length and may postpone long jobs.

  • First-Come, First-Served preserves arrival order and does not impose a recurring time quantum.

  • The Elevator policy is designed for disk-head request ordering rather than CPU allocation among interactive processes.

Cross-check

The defining mechanism required here is repeated CPU access through time quanta. Round Robin implements exactly that cyclic quantum-based mechanism, so the best-suited policy among the offered values is Round Robin.

optionFeedback.html: Shortest Job First selects the ready process with the smallest predicted CPU burst; its ordering is based on burst length and can delay long jobs.
Round Robin rotates the ready queue, gives each runnable process a fixed time quantum, and requeues an unfinished process after that quantum.
First-Come, First-Served admits ready processes in arrival order and lets the running process continue until it blocks or completes.
The Elevator policy moves a disk head through pending cylinder requests in one direction before reversing, so it schedules storage requests.

title: What is the primary factor that affects the performance of
subject: Operating System
text: What is the primary factor that affects the performance of Round Robin scheduling?
solution:
In Round Robin (RR) CPU scheduling, the time quantum is the fixed amount of time a process is allowed to run before being preempted and placed back at the end of the ready queue.

Choosing the right time quantum size is a delicate balancing act that directly dictates the efficiency and responsiveness of the operating system:

  • If the Time Quantum is too large: The algorithm behaves exactly like First-Come, First-Served (FCFS). Processes with long CPU bursts will hold onto the processor for their entire duration, causing shorter, interactive processes to experience high waiting times.

  • If the Time Quantum is too small: The CPU will switch between tasks incredibly quickly. While this provides excellent responsiveness (giving the illusion that all programs are running simultaneously), it triggers a massive amount of context switches. Since saving and loading process states takes CPU cycles, a tiny time quantum forces the system to waste most of its processing power on scheduling overhead rather than actual user programs.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. While context switch time adds overhead that can degrade performance, it is a constant architectural cost. The frequency and impact of these context switches are ultimately dictated by another, primary configuration factor.

Incorrect. I/O burst time affects how often a process relinquishes the CPU voluntarily to perform I/O operations. While it influences individual process behavior, it is an inherent characteristic of the workload, not the primary tuning knob that controls the Round Robin scheduler's overall performance.

Correct! The time quantum (or time slice) is the primary factor because the entire performance of Round Robin depends on its size. If it is too large, Round Robin degenerates into First-Come, First-Served (FCFS). If it is too small, the system spends more time switching between processes (context switching overhead) than executing actual work.

Incorrect. Traditional Round Robin scheduling is a preemptive, egalitarian algorithm that treats all processes equally by utilizing a circular First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue. It does not look at process priorities to make scheduling decisions.

title: In round robin CPU scheduling as time quantum is increased
subject: Operating System
text: In round robin CPU scheduling as time quantum is increased the average turnaround time
solution: Increasing the time quantum reduces context switch overhead, which lowers turnaround time. However, it also increases waiting times for short processes arriving after long ones. Since the net effect depends on specific process burst times and arrival patterns, the average turnaround time varies irregularly rather than following a fixed trend.

optionFeedback.html: Increasing the time quantum reduces context switching overhead, which might initially lower turnaround times. However, larger quanta can cause short processes to wait longer behind long-running tasks, making the relationship non-linear. You should consider how process burst times interact with scheduling decisions before concluding a trend exists.

While reducing context switch overhead often improves performance, simply increasing the quantum does not guarantee lower turnaround times for all processes. Shorter jobs may experience longer waiting periods if the quantum becomes too large relative to their burst times. Check how varying burst lengths affect average waiting time in your specific scenario.

Increasing the time quantum changes how processes share the CPU, affecting waiting times differently for each process. Context switch overhead decreases while average waiting time may increase depending on burst lengths, so the result is not constant.

Increasing the time quantum reduces context switch overhead, which tends to lower turnaround time. However, it also increases waiting times for short processes arriving behind long ones, potentially raising the average. Since the net effect depends on specific process burst times and arrival patterns, the turnaround time varies irregularly rather than following a fixed trend.

title: Match List with List II List (Algorithms) List II (Characteristics)
subject: Operating System
text:
Match List I with List II
List I (Algorithms) List II (Characteristics)

(A) First Come First Served (FCFS) (I) Each process is assigned a priority.

(B) Shortest Job First (SJF) (II) Ensures fair allocation of CPU time by assigning a time slice.

(C) Round Robin (RR) (III) Processes are executed in the order they arrive.

(D) Priority Scheduling (IV) Selects the process for execution with the smallest next burst time.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
solution:
Correct matching and brief explanations:

  • (A) First Come First Served (FCFS): Processes are executed in the order they arrive (III). FCFS does not use time slices or priorities.

  • (B) Shortest Job First (SJF): Selects the process with the smallest next CPU burst time (IV).

  • (C) Round Robin (RR): Ensures fair allocation of CPU time by assigning fixed time slices (II).

  • (D) Priority Scheduling: Each process is assigned a priority and scheduling is based on those priorities (I).

Therefore the correct mapping is: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

optionFeedback.html: The mapping "(A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)" is incorrect. First Come First Served (FCFS) does not use time slices; it executes processes in the order they arrive. Shortest Job First (SJF) selects the process with the smallest next CPU burst, not by arrival order. Round Robin (RR) is the algorithm that ensures fair allocation by assigning a time slice. Priority Scheduling assigns priorities to processes. The correct mapping is: FCFS → arrival order (III); SJF → smallest next burst (IV); RR → time-slice/fair allocation (II); Priority Scheduling → assigned priorities (I).

The mapping "(A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)" contains both correct and incorrect pairings. SJF→smallest next burst (B)-(IV) and Priority Scheduling→assigned priorities (D)-(I) are correct. However, FCFS does not use time slices (so A should be matched to arrival order (III)), and Round Robin is the algorithm that uses time slices to ensure fairness (so C should be matched to time-slice/fair allocation (II)).

title: Which of the following is true with respect to monitor?

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q106
subject: Operating System
text: What is the main disadvantage of Peterson’s solution for mutual exclusion?

options.html: It fails on modern multi-core CPUs due to memory reordering

solution:
A correct critical-section solution must satisfy three conditions: mutual exclusion, so no two processes execute in their critical sections at the same time; progress, so a process wanting to enter is not delayed indefinitely by processes not interested in entering; and bounded waiting, so there is a finite bound on how many times other processes enter before a waiting process is served. Peterson's algorithm achieves all three purely through ordinary shared variables — a turn variable and a per-process flag array — with no special hardware instructions, but its correctness proof rests on the memory-access model of the machine: it assumes reads and writes to shared variables complete in the exact order they appear in the program, a property known as sequential consistency.

Modern multi-core and multiprocessor systems do not guarantee that assumption by default. To improve performance, compilers reorder independent-looking instructions and CPUs use per-core caches, store buffers, and out-of-order execution, so a write one process makes to its flag or to turn may not become visible to another core in the same order it was issued, unless the program explicitly inserts a memory barrier or fence. Because Peterson's proof depends entirely on strict ordering of these reads and writes, running the unmodified algorithm on such hardware can let both processes enter the critical section at the same time, breaking mutual exclusion even though the algorithm's logic looks correct on paper.

Checking each remaining option against this reasoning:

  • It does not ensure progress — progress is a formally proven property of Peterson's algorithm under the classical, sequentially consistent model; the algorithm's construction, where each process yields via the flag and turn check, is specifically designed so a process not seeking entry never blocks another. This is not the property affected by moving to modern hardware.

  • It causes external fragmentation — external fragmentation is a memory-allocation phenomenon, the leftover unusable gaps between allocated blocks in contiguous or segmented memory schemes; Peterson's algorithm only reads and writes two small shared variables and has no relation to how memory blocks are allocated.

  • It requires high memory access time — memory access time is a hardware and memory-hierarchy property, governed by cache and RAM latency, independent of which synchronization algorithm a program uses; Peterson's algorithm does not impose any unusual memory-access cost.

Cross-checking against how real systems handle this: production synchronization primitives such as mutexes and spinlocks are built on hardware atomic instructions like test-and-set or compare-and-swap, combined with explicit memory fences, precisely because plain load and store based algorithms like Peterson's cannot be trusted to work correctly on modern multi-core CPUs without such support. This confirms that the main disadvantage lies in Peterson's incompatibility with modern multi-core hardware, not in progress, fragmentation, or memory-access time.

optionFeedback.html: Progress is one of the three formal correctness conditions for critical-section solutions, alongside mutual exclusion and bounded waiting: no process wanting to enter its critical section may be delayed indefinitely by processes that are not currently trying to enter. In a construction built from a shared turn variable and per-process flag array, such as Peterson's, this condition is a property of how the two variables are read and updated to decide which process's turn it is.

Modern multi-core and multiprocessor hardware, together with compiler optimizations, can reorder the loads and stores that a program issues to shared memory through out-of-order execution, per-core caches, and store buffers. In a construction built from a shared turn variable and per-process flag array, such as Peterson's, this reordering is a property of how those two variables are physically read and written across cores.

External fragmentation is the accumulation of small, non-contiguous free memory blocks that are individually too small to satisfy new allocation requests, arising in contiguous or segmented memory-allocation schemes as processes are loaded and removed over time. In a construction built from a shared turn variable and per-process flag array, such as Peterson's, this is a property of the memory allocator rather than of how the two variables themselves are read and written.

Memory access time is the duration the CPU takes to read or write a value at a given memory location, determined by the memory hierarchy — cache levels, RAM latency, and bus or interconnect speed. In a construction built from a shared turn variable and per-process flag array, such as Peterson's, this is a property of the underlying hardware rather than of how the two variables themselves are logically read and written.

title: Message passing system allows processes to [Asked in Hexaware] This
subject: Operating System
text: Message passing system allows processes to __________

options.html: communicate with each other without sharing the same address space
communicate with one another by resorting to shared data
name the recipient or sender of the message

solution:
Two classic IPC (Inter-Process Communication) models let processes coordinate: a shared-memory model, where processes map a common memory region and read/write it directly (needing explicit synchronization to avoid race conditions), and a message-passing model, where processes exchange information only through discrete send/receive messages routed by the OS, each keeping its own private address space.

The blank asks what a message-passing system specifically allows processes to do. By definition, message passing gives processes a way to communicate purely through message exchange, without ever sharing memory or address space -- that is exactly the capability being tested.

  • Resorting to shared data / sharing data directly describes the shared-memory model -- the alternate IPC technique, not message passing.

  • Naming the recipient or sender is only an addressing detail of how a message is routed (direct vs indirect addressing) -- not the core capability the blank is asking about.

So message passing systems allow processes to communicate with each other without sharing the same address space.

optionFeedback.html: This is the defining trait of message-passing IPC: each process keeps its own private address space, and all communication happens strictly through explicit send/receive message exchange handled by the OS -- no process ever reads or writes into another process's memory.

This describes the shared-memory IPC mechanism -- processes map a common memory region and read/write it directly, which requires the programmer to add explicit synchronization (locks or semaphores) to prevent race conditions; that coordination burden is the hallmark of this alternative technique.

Sharing data directly is the shared-memory approach to inter-process communication -- a common memory segment is mapped into each process's address space, and the OS provides no automatic protection against simultaneous conflicting access, so the processes' own code must manage consistency.

Naming the recipient or sender only concerns how a message is addressed (direct addressing needs an explicit process name; indirect addressing uses a shared mailbox/port) -- it is a detail of message delivery, not the core capability the blank is asking about.

title: Which of the following algorithms is used to solve the
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following algorithms is used to solve the critical section problem for n processes?
solution:
Concept

The critical-section problem requires a synchronization mechanism that guarantees three properties for processes sharing a resource: mutual exclusion (at most one process inside the critical section), progress (a waiting process eventually enters), and bounded waiting (no starvation). A general solution must hold for an arbitrary number of processes, n, not just two.

Applying it here

The Bakery algorithm (Lamport, 1974) gives a classic software solution that works for any number of processes n. Each process that wants to enter the critical section draws a numbered token, much like customers taking tickets at a bakery counter. The process holding the lowest token enters first; ties are broken deterministically by process id. Because every entrant gets a strictly ordered ticket, mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting all hold for n processes without special hardware.

Why the other choices fail

  • Peterson's algorithm: a correct critical-section solution, but defined only for exactly two processes; it does not generalise to n processes on its own.

  • Moore algorithm: there is no established critical-section technique by this name; it is more commonly associated with the Moore finite-state-machine model in sequential-circuit and automata theory, unrelated to process synchronization.

  • Banker's algorithm: a deadlock-avoidance method that decides whether a resource request keeps the system in a safe state; it does not provide mutual exclusion for a critical section.

optionFeedback.html: Peterson's algorithm is a valid mutual-exclusion solution, but it is defined for exactly two processes; it does not by itself extend to an arbitrary number n of processes.

There is no established algorithm called the "Moore algorithm" for the critical-section problem; the name is more commonly linked to the Moore finite-state-machine model used in sequential-circuit and automata theory, which has nothing to do with process synchronization.
Banker's algorithm performs deadlock avoidance by checking that resource allocations keep the system in a safe state; it manages resource requests, not mutual exclusion for a critical section.
The Bakery algorithm assigns each process an ordered numbered token and admits the lowest token first, so it provides mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting for any number of processes n.

title: Which of the following is true with respect to strict

Strict Alternation – Explanation

Strict alternation is a software-only mutual exclusion mechanism that forces two processes (P1, P2) to take turns while entering the critical section (CS).

    Only one process can be in CS at a time.

❌ Does NOT Guarantee

  • B does want to use it

Still, B is blocked because the rule says “It’s A’s turn.”

So B must wait unnecessarily → progress is violated ❌.

Conclusion: The statement "p2 terminates but p1 does not" is impossible.

Reason:

  • When p2 exits its loop it has set z to false by evaluating z = (x != y). That can only happen when x == y at that moment.

Possible and impossible outcomes with short interleavings:

  • p1 and p2 both terminate — possible. Example: p2 increments y to 2 but is paused before updating z; p1 then increments x until x == 2 and exits; when p2 resumes it computes z = (x != y) which is false, so p2 exits too.

  • p2 terminates but p1 does not — impossible, for the reason given above.

  • Both do not terminate — possible. Example: p2 keeps incrementing y faster than p1 increments x, so x never catches up and both loops continue forever.

This code implements Strict Alternation using a turn variable. While it successfully ensures Mutual Exclusion (only one process enters at a time) and Bounded Wait (processes strictly take turns, so no one waits forever if the other process is active), it fails to satisfy Progress.

Why Progress fails: Progress requires that if the Critical Section is empty and some processes want to enter, only those processes competing for entry should participate in the decision. In this code, if Pi​ (whose turn it is) decides not to enter the Critical Section, it blocks Pj​ indefinitely—even though the Critical Section is free and Pi​ has no interest in it. Because a process in the "remainder section" can stop another process from entering, the Progress condition is violated.

title: Assume that is the mutex semaphore. Which of the following
subject: Operating System
text: Assume that s is the mutex semaphore. Which of the following order of statements is/are deadlock or violation of mutual exclusion?(assume s=1)
solution:
Summary of which sequences are incorrect and why:

  • Signal(s); critical_section(); Wait(s);

    • Problem: Violation of mutual exclusion.

    • Reason: Signaling before entering increments the semaphore and allows entry into the critical section without an accompanying Wait (acquire). The critical section is not properly protected.

  • Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s);

    • Problem: None — this is the correct usage.

    • Reason: Waiting before entering ensures the semaphore is acquired, preserving mutual exclusion; signalling after leaving releases the mutex.

  • critical_section(); Signal(s);

    • Problem: Violation of mutual exclusion.

    • Reason: Entering the critical section without a Wait means the semaphore was never acquired; Signal afterward does not retroactively enforce mutual exclusion.

  • Wait(s); Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s); Signal(s)

    • Problem: Deadlock.

    • Reason: The first Wait decrements the mutex from 1 to 0; the second Wait blocks because the semaphore is 0. The process is blocked before it reaches its Signal calls, so it cannot release the semaphore and becomes deadlocked.

Final answer: The sequences that are incorrect (either violate mutual exclusion or cause deadlock) are: Signal(s); critical_section(); Wait(s);, critical_section(); Signal(s);, and Wait(s); Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s); Signal(s). The correct usage that preserves mutual exclusion without deadlock is Wait(s); critical_section(); Signal(s).

optionFeedback.html: This sequence signals before trying to enter the critical section, so the process enters the critical section without performing a Wait (acquire). That violates mutual exclusion because the semaphore is not used to protect entry into the critical section.

This is the correct standard pattern for using a mutex semaphore: perform Wait(s) to acquire the semaphore, execute the critical section, then perform Signal(s) to release it. It preserves mutual exclusion and does not cause deadlock.
Entering the critical section without performing a Wait violates mutual exclusion. The following Signal(s) alone does not prevent the immediate unauthorized entry into the critical section.

Performing Wait(s) twice on a single mutex initialized to 1 causes the second Wait to block (since the semaphore is already 0 after the first Wait). The blocked process can never reach the subsequent Signal(s) calls, producing a deadlock (self-deadlock).

title: Processes and have producer-consumer relationship, communicating by the use of
subject: Operating System
text:
Processes P1 and P2 have a producer-consumer relationship, communicating by the use of a set of shared buffers.

P1: repeat
    Obtain an empty buffer
    Fill it
    Return a full buffer
    forever
P2: repeat
    Obtain a full buffer
    Empty it
    Return an empty buffer
    forever

Increasing the number of buffers is likely to do which of the following?

I. Increase the rate at which requests are satisfied (throughput)

II. Decrease the likelihood of deadlock

III. Increase the ease of achieving a correct implementation
solution:
Concept

In a bounded-buffer producer-consumer system, buffer capacity and synchronization correctness are governed by different mechanisms. The number of buffer slots only sets how much a producer can get ahead of a consumer (or vice versa) before one must wait - it does not change the semaphore protocol (mutex, empty, full) that a correct implementation needs, and it does not change the order in which those semaphores are acquired, which is what determines whether the solution is deadlock-free.

Applying it to each statement

  • Statement I (throughput): with more buffer slots, P1 can fill several buffers before it must wait for P2 to empty one, and P2 can empty several before waiting on P1 - so both processes block on each other less often. Fewer blocking waits per unit time means more fill or empty operations complete in the same time, so throughput increases.

  • Statement II (deadlock): deadlock here would come from an incorrect order of acquiring the mutex and the empty or full semaphores (for example, holding mutex while blocked on empty or full). That ordering is a property of how the code is written, not of how many buffers exist - the same flawed order deadlocks whether there is one buffer or a thousand.

  • Statement III (ease of implementation): a correct solution still needs exactly the same three synchronization primitives (mutex, empty-count, full-count) and the same wait or signal pairing regardless of buffer count - adding slots changes only the initial value of a counting semaphore, not the reasoning required to get the logic right.

Cross-check

Consider the two extremes: a correctly-synchronized implementation with a single buffer is deadlock-free, and a correctly-synchronized implementation with many buffers is also deadlock-free - capacity did not change that outcome, only the rate of progress changed. Conversely, an incorrectly-ordered implementation can deadlock at any buffer count. This confirms only the throughput claim (Statement I) tracks with buffer count.

Therefore, increasing the number of buffers supports Statement I alone: higher throughput is the likely effect.

title: Bounded Buﬀer problem: There is set of buﬀers shared by
subject: Operating System
text:
Bounded Buﬀer problem: There is a set of buﬀers shared by producer and consumer processes. Producer inserts resources into the buﬀer, and consumer removes resources from the buﬀer. A producer goes to sleep if the buﬀer is full, and a consumer goes to sleep if the buﬀer is empty. Now, consider the following implementation:

Choose the appropriate answer

options.html: Cannot say, the implementation depends on the size of the buﬀer

solution:
Key issue: consumers can enter the critical section and try to remove a resource even when the buffer is empty because there is no semaphore tracking filled slots.

Why this fails:

  • The consumer only uses the mutex for mutual exclusion and does not wait for any indication that an item is available.

  • If a consumer runs when the buffer is empty it will attempt to remove an item from an empty slot (underflow) or otherwise behave incorrectly.

Correct fix:

  • Introduce a semaphore full initialized to 0 to count filled buffers.

  • Keep mutex for mutual exclusion and empty initialized to buffer size N for empty slots.

Initialization:

  • Semaphore mutex = 1

  • Semaphore empty = N

  • Semaphore full = 0

Corrected pseudocode:

  • Producer:

  • P(empty) // wait for an empty slot

  • P(mutex) // enter critical section

  • add resource to buffer

  • V(mutex) // leave critical section

  • V(full) // signal a filled slot

  • Consumer:

  • P(full) // wait for a filled slot

  • P(mutex) // enter critical section

  • remove resource from buffer

  • V(mutex) // leave critical section

  • V(empty) // signal an empty slot

Note: The existing solution text had a wording error saying the consumer should "wait until the buffer is empty". The correct requirement is that the consumer must wait until the buffer is not empty (i.e., until a filled slot exists).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This implementation is missing a semaphore that tracks the number of filled buffers. As written, a consumer immediately acquires the mutex and tries to remove a resource even if the buffer is empty, which can cause removal from an empty slot or incorrect behavior. To fix the protocol, add a 'full' semaphore (initialized to 0); the producer should signal it after producing, and the consumer must wait on it before removing.

Correct. The implementation is incorrect because consumers are not prevented from accessing the buffer when it is empty. The usual bounded-buffer solution uses three semaphores: a mutex for mutual exclusion, an empty-count initialized to buffer size, and a full-count initialized to 0. The producer waits on empty and signals full after producing; the consumer waits on full and signals empty after consuming.

Incorrect. The correctness does not depend on the numeric size of the buffer for this issue. Even for any finite buffer size, the implementation is flawed because it does not block consumers when there are no filled slots. Adding or changing buffer size does not remove the need for a semaphore that tracks filled slots.

Incorrect. Saying "None of these" is not appropriate because the correct choice is that the implementation is incorrect and why. The implementation should be fixed by adding a 'full' semaphore and adjusting producer/consumer operations accordingly.

title: Which of the classical IPC problems is not solved using
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the classical IPC problems is not solved using semaphore?
solution:
Answer: All of the listed problems can be solved using semaphores.

  • Producer–Consumer: Use a counting semaphore for empty slots (initialized to buffer size), a counting semaphore for filled slots (initialized to 0), and a mutex (binary semaphore) to protect buffer access. This ensures producers wait when the buffer is full and consumers wait when it is empty.

  • Sleeping Barber: Use a counting semaphore to track waiting customers (chairs), a semaphore to signal the barber's readiness, and a mutex for updating the waiting count. Customers block when chairs are available or leave if all chairs are occupied; the barber sleeps when there are no customers.

  • Dining Philosophers: Represent each fork with a binary semaphore and use a strategy to avoid deadlock (for example, a waiter semaphore that limits the number of philosophers who may pick forks, resource ordering, or letting one philosopher pick forks in reverse order). Semaphores model pickup and putdown actions.

Key point: Semaphores provide mutual exclusion and synchronization primitives that, when designed carefully to avoid deadlock and starvation, can be used to solve these classic IPC problems.

Careful ordering or a limit on simultaneous philosophers picking forks prevents circular wait.

Yes. The producer–consumer problem is commonly solved with semaphores: a counting semaphore for available empty slots, a counting semaphore for available items, and a mutex (binary semaphore) to protect buffer access. This ensures producers wait when the buffer is full and consumers wait when it is empty.

Yes. Customers either wait if chairs are available or leave if all chairs are full; the barber sleeps when there are no customers.

Correct. All of the listed classic IPC problems can be solved using semaphores. title: In producer-consumer scenario also known as Bounded-Buffer Problem, what would
subject: Operating System
text: In a producer-consumer scenario also known as Bounded-Buffer Problem, what would be the most appropriate synchronization primitive to ensure that the consumer waits when the buffer is empty?
solution:
Concept

Solving the bounded-buffer problem needs a primitive that does two things at once: keep a running count of how many units of a resource are available, and put a thread to sleep (block it) when the count it needs has reached zero, then wake it the instant the count is restored. A primitive that only enforces mutual exclusion, or that waits by spinning on the CPU, cannot satisfy both of these at the same time.

The primitive that natively provides exactly this count-and-block behaviour is the counting semaphore: an integer value accessed only through two atomic operations - wait (decrement; block the caller if the value would go below zero) and signal (increment; wake one blocked thread).

Application to the bounded buffer

The bounded-buffer (producer-consumer) problem is solved with two counting semaphores plus one for mutual exclusion:

  • empty, initialised to the buffer size N - the producer waits on it before inserting, so it blocks when the buffer is full.

  • full, initialised to 0 - the consumer waits on it before removing, so it blocks (sleeps) exactly when the buffer is empty and is woken by the producer's signal after an insert.

  • mutex, a binary semaphore, guards the critical section that touches the shared buffer.

The requirement in the stem - the consumer must wait when the buffer is empty - is met precisely by the consumer performing wait on full: with full starting at 0, the very first remove blocks until a producer signals.

Contrast with the other primitives

Primitive

Why it does not fit the requirement

Spinlock

Provides mutual exclusion only and waits by busy-looping on the CPU; it neither counts items nor lets a thread sleep until data arrives, so the consumer would burn CPU instead of waiting.

Mutex lock

A pure lock/unlock for one critical section; it carries no count of buffered items, so on its own it cannot make the consumer wait specifically for the buffer to become non-empty.

Monitors

A higher-level construct that can solve the same problem using condition variables, but the question asks for the basic primitive that natively combines a resource count with blocking - an abstraction layer rather than that primitive.

optionFeedback.html: A spinlock waits by busy-looping on the CPU, so a consumer using it would spin and waste cycles rather than sleep while the buffer has nothing to remove.

A mutex lock is a single-owner lock that only enforces one-at-a-time access to the critical section; by itself it keeps no record of how many items are buffered, so it cannot make the consumer wait specifically for the buffer to stop being empty.

A semaphore keeps an internal count of buffered items and blocks (sleeps) the consumer on a wait operation while that count is zero, waking it when a producer signals - exactly the count-and-block behaviour the empty-buffer condition requires.

Monitors are a higher-level synchronization construct built on top of locks and condition variables; while they can solve producer-consumer, they are an abstraction layer rather than the basic primitive the question asks for.

solution:
Concept: A semaphore only guarantees mutual exclusion when every process follows the same protocol: succeed at P(mutex) before entering, then execute the matching V(mutex) after leaving so a permit becomes available for someone else. “Present in the critical section” means a process has passed its own entry step and has not yet executed its own exit step — the CPU can be given to other processes in between, so several processes can be sitting inside the CS simultaneously as long as each one individually cleared its own entry.

Application: Trace one valid interleaving starting from mutex = 1, always letting a released waiter consume a signal before the next signal is issued:

  1. P₁ executes P(mutex): mutex is 1, so it succeeds and mutex becomes 0. P₁ enters the CS and is left paused there (it has not yet reached its own V(mutex)).

  2. P₈ executes V(mutex): mutex goes from 0 to 1. Since P₈'s code never calls P(mutex), it enters the CS unconditionally — P₁ and P₈ are now both inside together.

  3. With mutex back at 1, P₂'s waiting P(mutex) immediately succeeds (mutex: 1 → 0). P₂ enters and stays paused. (P₁, P₂, P₈ inside.)

  4. P₈ signals V(mutex) again to close this pass: mutex goes to 1, and P₃'s waiting P(mutex) immediately consumes it (mutex back to 0). P₃ enters and stays paused.

  5. Looping back, P₈ signals V(mutex) once more to open the next pass: mutex goes to 1, and P₄'s waiting P(mutex) immediately consumes it (mutex back to 0). P₄ enters and stays paused, and P₈ itself re-enters the CS for a second visit — P₁ through P₄ and P₈ (five processes) are now inside.

  6. Repeating this same signal-then-consume pattern twice more releases P₅ (after P₈'s next closing signal) and P₆ (after its next opening signal); each enters and stays paused exactly as before, while P₈ re-enters the CS for a third visit — P₁ through P₆ and P₈ (seven processes) are now inside.

  7. One more signal-then-consume releases P₇, who enters and stays paused. P₈ signals once again — with no waiters left, this final signal simply leaves mutex at 1 — and re-enters the CS for a fourth time.

  8. At this instant P₁ through P₇ (all seven ordinary processes) and P₈ are simultaneously present inside the CS — 8 processes in total. At every step, mutex never had to exceed 1: each of P₈'s signals was consumed by exactly one already-waiting process before the next signal was issued, so this works even under a strictly binary semaphore.

Cross-check: This count is also the maximum possible, because the scenario defines only eight processes in total — P₁ through P₇ running the ordinary code, plus P₈ — and a count of just 1 would only hold if mutex behaved as a correctly-paired binary lock, which it does not here, since P₈ signals without ever waiting.

title: Consider the following synchronization mechanism and choose the appropriate answer:
subject: Operating System
text: The image shows a synchronization mechanism intended for a uniprocessor. Which statement correctly describes how this mechanism behaves?

options.html: It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region.
It works on single CPU machines even when there are context switches within the critical region.
It does not work on single core CPU.

solution:
CONCEPT

On a uniprocessor, only one instruction stream executes at a time. Masking interrupts prevents timer- and interrupt-driven preemption, so the running thread keeps the CPU until interrupts are restored.

This technique can protect a short kernel critical section when the code does not voluntarily block or fault and the previous interrupt state is restored afterward. It does not by itself provide multiprocessor mutual exclusion because another CPU can continue executing.

APPLICATION

  1. Calling acquire masks interrupts on the only CPU before the critical section begins.

  2. While interrupts remain masked, the periodic timer cannot preempt the running thread, so an interrupt-driven context switch cannot place another runnable process on that CPU.

  3. The current thread therefore executes the critical section without another process entering it through preemptive scheduling.

  4. Calling release re-enables interrupts, after which ordinary preemption and context switching may resume.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

  • “It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region” matches the uniprocessor execution trace: masking interrupts removes the preemption route during that interval.

  • “It works on single CPU machines even when there are context switches within the critical region” assumes away the protection: if another process can be scheduled there, this code has no shared lock-state test to stop that process from entering.

  • “It does not work on single core CPU” conflicts with the mechanism’s intended setting; controlling interrupt-driven preemption on the sole CPU is precisely what makes this limited technique usable.

  • “None of these” does not apply because one concrete statement describes the traced behavior.

Therefore, the appropriate statement is: “It works on single CPU machines because it disables context switches within the critical region.”

optionFeedback.html: Mechanism trace: acquire masks interrupt-driven preemption on the sole CPU; the protected interval executes; release restores interrupt delivery.
Mechanism trace: a switch before release schedules another thread; acquire checks no ownership flag; that thread can proceed to the protected interval.
Mechanism trace: the sole CPU has no concurrently executing peer; masking its interrupts removes timer-driven preemption until release.
Mechanism trace: acquire changes the sole CPU interrupt state to masked; the protected interval runs under that state; release changes it back to enabled.
