text:
Consider the following given programs P1, P2 and P3 with execution time of process x,y and z being 4ms, 3ms and 5ms respectively:

Assume s and t are locks initially in free state and preemptive priority scheduling algorithm is used. Then average turnaround time is ___________: (round off 2 decimal places)
solution:
Key idea: simulate preemptive priority scheduling, track lock acquisition and blocking, then compute completion times and turnaround times.

  • 0–4: Program 1 runs process x (4 ms).

  • 4–5: Program 1 acquires lock s and starts process z (first 1 ms of z).

  • 5: Program 2 arrives (higher priority) and preempts Program 1.

  • 5–9: Program 2 runs its process x (4 ms).

  • 9: Program 2 attempts to lock s but finds it held by Program 1, so Program 2 blocks.

  • 9–13: Program 1 resumes and completes remaining 4 ms of z, then unlocks s.

  • 13: Program 2 (waiting) acquires s and then t, starts its process z at 13.

  • 13–15: Program 2 runs 2 ms of z (of 5 ms).

  • 15: Program 3 arrives (highest priority) and preempts Program 2.

  • 15–19: Program 3 runs its process x (4 ms), then at 19 it tries to lock s but s is held by Program 2, so Program 3 blocks.

  • 19–22: Program 2 resumes and completes remaining 3 ms of z, then unlocks s and t at 22.

  • 22–27: Program 3 (waiting) acquires s and t, runs its z for 5 ms.

  • 27–30: Program 3 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 30.

  • 30–33: Program 2 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 33.

  • 33–36: Program 1 runs its process y (3 ms) and completes at time 36.

Turnaround times:

  • Program 1: completion 36 − arrival 0 = 36 ms

  • Program 2: completion 33 − arrival 5 = 28 ms

  • Program 3: completion 30 − arrival 15 = 15 ms

Average turnaround = (36 + 28 + 15) / 3 = 79 / 3 = 26.333... → 26.33 ms (rounded to 2 decimals).

title: Which of the following is/are true:
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following is/are true:

options.html: Kernel is not aware about the behaviour of every user level thread
User threads can switch faster than Kernel threads
Test and set lock guarantees progress and mutual exclusion
User level threads are not suitable for non blocking tasks.

solution:
Final answer: The true statements are:

  • Kernel is not aware about the behaviour of every user level thread

  • User threads can switch faster than Kernel threads

  • Test and set lock guarantees progress and mutual exclusion

Detailed explanation:

  1. Kernel awareness of user-level threads: True because user-level threads are managed by a user-space library; the kernel typically only knows about the enclosing process. Consequently, kernel scheduling and blocking system calls act on the whole process, not on individual user-level threads.

  2. Context switch speed: True because switching user-level threads avoids a kernel-mode switch and scheduler overhead, making the switch faster. This applies when no kernel involvement is required; user-level threads cannot exploit multiple CPUs unless the kernel schedules them as kernel threads.

  3. Test-and-set lock properties: The test-and-set lock enforces mutual exclusion and, under the usual progress criterion (if the critical section is free and threads want to enter, one will succeed), allows progress. However, it does not guarantee bounded waiting or fairness; threads may busy-wait and suffer starvation depending on scheduling.

  4. Why the remaining statement is false: The claim that user-level threads are not suitable for non-blocking tasks is incorrect. User-level threads are well suited for non-blocking and CPU-bound work because they are lightweight and fast to switch. The main drawbacks are inability to run on multiple CPUs (unless kernel support exists) and that blocking system calls can block the entire process.

optionFeedback.html: True. User-level threads are scheduled by a user-space thread library, so the kernel typically sees only the single process and is not aware of each user-level thread's state or scheduling. As a result, a blocking system call in one user-level thread can block the entire process unless the thread library handles it specially.

True. Switching between user-level threads does not require a transition to kernel mode, so context switches are cheaper and faster than kernel-thread context switches. This is true when switching within the same process and when no kernel involvement (e.g., no system call) is required. Note that user-level threads cannot run on multiple CPUs concurrently unless supported by the kernel.

True, with a caveat. A test-and-set lock enforces mutual exclusion by allowing only one thread to hold the lock at a time, and under the usual progress condition it permits a waiting thread to eventually acquire the lock when the lock is free. However, test-and-set does not guarantee bounded waiting or fairness: threads may busy-wait and suffer starvation depending on scheduling.

False. User-level threads are suitable for non-blocking and CPU-bound tasks because they are lightweight and have fast context switches. The main limitations are that blocking system calls can block the whole process and user-level threads usually cannot utilize multiple CPUs unless the kernel is aware of them.

title: Which makes more sense when it comes to critical section
subject: Operating System
text:
Which makes more sense when it comes to critical section problem?

1. “ Spin lock with single core cpu”

2. “Spin lock with multi core cpu”
solution:
Answer: Spin lock with multi core CPU is the better choice in typical cases.

Key idea: spin locks cause busy-waiting; whether that is acceptable depends on the CPU topology and expected wait time.

  • Single-core systems: Busy-waiting blocks the only runnable core. If a thread spins, it prevents the lock holder from running and releasing the lock, so progress stalls. Use blocking synchronization (mutexes or condition variables) instead.

  • Multi-core systems: Other cores can run the thread that will release the lock while one thread spins. For very short critical sections and low contention, spinning can be cheaper than the overhead of sleeping and waking threads.

  • Rule of thumb: Use spin locks only when the expected wait is very short (microseconds) and the overhead of blocking is higher than spinning. Otherwise prefer blocking locks.

optionFeedback.html: Spin locks on a single-core CPU are usually a poor choice. A spin lock makes a thread busy-wait while polling the lock; on a single core that busy-wait prevents the thread that might release the lock from running, so the system cannot make progress. Use a blocking lock (mutex) or other sleep-based synchronization on single-core systems or when wait times may be long.

Spin locks on multi-core CPUs can make sense when the critical section is very short and contention is low. Because other cores can continue running, spinning wastes some CPU cycles but may be cheaper than the overhead of putting a thread to sleep and waking it. Use spin locks selectively for short waits on multicore systems.

Using spin locks in both single-core and multi-core scenarios is not equally appropriate. While spin locks can be useful on multi-core systems for short critical sections, they are generally inappropriate on single-core systems for the reasons explained above. So the blanket choice 'both' is misleading.

Saying 'none' is incorrect because spin locks do make sense in some contexts — specifically on multi-core systems for very short critical sections. The statement should be qualified rather than rejected entirely.

title: Which of the below statements is/are false? Mutual statement is
subject: Operating System
text:
Which of the below statements is/are false?

1. Mutual statement is guaranteed
2. Deadlock free algorithm
3. Progress is guaranteed
solution:
Assumption: occupied and blocked are initialized to 0, and wakeup unblocks exactly one waiting process. Under these usual assumptions, none of the three statements is false — mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom, and progress are all satisfied. Explanation:

  • Mutual exclusion: Only a process that finds occupied == 0 executes occupied = 1 and proceeds into the critical section. Any process that finds occupied == 1 increments blocked and sleeps. On exit, the exiting process sets occupied = 0 and wakes exactly one waiting process, which is the only waiter that will continue into the critical section next. Therefore at most one process is in the critical section at a time.

  • Deadlock freedom: There is no cycle of processes waiting indefinitely for each other. If a process is in the critical section it will eventually execute the exit code, set occupied = 0 and wake one blocked process. If no process is in the critical section, any arriving process will set occupied = 1 and enter. Because exit always wakes a waiter when one exists, blocked processes are eventually awakened, so the system cannot enter a deadlock where no one can make progress.

  • Progress: If some process wishes to enter and no one is in the critical section, that process sets occupied = 1 and proceeds immediately. If the critical section is occupied, waiting processes are queued conceptually via the blocked count; each exit wakes one waiter, so waiting processes will eventually be woken and enter. Thus a waiting process will make progress rather than being permanently blocked (assuming wakeup is reliable and scheduler eventually runs the woken process).

Caveats and required assumptions: The conclusions rely on occupied and blocked being initialized (commonly to 0), that the check/update of occupied and blocked within the Enter/Exit region is performed atomically as shown, and that wakeup reliably unblocks exactly one waiting process. If those assumptions are violated, behavior can differ.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Not all three statements are false. Assuming occupied = 0 and blocked = 0 initially and that wakeup unblocks exactly one waiting process, the code enforces mutual exclusion, is deadlock-free, and guarantees progress. See the improved solution for a step-by-step explanation.

Incorrect. The claims that deadlock freedom and progress are false are not correct. With occupied and blocked initialized to 0 and wakeup waking a single waiting process, the algorithm wakes one waiter on exit so it cannot deadlock and waiting processes eventually make progress. See the solution for details.

Incorrect. Mutual exclusion is guaranteed. Only a process that finds occupied == 0 sets occupied = 1 and enters the critical section; any other process increments blocked and sleeps. Exit wakes exactly one waiting process, ensuring only one process is in the critical section at a time. See the solution for the full argument and assumptions.

Correct. Assuming typical initial values occupied = 0 and blocked = 0 and that wakeup unblocks exactly one waiting process, the code ensures mutual exclusion, is deadlock-free, and guarantees progress. See the detailed explanation in the solution.

title: Which mechanism allows processes to exchange data and messages directly
subject: Operating System
text: Which mechanism allows processes to exchange data and messages directly?
solution: Shared memory is the correct mechanism because it allows multiple processes to access a common region of physical memory, enabling them to exchange data directly without the overhead of kernel-mediated copying. When processes map the same memory segment, they can read and write data instantly, making it highly efficient for high-volume communication. In contrast, semaphores are synchronization primitives used to control access to shared resources but do not transfer data themselves. Pipes facilitate communication through a unidirectional byte stream, typically requiring the kernel to buffer and relay data between processes rather than allowing direct access. Signals are asynchronous notifications used to alert a process of an event but carry minimal data payload, making them unsuitable for direct message exchange. Therefore, shared memory uniquely supports the requirement of direct data and message exchange between processes.

optionFeedback.html: Semaphores are synchronization primitives used to control access to shared resources but do not transfer data themselves.

Shared memory is the correct mechanism because it allows multiple processes to access a common region of physical memory, enabling them to exchange data directly without the overhead of kernel-mediated copying.
Pipes allow data exchange but typically through a kernel buffer rather than direct memory access.
Signals are asynchronous notifications used to alert a process of an event but carry minimal data payload, making them unsuitable for direct message exchange.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q92
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following ensures mutual exclusion in concurrent processes?
solution:
Mutual exclusion requires that when multiple processes or threads share a critical section, at most one of them executes inside it at any instant. Operating systems achieve this through several general mechanisms — semaphore-based blocking, software algorithms such as Peterson's solution, and atomic hardware instructions. Hardware-based approaches use an operation that reads a shared lock variable and updates it in a single indivisible step, so no other process can see or act on an in-between state; the classic hardware primitive for this is the Test-and-Set (TSL) instruction.

Trace how a spinlock built on test-and-set enforces this in practice:

  1. The lock variable starts at false (unlocked), and every process trying to enter the critical section repeatedly calls TestAndSet(&lock) until it returns false.

  2. TestAndSet atomically reads the current value of lock, sets lock to true, and returns the value it read — the read and the write happen as one uninterruptible hardware step.

  3. The first process to call TestAndSet gets back false (lock was unlocked), so its loop exits and it proceeds into the critical section, and lock is now true.

  4. Any other process calling TestAndSet while the first is inside the critical section reads back true (lock is already held), so its loop keeps spinning instead of entering — it can never slip in during the gap between the read and the write, because there is no gap.

  5. When the first process finishes, it sets lock back to false, allowing exactly one waiting process to succeed on its next TestAndSet call.

boolean TestAndSet(boolean *target) {
    boolean rv = *target;
    *target = true;
    return rv;
}

// Each process:
while (TestAndSet(&lock))
    ;              // busy-wait
// critical section
lock = false;

Contrast with the other options: unbuffered I/O only controls when a single process's output is flushed to a device, not how multiple processes coordinate; environment variables are key-value settings copied into a process's own address space at creation time; command-line arguments (argv) are launch-time parameters whose values are fixed when a program starts, though the process may go on reading them repeatedly during its run. None of these three involve a shared, atomically-updated variable, so none can serialize access between concurrently running processes.

Among the options offered here, only an atomic hardware instruction such as test-and-set removes the window in which two processes could both see the lock as free at once; the other three options never touch any shared, atomically-updated variable at all, so none of them can serialize access between concurrent processes.

optionFeedback.html: Unbuffered I/O is a mode that writes a process's output directly to a device as each write call executes, rather than accumulating it in an in-memory buffer for a later flush; it is a per-stream I/O timing setting configured on a single process's file descriptor.
A test-and-set instruction is a hardware operation that reads a lock variable's current value and overwrites it with a new value within that same operation, then returns the value that was read.

Environment variables are key-value pairs (such as PATH or HOME) that the operating system copies into a process's address space at the moment that process is created, forming part of that process's own runtime configuration.

Command-line arguments are the string tokens passed into a program's argv array at the moment it is launched via exec; the process can read this array as many times as it likes during its run, but the values themselves are fixed at launch.

title: Disabling an interrupt is known as
subject: Operating System
text: Disabling an interrupt is known as ______.
solution:
Concept

In an interrupt-driven system, the CPU can selectively ignore an interrupt request by setting a bit in an interrupt-mask register. This act of switching off (disabling) recognition of an interrupt source is called masking. A masked interrupt remains pending or is ignored — the CPU does not jump to its service routine.

Application

"Disabling an interrupt" is, by definition, masking it: the mask bit for that interrupt is set so the processor stops responding to that signal even when it is asserted. Masking can be done in hardware (mask pins/registers on the interrupt controller) or in software (writing the mask register).

Contrast

  • Run, Stop, and Halt all describe execution states of a process or the CPU — whether instructions are being executed — and have nothing to do with switching an interrupt line on or off.

  • Only masking names the mechanism that controls (enables/disables) which interrupt signals the CPU will recognize.

optionFeedback.html: Masking is the standard term for disabling an interrupt: a mask bit is set so the CPU stops recognizing that interrupt source even when its signal is asserted.
"Run" describes a process actively executing instructions — an execution state, not the hardware/software mechanism that switches an interrupt line on or off.
"Stop" names a process execution state (execution suspended), not the mechanism that controls which interrupt signals the CPU recognizes.
"Halt" refers to the CPU/process ceasing execution — an execution state — and does not describe controlling or disabling interrupt signals.

title: What is the output of the following code?
subject: Operating System
text: How many processes execute the statement printf("4 ") in the following C program?
solution:
Concept: A successful fork() creates one child process, and both parent and child continue from the statement after that fork. A statement placed after all branches executes once in every process that reaches it.

  1. The first fork() creates two processes: the original parent enters the outer if branch, while its child enters the outer else branch and then reaches the final printf("4 " ).

  2. Only the original parent executes the second fork() inside if (!fork()). This creates one more process, so three processes now exist.

  3. The child created by the second fork() satisfies !fork() and executes the third fork(), creating one additional process. The total is therefore four processes.

  4. The final printf("4 " ) is outside every conditional block, so each of the four processes executes it once.

title: Consider the following code segment: main(){ for(int if(i%2==0) fork(); printf(“hello”);
subject: Operating System
text:
Consider the following code segment:
main(){
for(int i=0; i≤9; i++){
if(i%2==0) fork();
printf(“hello”);
}
}
How many times printf will be executed by the child process?
solution:
Clarification: fork() is executed when i is 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 — five times in total.

Because fork() is called before printf in each relevant iteration, the number of processes that execute printf in a given iteration depends on how many forks have already happened.

  • i = 0 (fork): 2 processes print -> child prints = 1

  • i = 1 (no fork): 2 processes print -> child prints = 1

  • i = 2 (fork): 4 processes print -> child prints = 3

  • i = 3 (no fork): 4 processes print -> child prints = 3

  • i = 4 (fork): 8 processes print -> child prints = 7

  • i = 5 (no fork): 8 processes print -> child prints = 7

  • i = 6 (fork): 16 processes print -> child prints = 15

  • i = 7 (no fork): 16 processes print -> child prints = 15

  • i = 8 (fork): 32 processes print -> child prints = 31

  • i = 9 (no fork): 32 processes print -> child prints = 31

Sum across all iterations: total printf executions by all processes = 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 8 + 16 + 16 + 32 + 32 = 124.

The original parent prints once each iteration (10 times total), so the printf calls executed by child processes collectively = 124 - 10 = 114.

Also useful: the number of child processes created is 2^5 - 1 = 31.

Final answers: total printf calls executed by child processes (collectively) = 114; number of child processes created = 31.

title: When process is created using fork system call, then which
subject: Operating System
text: When a process is created using fork system call, then which of the following is shared between both child and parent process?
solution:
Answer: Shared memory segments are shared between parent and child.

Explanation: When fork creates a new process, the child gets copies of the parent's memory and execution context. Modern kernels use copy-on-write, so physical pages may be shared until either process modifies them, but logically the stack and heap are separate.

  • Stack — copied for the child; each process has its own stack.

  • Heap — copied for the child (typically via copy-on-write); not shared unless explicit shared memory mechanisms are used.

  • Shared memory segments — remain shared between parent and child, so both can access the same memory region.

  • Other related resource: file descriptors are duplicated but refer to the same underlying open file, so file offset and flags are shared unless changed.

Therefore, from the given choices, only shared memory segments are actually shared between parent and child after fork.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The stack is copied for the child process. After fork, the child has its own stack and changes to the stack in one process do not affect the other.
Incorrect. The heap is copied for the child process (modern systems typically use copy-on-write), so the child gets its own heap space unless explicit shared memory is used.
Correct. Shared memory segments remain shared between parent and child after fork, so both processes can access the same memory region.

Incorrect. Although shared memory segments are shared, the heap is not shared by default. The child receives a copy of the heap (usually via copy-on-write), so saying both heap and shared memory are shared is wrong.

title: When process creates new process using the fork() operation, which
subject: Operating System
text: When a process creates a new process using the fork() operation, which of the following is shared between the parent process and the child process?
solution:
The parent and child share only the shared memory segments. Everything else is duplicated, but the child has its own versions.

  • Address space (stack and heap) is duplicated.

  • Page tables are not shared; the kernel gives the child its own page tables. Many systems use copy-on-write so physical pages are copied only when written.

  • Shared memory segments remain shared across parent and child (for example, SysV shared memory or mmap with MAP_SHARED). Changes in that region are visible to both processes.

  • Open file descriptors are duplicated in the child, but they refer to the same underlying file table entry, so file offsets and flags are shared.

  • Summary: the correct shared resource is shared memory segments; stacks, heaps, and page tables are duplicated (often implemented with copy-on-write).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Page tables are not shared. fork creates a separate address space for the child and the kernel gives the child its own page tables (many systems use copy-on-write so physical pages are only duplicated when written).

Correct. Shared memory segments (for example SysV shared memory or mmap with MAP_SHARED) remain mapped into both processes so changes are visible to both. Note that other memory regions like the heap and stack are duplicated for the child; open file descriptors are duplicated but refer to the same underlying file table entry.

Incorrect. The stack is part of each process's private address space. After fork the child gets its own stack (initially implemented with copy-on-write), so changes to one process's stack are not seen by the other.
Incorrect. The heap is duplicated for the child process. Heap memory is private to each process after fork unless specifically allocated as shared memory.

title: Consider the following segment of codes related to process creation.
subject: Operating System
text:
Consider the following segment of codes related to process creation. How many times the message “child process created” will be printed?

#include <stdio.h>

void main()

{

fork();
fork();
fork();

printf("child process created");

}
solution:
fork() splits the process that calls it into two independent processes — the original process and a new copy — and both processes resume execution from the very next statement onward. If a program executes fork() n times in succession with no condition on its return value, every process alive at each call also executes that same call, so the total number of processes doubles at each of the n calls, giving 2n processes overall. Every one of those processes then independently executes any statement that follows — including a printf() — exactly once.

  1. Before the first fork(): exactly 1 process is running.

  2. First fork() executes: the 1 running process becomes 2 processes — the original process and a new copy.

  3. Second fork() executes: each of the 2 currently running processes calls fork() independently, so 2 processes become 4.

  4. Third fork() executes: each of the 4 currently running processes calls fork() independently, so 4 processes become 8.

  5. All 8 processes then reach the printf("child process created") statement — it has no condition on the fork() return value, so every one of the 8 processes executes it exactly once.

As an independent check: counting only the processes newly spawned by the three fork() calls gives 23 − 1 = 7 new child processes; adding back the single original process, which also survives and reaches the printf() statement, gives 7 + 1 = 8 processes in total — the same count reached by direct doubling above.

Therefore, the message “child process created” is printed 8 times in total.

optionFeedback.html: This total is the count reached by squaring the number of fork() calls (32 = 9).
This total is the count reached by doubling the number of fork() calls and adding one (2 × 3 + 1 = 7).
This total is the count reached by doubling the number of fork() calls and adding two (2 × 3 + 2 = 8).
This total is the count reached by taking the number of fork() calls directly as the total (3).

title: Which of the following statements correctly describe the return values
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following statements correctly describe the return values of the fork() system call in a Unix-like operating system?

options.html: 0 to the child process and a positive value (child's PID) to the parent process
1 to the child process and 0 to the parent process
A negative value if the fork fails

solution:
Concept

The fork() system call creates a new process by duplicating the calling (parent) process. It is called once but returns twice — once in the parent and once in the newly created child. The single return value is what lets each process discover which role it is playing after the duplication.

Return-value rule

On a successful fork(), the kernel hands back three distinct outcomes:

  • In the child process the return value is 0. The child has no need to learn its own PID this way — it can always obtain it with getpid().

  • In the parent process the return value is the PID of the newly created child, which is a positive integer. This lets the parent track or wait for that specific child.

  • If fork() fails (for example, the process table is full), no child is created and the call returns a negative value, conventionally -1, in the parent, with errno set.

Applying it here

The statement "0 to the child and a positive value (the child's PID) to the parent" matches the success behaviour exactly, so it is correct. The statement "a negative value if the fork fails" matches the failure behaviour exactly, so it is also correct. The statement "1 to the child and 0 to the parent" inverts and misstates the values — the child receives 0, not 1, and the parent receives a positive PID, not 0 — so it is wrong. Because two of the listed statements are individually correct, the choice that affirms both of those statements together is the right answer.

Cross-check

A standard idiom confirms this: pid = fork(); if (pid < 0) handle_error(); else if (pid == 0) child_code(); else parent_code();. The three branches — negative, zero, positive — correspond exactly to failure, child, and parent, which is precisely what the two correct statements together describe.

optionFeedback.html: This option commits to a single description of what fork() returns and stops there. The prompt asks which statements correctly describe the return values, so the right approach is to test every statement on its own merits before settling on a choice. Picking one description after a quick read, without weighing the others, is the trap this option sets.

This misremembers the convention. The child does not receive 1 — it receives 0 — and the parent does not receive 0; it receives the child's PID, a positive value. Confusing fork()'s return contract with a generic "success equals nonzero" habit produces these inverted numbers, which no Unix-like kernel returns.

This option locks onto a single description of fork()'s behaviour and stops there. The prompt asks which statements correctly describe the return values, so each statement deserves to be checked on its own before you commit. Settling on one description without weighing the rest is exactly the shortcut this option rewards.

Read each statement on its own and two of them describe fork()'s return contract correctly: on success the child gets 0 while the parent gets the child's positive PID, and on failure the parent gets a negative value. This choice is the one that brings those two accurate descriptions together, covering every way fork() can return.

"None" claims that not a single listed statement gives a correct account of fork()'s return values. Checked one by one, at least one of the statements does state the return behaviour accurately, so a correct description is present among the choices and "none" is too strong to hold.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2019 — Q26
subject: Operating System
text: The fork() system call is used for:
solution:
Concept

In Unix-like operating systems, fork() is a process-creation system call.

It duplicates the calling process to create a child process with a new process identifier; after the call, the parent and child can continue independently.

Application

  1. Suppose a process P with process identifier 1200 calls fork().

  2. The operating system creates a child process C with a different process identifier and copies the calling process state.

  3. The call returns the child's process identifier to the parent and 0 to the child, so the two processes can follow separate execution paths.

Cross-check and contrast

The nearby concepts describe different operating-system actions:

  • Task dispatching selects an existing ready task for CPU execution.

  • Job creation defines a workload at a broader job-management level.

  • Process creation establishes a new child execution context.

  • Priority adjustment changes a scheduling attribute of an existing task.

Therefore, fork() is used for the creation of a new process.

optionFeedback.html: In the fork() context, task dispatching is a scheduler action that selects an existing ready task for CPU execution.
In the fork() context, job creation is a job-management action that defines a new batch or workload unit.
In the fork() context, process creation is a process-management action that establishes a new execution context with its own process identifier.
In the fork() context, priority adjustment is a scheduler action that changes an existing task's scheduling attribute.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q13
subject: Operating System
text: A process executes the following code: fork(); fork(); fork(); How many child processes are created in total?
solution:
Concept

Each successful fork() duplicates every process that reaches the call. Starting with one process, n unconditional sequential calls therefore produce 2n total processes and 2n − 1 newly created child processes.

Application

  1. Before any call, there is 1 process.

  2. After the first fork(), 1 × 2 = 2 processes exist.

  3. After the second fork(), 2 × 2 = 4 processes exist.

  4. After the third fork(), 4 × 2 = 8 processes exist.

  5. Of these 8 processes, 1 is the original process, so the number created as children is 8 − 1 = 7.

Cross-check

The three calls create 1, then 2, then 4 new children; 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. Therefore, the total number of child processes created is 7.

optionFeedback.html: The value 3 corresponds to counting one newly created child for each written fork() call.
The value 4 is the number of processes present immediately after two successful fork() calls.
The value 7 comes from eight final processes after excluding the one original process.
The value 8 is the total number of processes present after three successful fork() calls, including the original process.

title: Which of the following best describes the major difference between
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following best describes the major difference between UNIX fork() and Windows CreateProcess?

options.html: CreateProcess creates a new thread in the same process
fork() copies the current process; CreateProcess creates a new one from scratch

solution: The correct answer is Option D. The fundamental difference lies in how each system handles process creation. UNIX's fork() creates a new process by duplicating the calling process, resulting in two nearly identical processes that share memory until one writes to it. In contrast, Windows CreateProcess does not duplicate the current process; instead, it loads a new executable from disk and creates an entirely fresh process with its own memory space. This distinction makes fork() efficient for immediate execution of existing code, while CreateProcess is designed to launch new programs. Option A is incorrect because fork() and CreateProcess create processes, not threads within the same process. Option B is false as their mechanisms differ significantly. Option C is wrong because fork() operates in both command-line and GUI environments on UNIX systems.

optionFeedback.html: incorrect. As the name explicitly implies, CreateProcess allocates a brand-new, isolated process with its own dedicated virtual address space and resources. If a Windows developer wants to spin up a new thread inside the same process space, they would use the CreateThread API instead.

incorrect. Their foundational mechanics are completely opposite. UNIX uses a two-step cloning architecture (fork() to duplicate, then exec() to load a new binary), whereas Windows handles process generation in a single, distinct action by constructing a completely fresh environment around a specified executable file.

incorrect. fork() is a core POSIX/UNIX system call that functions at the fundamental operating system kernel level. It operates entirely independently of user interfaces and is heavily utilized in command-line tools, background daemons, and headless server architectures.

Correct
fork() duplicates the parent process's memory space, variables, and execution state entirely (using Copy-on-Write optimization) so that both continue from the exact same line of code. Conversely, Windows' CreateProcess ignores the parent's memory layout and sets up a clean, blank slate initialized straight from a specified .exe application file.

title: Which system call can be used by parent process to

title: Which of the following statements are true?
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: Creating a thread is more efficient than creating a process.
Creating a thread is less efficient than creating a process.
Each thread has its own set of registers.
Communication between threads is easier than communication between processes.

solution:
Statement: Creating a thread is more efficient than creating a process. True. Threads share the process address space and many resources (such as open file descriptors and memory mappings), so creating and switching threads usually has lower overhead than creating or switching processes.

Statement: Creating a thread is less efficient than creating a process. False. This contradicts the previous statement: creating a thread is typically lighter weight than creating a process because processes require separate address spaces and more kernel-side setup.

Statement: Each thread has its own set of registers. True. Each thread maintains its own CPU register context (including the program counter and stack pointer), allowing independent execution. Threads share memory but have separate execution state.

Statement: Communication between threads is easier than communication between processes. True, with caveats. Because threads share the same memory, data sharing is usually simpler and faster than inter-process communication. However, shared-memory communication requires explicit synchronization (locks, atomics) to avoid data races, whereas processes are isolated and rely on IPC mechanisms.

Correct answers: The true statements are: creating a thread is more efficient than creating a process; each thread has its own set of registers; and communication between threads is easier than communication between processes.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Creating a thread is generally more efficient than creating a process because threads in the same process share the address space and many resources (open file descriptors, memory mappings). Thread creation and context switching typically incur less overhead than creating or switching entire processes.

Incorrect. Creating a thread is usually more efficient than creating a process. New processes require separate address space and more kernel setup, which makes process creation and switching heavier than thread creation and switching.

Correct. Each thread has its own CPU register context (for example, its own program counter, stack pointer, and general-purpose registers). Threads share the process memory space but maintain separate register/state so they can execute independently when scheduled.

Correct (with nuance). Communication between threads is typically easier and faster because threads share the same memory space, allowing direct data sharing without IPC mechanisms. However, shared memory requires synchronization (locks, atomics) to avoid data races, whereas processes are isolated and need explicit IPC.

title: Which of the following can be shared between two threads
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following can be shared between two threads of the same process?
solution:
Answer: Data section, Code section, and I/O files can be shared; the Stack section cannot be shared.

Explanation: Threads of the same process share the process address space and resources, but each thread keeps its own execution context.

  • Code section: The program's instructions are loaded once and are shared by all threads (usually read-only).

  • Data section: Global and static variables (and the heap) are part of the shared address space and accessible to all threads.

  • Stack section: Each thread has a private stack for local variables, return addresses, and its register context. Stacks cannot be shared because doing so would corrupt per-thread local state and control flow.

  • I/O files: Open file descriptors and handles are shared within the process, so threads can read/write the same files, but concurrent access typically requires synchronization.

Summary: Because threads share the process address space they can share code, global data, and open I/O files. Each thread, however, needs its own stack and register context (including program counter) to maintain independent execution.

optionFeedback.html: Data section (global and static variables) is shared among threads because threads in the same process share the same address space. That means global variables and the heap are accessible to all threads.

Code section (the program text) is shared by threads. The executable instructions are loaded once into the process address space and all threads execute the same code; this is typically read-only and shared.

Stack section is not shared. Each thread gets its own stack to hold local variables, return addresses, and the thread's program counter/register context. Sharing a stack would corrupt local state and control flow.
I/O files (open file descriptors/handles) are shared between threads of the same process. Threads can use the same open files, though access should be synchronized to avoid race conditions.

title: Which of the following multithreading model is followed in Linux
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following multithreading model is followed in Linux OS?

options.html: One User Thread mapping to One Kernel Thread
Many User Threads mapping to One Kernel Thread
One User Thread mapping to Many Kernel Threads
Many User Threads mapping to Many Kernel Threads

solution:
Concept

A multithreading model describes how user-level threads (created by a thread library) are mapped onto kernel-level threads (the entities the operating-system scheduler actually dispatches). Three classical mappings exist:

  • One-to-one (1:1): every user thread is backed by its own kernel thread, so the kernel schedules each one independently.

  • Many-to-one (M:1): many user threads share a single kernel thread, scheduled in user space.

  • Many-to-many (M:N): M user threads are multiplexed over a smaller pool of N kernel threads by a two-level scheduler.

Application to Linux

Modern Linux implements POSIX threads through the Native POSIX Thread Library (NPTL), which uses the one-to-one model. Each pthread the application creates is realised as a distinct kernel scheduling entity (a task created via the clone() system call sharing the address space). Therefore the answer is “One User Thread mapping to One Kernel Thread”.

Why the one-to-one model fits Linux

  • Independent scheduling: the kernel sees and schedules every thread, so threads can run on different CPU cores for genuine parallelism.

  • No convoy on blocking: if one thread issues a blocking system call, only that kernel entity blocks; the others keep running.

  • Historical fit: NPTL replaced the older Linux threading implementations (the original LinuxThreads and the experimental M:N NGPT project) because a clean, direct mapping scales better on SMP hardware than a two-level scheme.

Cross-check (contrast with the other models)

  • Many-to-one would let a single blocking call stall every thread and cannot use multiple cores — not what Linux does.

  • Many-to-many is the hybrid two-level scheme (for example, classic Solaris); the Linux kernel does not run such a user-space scheduler over a smaller kernel-thread pool.

  • One-to-many is not a usable model at all, since one thread of control cannot execute on several kernel entities simultaneously.

optionFeedback.html: A one-to-one mapping is exactly what the Native POSIX Thread Library (NPTL) implements: each user thread is bound to its own kernel scheduling entity, so the kernel schedules every thread independently and a blocking call in one thread does not stall the others.

A many-to-one mapping multiplexes several user threads onto a single kernel thread through a user-space scheduler; because the kernel sees only one schedulable entity, one blocking system call would freeze all the threads and true multiprocessor parallelism is impossible. This is the classic user-level (green-thread) design, not how the Linux kernel schedules threads.

Mapping a single user thread onto many kernel threads is not a real threading model: one logical thread of control cannot run on several kernel entities at once, so no mainstream operating system, including Linux, is built this way.

A many-to-many mapping multiplexes M user threads over N kernel threads via a two-level (hybrid) scheduler, as in older Solaris. The Linux kernel does not schedule threads this way: it does not run a user-space two-level scheduler on top of a smaller kernel-thread pool.

title: With single resource, deadlock occurs

text: If the system contains exactly one non-shareable resource instance in total, deadlock among competing processes occurs:

options.html: when more than two processes compete for that resource instance
when exactly two processes compete for that resource instance
when exactly one process competes for that resource instance

solution:
Concept

A deadlock is a permanent circular wait: each process in a cycle waits for a resource held by the next process in that cycle.

Contention alone is not deadlock. When the system has only one non-shareable resource instance in total, its holder has no different resource in this model to wait for, so a circular wait among competing processes cannot form.

Application

Represent the situation with a wait-for graph.

  1. If one process holds the single resource instance, every other competing process can only wait for that holder.

  2. The holder has no second resource in this model to wait for, so no edge can lead from the holder back to a waiting process.

  3. Therefore, the graph has waiting edges but no directed cycle, regardless of whether one, two, or more than two processes compete.

Contrast

  • More than two processes: several processes may queue behind one holder, but the queue does not create a cycle.

  • Exactly two processes: one may wait for the holder, but there is no return wait that closes a cycle.

  • Exactly one process: there is no inter-process waiting cycle.

  • None of these cases: process count alone cannot create circular wait with a single resource instance.

Cross-check

All four Coffman conditions are necessary for deadlock. The circular-wait condition is absent here, so the result is none of these cases.

title: The algorithm which is prone to deadlock is
subject: Operating System
text: The algorithm which is prone to deadlock is —
solution:
Concept: A distributed mutual-exclusion algorithm is deadlock-free only if it forces one global order on all pending requests, so no set of processes can end up circularly waiting on each other's permissions. Timestamp-based total-ordering schemes guarantee this; permission/voting-based schemes in which each process waits on only an overlapping subset of the others do not guarantee it unless extra ordering or priority rules are added.

Algorithm

How permission is granted

Deadlock-free?

Lamport's algorithm

Every request is placed on one shared logical-timestamp-ordered queue; a process enters its critical section only when its own request is at the head everywhere.

Yes — a single total order rules out any circular wait.

Ricart–Agrawala's algorithm

A process replies immediately to any request whose timestamp is later than its own pending request, and defers only requests it must logically precede.

Yes — the same timestamp ordering rules out any cycle.

Maekawa's algorithm

A process needs permission from only a subset of processes (its voting set); voting sets overlap pairwise but are not globally ordered.

No — in its basic form, two processes can each hold part of the other's needed votes and wait on each other, forming a cycle.

Cross-check: Lamport's and Ricart–Agrawala's algorithms are both provably deadlock-free because of their total ordering, and among the given choices only one other named algorithm remains besides “none of these” — so the deadlock-prone one must be that remaining algorithm, which also rules out “none of these.”

Therefore, the algorithm prone to deadlock is Maekawa's algorithm.

optionFeedback.html: Maekawa's algorithm requires a process to collect permission only from a subset of processes (its voting set) rather than from everyone, and these voting sets overlap only pairwise. Two processes can each hold permission from part of their own set while waiting on the other's remaining votes, producing a circular wait — so in its basic form this algorithm is prone to deadlock unless extended with a priority or timestamp-based ordering.

The Ricart–Agrawala algorithm totally orders every request using logical timestamps: a process replies to a conflicting request only after its own earlier-timestamped request is satisfied, and no process is ever kept waiting indefinitely on a request with a lower timestamp. This total ordering rules out any circular wait, so Ricart–Agrawala's algorithm is deadlock-free.

Lamport's algorithm places every request in a global logical-timestamp-ordered queue that all processes agree on, and grants access strictly in that order. Because every process's requests are served in one common order, no process can end up waiting in a cycle, so Lamport's algorithm is deadlock-free.

This choice assumes every algorithm named in the option list is guaranteed to avoid deadlock, but that guarantee does not automatically hold for every distributed mutual-exclusion design — different algorithms give different guarantees, and at least one of the algorithms offered here does not guarantee deadlock-freedom. So it is not correct to say that none of the listed algorithms can deadlock.

  4. Therefore add one extra unit to prevent that scenario: minimum units = n × (m − 1) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.

Answer: Deadlock can never occur. Here is a constructive example and a short formal argument.

Example safe sequence (one possible allocation):

  • Suppose the current allocation is P1 = 2, P2 = 1, P3 = 1 (all 4 resources are allocated).

  • The process holding 2 units has reached its maximum and needs 0 more resources, so it can execute and release its 2 units.

  • After it releases, there are at least 2 units available, allowing the remaining processes to complete. Thus a safe sequence exists.

Formal case-based argument:

  • Case 1 — Available = 0: If no resources are available then all 4 units are allocated. It is impossible for every process to still need at least one more unit because that would require each process to have allocated at most 1 unit, giving total allocated ≤ 3, a contradiction. Therefore at least one process has remaining need 0 and can run to completion, releasing resources.

  • Case 2 — Available ≥ 1: If at least one unit is available, then any process whose remaining need is ≤ 1 can be satisfied. Since each process's maximum remaining need is at most 2 and some processes may already hold resources, there will always be at least one process whose remaining need ≤ available. That process can run and release resources.

In every possible allocation one of the above cases applies, so at least one process can always proceed and eventually all processes can complete. Hence deadlock can never occur.

title: Which of the following is/are condition for deadlock prevention in
subject: Operating System
text:
Which of the following is/are condition for deadlock prevention in given below:
S1: Each process request resource in either in increasing order or in decreasing order only

solution:
Answer: Statements S1 and S3 only.

Key idea: Deadlock prevention works by ensuring that at least one of the necessary conditions for deadlock cannot occur. The four necessary conditions are:

  • Mutual exclusion (some resources are non-shareable).

  • Hold and wait (a process holds resources while waiting for others).

  • No preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken away).

  • Circular wait (a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next).

How the given statements relate:

  • S1 — Requiring each process to request resources in a global increasing or decreasing order prevents circular wait by design (no cycles can form).

  • S3 — Requiring a process to release all currently held resources before requesting new ones removes the hold-and-wait condition (or enables preemption), preventing deadlock.

  • S2 — The Banker’s algorithm is a deadlock avoidance strategy: it permits resource allocation only when the system remains in a safe state. That is not the same as prevention.

Conclusion: Because S1 eliminates circular wait and S3 eliminates hold-and-wait (or provides preemption), they are valid deadlock prevention techniques. S2 is an avoidance algorithm, so the correct prevention statements are S1 and S3 only.

title: Computer has tape drives with processes competing for them. Each
subject: Operating System
text: A computer has 6 tape drives with n processes competing for them. Each process may need 2 drives. What is the maximum value of n for the system to be deadlock free ?
solution: To ensure a system remains deadlock-free, we must guarantee that at least one process can always complete its execution. The worst-case scenario for deadlock occurs when every process holds the maximum number of resources it can hold without completing. Here, each process needs 2 tape drives but will be stuck holding only 1 drive while waiting for the second. With n processes, the maximum number of drives held without completing is n * (2 - 1) = n. To prevent deadlock, the total available resources must be greater than this worst-case sum by at least 1. Using the formula: Total Resources >= n * (Max Need - 1) + 1, we substitute the values: 6 >= n * (2 - 1) + 1. Simplifying gives 6 >= n + 1, which means n <= 5. Therefore, the maximum number of processes is 5. If there were 6 processes (Option D), each holding one drive would consume all resources, leaving none for any process to acquire the second needed drive, causing a deadlock. Similarly, while 3 or 4 processes (Options A and B) would also be safe, they are not the maximum possible value.

title: What is the purpose of banker’s algorithm?
subject: Operating System
text: What is the purpose of banker’s algorithm?
solution:
Concept. An operating system can deal with deadlock in four distinct ways, and standard OS theory keeps them separate. Prevention designs the request protocol so that one of the four Coffman conditions — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — can never hold. Avoidance leaves those conditions intact and instead examines each request at run time, granting it only if the resulting state is still safe, that is, only if some ordering of the processes lets every one of them finish with the resources that remain. Detection lets a deadlock form and then searches the allocation state for a circular wait, and recovery breaks an identified deadlock by aborting or preempting processes.

Application. The Banker's algorithm implements the second of these. Every process declares its maximum claim in advance, and on each resource request the algorithm proceeds as follows:

  1. Compare the request with the process's remaining Need and with the currently Available units; if it exceeds either, the process waits.

  2. Tentatively allocate the requested units and recompute the Available, Allocation and Need matrices for that hypothetical state.

  3. Run the safety algorithm on that state: repeatedly find a process whose Need is less than or equal to Available, mark it as able to finish, and add its Allocation back to Available.

  4. If every process can be marked in some order, the state is safe and the allocation is committed; if no such order exists, the tentative allocation is undone and the requester blocks.

Nothing in that procedure negates a Coffman condition, searches for a cycle that has already formed, or aborts a running process. The algorithm simply refuses any grant that would move the system out of a safe state, which is precisely the definition of deadlock avoidance.

Cross-check. Comparing that behaviour with each purpose offered:

Offered purpose

What that strategy does

Banker's algorithm?

To detect deadlock

Searches the allocation state for a circular wait after one may already exist

No — it runs before each grant and never reports an existing cycle

To prevent deadlock

Statically negates one of the four Coffman conditions by protocol design

No — all four conditions remain possible; only unsafe grants are refused

To solve deadlock

Terminates or preempts processes to break a deadlock that already exists

No — it never aborts or rolls back a process

None of these

Catch-all for a purpose outside the three above

Yes — the purpose is deadlock avoidance, which is not listed

Result. The purpose of the Banker's algorithm is deadlock avoidance, and none of the three named purposes is avoidance, so “None of these” is the choice that holds. Some texts do use “prevention” loosely for any technique that stops a deadlock from arising; in the standard four-way classification used by this syllabus, and with an explicit “None of these” option on offer, avoidance and prevention remain separate categories, so that loose reading does not apply here.

optionFeedback.html: Detection is the strategy of granting requests freely and then running a separate routine over the current Allocation and Request state — a cycle search on the resource-allocation graph, or the detection-matrix algorithm — to identify processes already blocked in a circular wait. It acts after the fact and reports which processes are stuck, rather than deciding whether a pending request may be granted.

Prevention is the strategy of designing the resource protocol so that one of the four Coffman conditions can never hold: requiring a process to acquire all its resources at once negates hold-and-wait, allowing forced release negates no-preemption, and imposing a global ordering on resource types negates circular wait. It is a static structural restriction, fixed in advance and independent of the current allocation state.

Solving, in the sense of recovery, is the strategy applied once a circular wait has already been identified: it breaks the cycle by terminating one or more of the deadlocked processes, or by preempting the resources they hold and rolling those processes back to an earlier checkpoint. It restores progress in a system that is already stuck, rather than governing how requests are granted.

This is a catch-all option rather than a named strategy: it asserts only that the purpose in question matches none of the three categories listed in the other options. It has no mechanism, timing, or algorithm of its own to describe; its content is entirely the negation of those three named categories.

title: The Banker's Algorithm is critical deadlock avoidance method in operating
subject: Operating System
text:
The Banker's Algorithm is a critical deadlock avoidance method in operating systems, designed to facilitate resource allocation without causing deadlock. It operates by maintaining information about the maximum resources Each process may require, the current allocated resources and the available resources in the system. The algorithm checks each resource request to determine, if granting it would leave the system in a safe state, meaning that there is always a sequence in which all processes can complete their execution without getting stuck due to resource unavailability. Each process must specify its maximum demand for each resource type before it starts execution. When a process requests additional resources, the algorithm checks if granting the request will keep the system in a safe state. If so, the resources are allocated otherwise the process must wait until its request can be safely fulfilled.
What is the significance of the Banker's algorithm in terms of resource management ?

options.html: It ensures that all processes can finish their execution without deadlock.
It eliminates the need for processes to request resources.
It accelerates the execution of critical sections in processes.
It minimizes the number of context switches between processes.

solution:
Significance of the Banker's algorithm: it provides a conservative method to manage resources so that deadlock cannot occur.

  • Prevents deadlock by ensuring safety: before granting a request, the algorithm simulates the allocation and checks whether the system would remain in a safe state (i.e., there exists a sequence in which all processes can complete).

  • Requires knowledge of maximum demands: each process must declare its maximum resource needs; the algorithm uses Available, Allocation, and Need information to perform safety checks.

  • Guarantees a safe completion sequence: if the system is in a safe state, the algorithm can identify an order in which all processes can finish without deadlock.

  • Trades concurrency for safety: it may delay granting certain requests even when resources are currently free to avoid entering an unsafe state.

  • Limitations: requires prior knowledge of maximum needs, adds runtime overhead for safety checks, and is not practical when resource demands are unknown or highly dynamic.

  • Does not eliminate requests or speed up critical sections nor directly reduce context switches: it strictly governs whether a resource request can be safely granted.

In summary, the Banker's algorithm is significant because it provides a practical safety check that prevents deadlocks by allowing only those allocations that preserve a safe state, at the cost of reduced concurrency and additional bookkeeping.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The Banker's algorithm ensures the system only grants resource requests that keep the system in a safe state. By simulating allocations and checking for a safe completion sequence, it guarantees there exists an order in which all processes can finish, preventing deadlock.

Incorrect. The Banker's algorithm does not remove the need for processes to request resources. Processes must still request resources and declare their maximum needs; the algorithm decides whether to grant a request immediately or make the process wait to keep the system in a safe state.

Incorrect. The Banker's algorithm is about safe resource allocation to avoid deadlocks, not about improving the speed of critical section execution. It may even delay some requests to maintain safety, so it does not accelerate critical sections.

Incorrect. The Banker's algorithm does not aim to minimize context switches. Its purpose is to manage resource allocations to avoid unsafe states and deadlock. Context switching is a scheduling concern and is not directly addressed by this algorithm.
