subject: Operating System
text:
Consider a system with five processes 𝑃0 through 𝑃4 and three resource types 𝑅1, 𝑅2 and 𝑅3 . Resource type 𝑅1 has 10 instances, 𝑅2 has 5 instances and 𝑅3 has 7 instances. Suppose that at time 𝑇0, the following snapshot of the system has been taken :

 Allocation

         𝑅1         𝑅2          𝑅3

𝑃0     0            1             0

𝑃1     2            0             0

𝑃2     3            0             2

𝑃3     2            1             1

𝑃4     0            2             2

 Max

𝑅1         𝑅2           𝑅3

7            5              3

3            2              2

9            0              2

2            2              2

4            3              3

Available

𝑅1         𝑅2            𝑅3

3             3               2

Assume that now the process 𝑃1 requests one additional instance of type 𝑅1 and two instances of resource type 𝑅3. The state resulting after this allocation will be
solution:
Answer: The system will be in a safe state.

Reasoning (Banker's algorithm):

  • Total instances: R1 = 10, R2 = 5, R3 = 7.

  • Initial Allocation matrix (P0..P4):

    P0 (0,1,0), P1 (2,0,0), P2 (3,0,2), P3 (2,1,1), P4 (0,2,2).

  • Max matrix (P0..P4):

    P0 (7,5,3), P1 (3,2,2), P2 (9,0,2), P3 (2,2,2), P4 (4,3,3).

  • Compute Need = Max - Allocation:

    P0 (7,4,3), P1 (1,2,2), P2 (6,0,0), P3 (0,1,1), P4 (4,1,1).

  • Initial Available: (3,3,2). P1 requests (1,0,2).

  • Check request <= Need for P1: (1,0,2) <= (1,2,2) — allowed.

    Check Available >= request: (3,3,2) >= (1,0,2) — allowed.

  • Tentatively grant request: new Available = (3,3,2) - (1,0,2) = (2,3,0). New Allocation for P1 = (3,0,2). New Need for P1 = (0,2,0).

Safety check (find a sequence where each process's need <= current work):

  1. Start with Work = Available = (2,3,0). P1 need (0,2,0) <= Work, so P1 can finish. Release P1 allocation (3,0,2) -> Work becomes (5,3,2).

  2. With Work = (5,3,2), P3 need (0,1,1) <= Work, so P3 finishes. Release (2,1,1) -> Work becomes (7,4,3).

  3. With Work = (7,4,3), P0 need (7,4,3) <= Work, so P0 finishes. Release (0,1,0) -> Work becomes (7,5,3).

  4. With Work = (7,5,3), P2 need (6,0,0) <= Work, so P2 finishes. Release (3,0,2) -> Work becomes (10,5,5).

  5. With Work = (10,5,5), P4 need (4,1,1) <= Work, so P4 finishes. All processes can finish.

Therefore a safe sequence exists (one such sequence is P1 -> P3 -> P0 -> P2 -> P4), so the system is in a safe state after the requested allocation.

optionFeedback.html: Calling the resulting global condition a "Ready state" is misleading. "Ready" usually describes an individual process that can run; the question asks whether the system is safe after granting the request. After granting the requested resources the system is not merely "ready" or blocked — it is in a safe state because a safe completion sequence exists. Therefore this answer is incorrect.

Correct. After granting P1 the additional (1 of R1 and 2 of R3), available becomes (2,3,0). Using the Banker's safety check we can find a safe completion sequence: P1 -> P3 -> P0 -> P2 -> P4. Since every process can finish in turn, the system is in a safe state.

"Blocked state" is not correct. A blocked state would imply processes cannot all eventually complete and are waiting indefinitely. In this case, after granting the request a safe sequence exists (for example P1, P3, P0, P2, P4), so processes can complete without deadlock. Therefore the system is not blocked.

"Unsafe state" is incorrect here. An unsafe state would mean no safe sequence exists and the system may lead to deadlock. After the requested allocation the Banker's algorithm finds a safe sequence (P1 -> P3 -> P0 -> P2 -> P4), so the state is safe, not unsafe.

title: Consider the following snapshot of system running concurrent processes. Process
subject: Operating System
text: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process i is holding Xi instances of a resource R, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all i, process i can place a request for at most Yi additional instances of R while holding the Xi instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that Yp = Yq = 0. Which one of the following conditions guarantees that no other process apart from p and q can complete execution?

options.html: Xp + Xq < Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Xp + Xq < Max{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Min(Xp, Xq) ≥ Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Min(Xp, Xq) ≤ Max{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}

solution:
Concept. This item uses the maximum-claim model of deadlock avoidance: every process declares the largest additional amount it may still request, and because the system cannot know in advance that a process will ask for less, a process counts as able to complete only when the free pool can cover that full declared amount. The pool itself grows only when some process finishes and hands back everything it was holding. To block an entire group of processes at once, compare the pool that will actually become available against the smallest declared demand in that group: a pool strictly below that minimum is strictly below every demand in the group, so no claim in the group can be granted — and because nothing finishes, no further release ever occurs and the pool never grows. That permanence is what turns a momentary shortage into a guarantee.

Applying it to this snapshot.

  1. All instances of R are already in use, so the free pool starts at 0. With no free instances, any process k whose declared outstanding demand Yk is greater than 0 cannot be granted its claim and is stuck immediately.

  2. Exactly two processes, p and q, have Yp = Yq = 0. They need nothing further, so they run to completion and hand back everything they hold. The free pool therefore becomes Xp + Xq.

  3. A remaining process k (k ≠ p, q) counts as able to finish only if that pool covers its full declared demand, that is only if Xp + Xq ≥ Yk; the worst case the model must assume is that k asks for all Yk at once.

  4. To block every remaining process at the same time we need Xp + Xq < Yk for all k ≠ p, q. A quantity lies below every member of a set exactly when it lies below the smallest member, so this collapses to Xp + Xq < Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}.

  5. Since nothing else can proceed, no further resources are ever released and the pool stays at Xp + Xq forever. The blockage is therefore permanent, which is exactly what “guarantees” demands.

Cross-check and contrast.

  • Comparing against the maximum instead: Xp + Xq < Max{Yk | k ≠ p, q} says only that the pool falls short of the single hungriest claim. Take a released pool of 3 with remaining demands Yr = 2 and Ys = 9 — here Max{2, 9} = 9, so 3 < 9 holds, yet the pool of 3 already covers r’s claim of 2 and r completes. The condition can hold while another process still finishes, so it guarantees nothing.

  • Using Min(Xp, Xq) in place of the sum: the pool that is actually released is Xp + Xq, not the smaller of the two holdings. Bounding Min(Xp, Xq) says nothing about how large Xp + Xq can be, so it cannot cap the pool.

  • Direction of the inequality: Min(Xp, Xq) ≥ Min{Yk | k ≠ p, q} makes a holding at least as large as a demand, which permits a process to be satisfied instead of blocking it, while Min(Xp, Xq) ≤ Max{Yk | k ≠ p, q} is almost always true and constrains nothing at all.

  • Numeric check: take n = 4 with Xp = 2, Xq = 1 and remaining demands Yr = 4, Ys = 9. The released pool is 3 and Min{4, 9} = 4, so 3 < 4 holds and neither r nor s can proceed. Lower Yr to 3 and the pool of 3 now covers r — and correspondingly 3 < Min{3, 9} = 3 is false.

Result. The guarantee is exactly Xp + Xq < Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}.

optionFeedback.html: On the left is the sum Xp + Xq, built from the holdings of the two processes whose additional demand is 0. On the right is Min{Yk | k ≠ p, q}, the smallest additional demand among the other processes — the member of that set no other member falls below. The strict < asserts that the sum stays under that value.

The left side is again the total Xp + Xq held by the two processes with additional demand 0, and the right side is Max{Yk | k ≠ p, q}, the largest additional demand among the other processes — the member of that set no other member rises above. The strict < asserts that this total remains below that value.

On the left is Min(Xp, Xq), the smaller of the two individual holdings taken on its own rather than added together. On the right is Min{Yk | k ≠ p, q}, the smallest additional demand among the other processes. The ≥ asserts that this single holding is at least as large as that value, fixing how small the holding may be.

The left side is again Min(Xp, Xq), the smaller of the two individual holdings taken on its own, and the right side is Max{Yk | k ≠ p, q}, the largest additional demand among the other processes. The ≤ asserts that this single holding is no larger than that value, fixing how large the holding may be.

This is the HPSC answer-sheet entry used for leaving an item unanswered. It carries no relation between the holdings X and the outstanding demands Y, so it states nothing about which processes can finish.

title: When process is rolled back as result of deadlock the
subject: Operating System
text: When a process is rolled back as a result of deadlock the difficulty which arises is
solution:
When a deadlock is detected, one recovery strategy involves rolling back or aborting one of the involved processes to release resources.

The primary difficulty arising from this approach is starvation. If the system repeatedly selects the same process for rollback due to cost factors or priority, that process may never complete its execution.

To mitigate this, operating systems implement mechanisms like aging or cost analysis to ensure fair resource allocation during deadlock resolution.

optionFeedback.html: Starvation occurs when a process is repeatedly rolled back and fails to make forward progress indefinitely.
While deadlock resolution impacts throughput, the specific difficulty of process rollback concerns individual progress guarantees.
This option describes a system performance metric, not the specific risk associated with repeated process rollback during deadlock resolution.
Cycle stealing is a technique used in DMA operations, unrelated to the consequences of process rollback in deadlock handling.

title: Which of the one of the following statement is FALSE
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the one of the following statement is FALSE

options.html: Code that can deadlock is not guaranteed to make progress in all cases.
Race conditions and deadlocks are separate kinds of coding errors.
If the code is vulnerable to starvation, then that will result in deadlock.
To guarantee no deadlock, it is sufficient to negate just one of the four conditions that contribute to avoid deadlock.

solution: False. Deadlock can result in starvation, but starvation can happen without deadlock.

optionFeedback.html: This statement is true. Deadlock means two or more threads or processes are waiting indefinitely for each other’s resources, so code that can deadlock is not guaranteed to make progress in every execution.

This statement is true. Race conditions and deadlocks are different problems: a race condition produces incorrect or unpredictable results due to unsynchronized access to shared data, while a deadlock is a situation where threads wait forever for resources and no progress occurs.

This statement is false. Starvation means a thread or process is repeatedly denied resources or scheduling and may never make progress, while other threads can still run. Deadlock requires a circular wait where the involved threads are all blocked. Starvation can occur without deadlock (for example, a low-priority task never scheduled), and deadlock can cause starvation for some tasks, but starvation does not necessarily imply deadlock.

This statement is true. The four Coffman conditions for deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. If you prevent (negate) any one of these conditions you eliminate the possibility of deadlock. For example, preventing circular wait by imposing a global resource ordering avoids deadlocks.

title: Which technique can be applied to resolve deadlock after it
subject: Operating System
text: Which technique can be applied to resolve a deadlock after it has been detected?
solution: After a deadlock has been detected, we can apply either Process Termination or Resource Preemption to resolve it. The Banker's algorithm is a prevention/avoidance technique, not a resolution technique.

optionFeedback.html: Process termination is a valid technique to resolve deadlocks by terminating one or more processes involved in the deadlock cycle.
Resource preemption is a valid technique to resolve deadlocks by forcibly taking resources from processes and reallocating them.
Banker’s algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance, not resolution after detection.
This option includes techniques like process termination and resource preemption, which resolve deadlocks after detection.

title: Question 11611
subject: Operating System
text: Overlaying

options.html: allows larger programs, but requires more effort

solution:
Overlaying is a memory-management technique used on systems that lack (or predate) virtual memory: only the code and data a running process needs at a given moment are kept in main memory, while the rest stays on secondary storage and is swapped in only when required. The operating system does not do this swapping automatically — the programmer, or a linker-driven overlay manager, must divide the program into overlay segments and control when each segment is loaded and unloaded.

For this item, that dual nature is exactly what the correct completion captures: overlaying lets a program whose total size exceeds physical memory still execute, because at any moment only the overlay segments that are mutually exclusive in use need to share the same memory region — typically alongside a small permanently resident root segment — while the rest wait on secondary storage until called for. Achieving this needs deliberate design work: identifying which routines can safely share the same memory region and inserting the calls that trigger each swap. So overlaying "allows larger programs, but requires more effort" is the accurate characterization.

  • requires use of a loader — a loader participates in launching any program, overlaid or not; it is not the property that distinguishes overlaying from ordinary program execution.

  • is most used on large computers — the opposite is true: overlaying became necessary specifically on machines with small physical memory, to fit programs that would not otherwise run.

  • is transparent to the user — that describes fully OS-managed schemes such as demand paging, introduced later; here "user" means whoever writes and manages the program (not the end user running the finished application), and overlaying does not carry that same invisibility to that person, since it is that person who must lay out the segments and code the swap calls.

So overlaying is the technique that lets a program exceed physical memory size, at the cost of extra design effort from whoever writes it.

optionFeedback.html: A loader participates in launching every program, whether or not it uses overlays, so this doesn't capture what is distinctive about the overlay technique itself.

This matches how overlaying works: only the segment needed at a given moment sits in memory, so a program bigger than physical memory can still run, but the developer must design and trigger every segment swap.

The relationship runs the other way: overlaying became necessary specifically on machines with small, limited physical memory, so a program could still run despite that hardware constraint — not because of large computers.
This description matches demand paging and virtual memory — later memory-management schemes distinct from the classic overlay technique this question is testing.

title: The operating system and the other processes are protected from
subject: Operating System
text: The operating system and the other processes are protected from being modified by an already running process because

options.html: they run at different time instants and not in parallel
they use a protection algorithm in the scheduler
every address generated by the CPU is being checked against the relocation and limit parameters

solution: Modern operating systems protect the OS and other processes from modification by running processes through hardware support, specifically the Memory Management Unit (MMU). The MMU enforces strict memory boundaries by checking every CPU-generated address against relocation and limit registers. This hardware enforcement ensures isolation, preventing any process from accessing or modifying protected kernel memory or the memory space of other processes.

optionFeedback.html: This option describes scheduling behavior. Protection relies on memory isolation and privilege levels, not just execution timing.
Logical address separation is part of virtual memory, but hardware enforcement is required to prevent unauthorized modifications.

Memory protection is enforced by hardware mechanisms like the MMU using limit registers, not solely by scheduler algorithms. The CPU checks every address against these limits to prevent unauthorized access.
This describes how hardware memory management units enforce boundaries by checking every address against limit registers, preventing unauthorized access to protected system areas.

title: The working set model is used in memory management to
subject: Operating System
text: The working set model is used in memory management to implement the concept of:
solution:
The working set model is explicitly based on the principle of locality. This principle states that as a process executes, it moves from one locality (a set of pages that are actively used together) to another. By tracking and keeping the active pages (the working set) of a process in main memory, the operating system effectively minimizes page faults and prevents thrashing.

Thus, the correct option is A.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The working set model directly utilizes the temporal and spatial locality of a process to dynamically define its memory requirements within a specific time window
Incorrect. Thrashing is a severe performance degradation that occurs when a system spends more time paging than executing; the working set model is used to prevent thrashing, not implement it.
Incorrect. Paging is a fundamental hardware-supported memory management scheme that maps virtual addresses to physical frames; the working set is a high-level policy overlaying demand paging.

Incorrect. Segmentation is a memory management scheme based on logical logical units (like functions or objects), whereas the working set model tracks page references regardless of physical segmentation.

title: What is the primary function of the memory manager in
subject: Operating System
text: What is the primary function of the memory manager in an operating system ?
solution: The primary function of the memory manager in an operating system is to allocate and manage memory space.

optionFeedback.html: This option describes CPU scheduling, not memory management. The memory manager handles RAM allocation and deallocation for processes.
This option correctly identifies the core responsibility of a memory manager.
File access permissions are handled by the file system, not memory management.
I/O operations are managed by device drivers, not the memory manager.

title: What is buffer in operating systems?
subject: Operating System
text: What is buffer in operating systems?
solution: A buffer is a region of memory used to temporarily store data during transfer between devices or processes. It facilitates smooth data flow by handling speed mismatches.

optionFeedback.html: A buffer acts as a temporary storage region within main memory to hold data during transfer between devices or processes. This mechanism helps synchronize speed differences and ensures smooth data flow without requiring immediate processing by the destination.

Registers are hardware components for immediate processing, not temporary storage zones for data transfer. Buffers handle speed mismatches between devices or processes using different mechanisms than registers. Review the distinction between hardware components and temporary data holding areas next.

This option incorrectly identifies the buffer as secondary storage like a hard drive. Buffers are actually temporary regions within main memory (RAM) used to hold data between devices or processes efficiently. You should verify the volatility and location of the storage area next.

This option is incorrect because Read-Only Memory cannot be written to during data transfer operations. A buffer requires a writable memory space in RAM to temporarily hold changing data between devices or processes efficiently. Check the read-write capabilities of memory types next.

title: With regard to computer memory, which of the following statement(s)
subject: Operating System
text:
With regard to computer memory, which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

(A) Cache memory is 'volatile' memory.
(B) Magnetic memory is 'volatile' memory.
(C) Flash memory is 'volatile' memory.
(D) RAM is 'volatile' memory.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Concept

Memory is classified as volatile or non-volatile by what happens when power is removed. Volatile memory loses its stored contents the moment power is cut off; non-volatile memory keeps its contents without any power. Whether a technology is volatile depends on its physical storage mechanism - not on how fast it is or where it sits in the memory hierarchy.

Applying it to each memory type

Memory

Storage mechanism

Keeps data without power?

Volatile?

Cache

SRAM - transistor flip-flop cells that need power to hold state

No

Yes

Magnetic (HDD, tape)

Magnetised regions on a physical surface

Yes

No

Flash

Electrons trapped in floating-gate cells

Yes

No

RAM (DRAM)

Charge on tiny capacitors that must be powered and refreshed

No

Yes

Result

Cache and RAM both rely on powered transistor or capacitor cells, so they lose their contents when power is removed - both are volatile. Magnetic storage and flash store data physically (magnetisation and trapped charge respectively) and keep it without power, so both are non-volatile. The only true statements are therefore that cache is volatile and that RAM is volatile; magnetic memory and flash being called volatile are both false.

Cross-check

Sanity check: anything you can switch off and still find your files on afterwards - a hard disk, a USB or SSD flash drive - must be non-volatile, which rules out magnetic and flash being volatile. Anything wiped on a reboot, such as the live working contents of RAM and cache, is volatile.

optionFeedback.html: This grouping calls magnetic memory volatile. Magnetic media such as hard disks and tape store each bit as a physical magnetised region on the platter or strip, and that magnetisation stays put when the power is gone - which is precisely why a hard disk still holds your data after shutdown. A medium that survives a power cut is non-volatile, so classing magnetic memory as volatile misreads how it stores bits.

This selection reflects a common shortcut: RAM is the most frequently cited example of power-dependent memory, so a learner may stop at RAM without separately working out how the other three named technologies - cache, magnetic storage, and flash - actually hold a bit. Each of the four claims in this question has to be checked against its own physical storage mechanism (a powered transistor or capacitor cell behaves differently from a magnetised region or a trapped charge on an insulated floating gate); treating RAM as the sole relevant case here skips that per-technology check for cache, magnetic storage, and flash alike.

Both of the memories named here keep their bits only while powered: SRAM cache holds each bit in a transistor flip-flop, and DRAM main memory holds each bit as charge on a capacitor that must be refreshed. Remove the supply and both relax to nothing - the defining behaviour of volatile memory. The technologies left out store bits physically and survive a power cut, so they do not belong in this group.

This grouping calls flash volatile. Flash stores each bit as electrons trapped on a floating gate, insulated so the charge stays for years with no power at all - this is exactly why a USB stick or SSD keeps your files after it is unplugged. Retaining data without power is the definition of non-volatile, so treating flash as volatile mistakes a persistent storage technology for a transient one.

title: Computer has of main memory. The jobs arrive and finish
subject: Operating System
text: A computer has 1000 K of main memory. The jobs arrive and finish in the sequence Job 1 requiring 200 K arrives Job 2 requiring 350 K arrives Job 3 requiring 300 K arrives Job 1 finishes Job 4 requiring 120 K arrives Job 5 requiring 150 K arrives Job 6 requiring 80 K arrives Among best fit and first fit, which performs better for this sequence?
solution: First Fit successfully allocates all jobs in the sequence, whereas Best Fit fails to allocate Job 6. With First Fit, Job 4 occupies the hole left by Job 1 (200K), leaving an 80K fragment that accommodates Job 6. Best Fit places Job 4 in the smallest sufficient hole (150K), fragmenting memory into unusable pieces for Job 6. Thus, First Fit performs better for this specific sequence of arrivals and finishes.

optionFeedback.html: First Fit allocates the first available hole large enough, preserving contiguous space for later jobs like Job 6 in this sequence.
Best Fit selects the smallest sufficient hole, which can create small unusable fragments that prevent later jobs from fitting.
First Fit and Best Fit allocate memory differently. In this sequence, their hole selection strategies lead to different fragmentation results.
Since the algorithms produce different allocation outcomes for this sequence, there is a clear performance difference between them.

title: The Operating System of computer may periodically collect all the
subject: Operating System
text: The Operating System of a computer may periodically collect all the free memory space to form contiguous block of free space. This is called:
solution:
Free memory in a system often ends up scattered as many small unused holes between allocated blocks — external fragmentation — even when the total free space is large enough for a request, because no single hole may be big enough to satisfy it. One class of memory-management technique addresses this by relocating currently-used (live) memory together and merging every freed hole into one large contiguous block.

For this item, that periodic “gather every free hole into one contiguous block” operation is what a compacting garbage collector performs: it identifies the memory still referenced (in use), moves that live data together toward one end, and leaves the remaining space as a single free region. Contrasting against the offered choices by what each actually means:

  • Garbage collection — reclaims unused memory and compacts the surviving data, merging the freed space into one contiguous block, which matches the stem.

  • Concatenation — joins data sequences together; it says nothing about consolidating free memory regions.

  • Collision — a hash-table or networking conflict between two items, unrelated to memory consolidation.

  • Dynamic Memory Allocation — hands memory out to a process on request, the opposite direction of gathering free memory back.

Cross-checking against the official ISRO CS 2018 answer key for this exact previous-year question confirms Garbage collection as the keyed choice, consistent with the mark-compact garbage-collection model above.

optionFeedback.html: Concatenation means joining sequences — strings, lists, or data blocks — end to end; it describes combining data, not the operating system consolidating already-free memory into one contiguous region.

A compacting garbage collector periodically identifies memory that is no longer in use and relocates the still-live data so that every freed region merges into a single contiguous block — exactly the operation the stem describes.
A collision is a conflict — two keys mapping to the same hash-table slot, or two signals contending for the same channel — a data-structure or networking term, not a memory-consolidation technique.

Dynamic memory allocation is the runtime process of handing out memory to a program on request; it explains how memory gets assigned, not how the operating system gathers already-free space back into one contiguous block.

title: What is compaction refers to
subject: Operating System
text: What is compaction refers to
solution: Compaction is a memory management technique used to address external fragmentation. It works by rearranging the contents of main memory, moving allocated blocks together to create a single large block of free memory.

optionFeedback.html: Compaction is used to solve external fragmentation by moving processes in memory. Internal fragmentation happens inside allocated blocks and isn't fixed by rearranging them.
Compaction applies to contiguous memory allocation schemes. Paging uses fixed-size blocks and does not rely on compaction to manage free space.
Compaction rearranges memory contents to consolidate free space, which is the standard method for resolving external fragmentation.
Compaction rearranges memory blocks to create contiguous free space, not compressing data size.

title: Memory system of bytes size is organized using contiguous dynamic
subject: Operating System
text:
A memory system of 200K bytes size is organized using contiguous dynamic management. P, Q, R, and S are processes running with the following allocation and deallocation requests:

(a) P requests 32KB

(b) Q requests 38KB

title: Consider five memory partition of size KB, KB, KB, KB,
subject: Operating System
text: Consider five memory partitions of size 150 KB, 400 KB, 550 KB, 220 KB, 280 KB in the same order. If sequences of requested blocks of size 200 KB, 350 KB, 220 KB, 180 KB, 300 KB, in the same order come and partitioning can be done in blocks, then which of the following algorithms satisfies all the block requests?
solution:
Answer: none of them

Reason: Step-by-step allocation shows both first-fit and best-fit fail to satisfy the final 300 KB request.

Best-fit allocation (choose the smallest partition that fits each request):

  1. Initial partitions: 150 KB, 400 KB, 550 KB, 220 KB, 280 KB

  2. Request 200 KB → allocate 220 KB (smallest fit). Remaining free: 150 KB, 400 KB, 550 KB, 280 KB.

  3. Request 350 KB → allocate 400 KB (smallest fit). Remaining free: 150 KB, 550 KB, 280 KB.

  4. Request 220 KB → allocate 280 KB (smallest fit). Remaining free: 150 KB, 550 KB.

  5. Request 180 KB → allocate 550 KB (only fit). Remaining free: 150 KB.

  6. Request 300 KB → cannot be allocated (only 150 KB remains). Best-fit fails.

First-fit allocation (choose the first partition in order that fits each request):

  1. Initial partitions: 150 KB, 400 KB, 550 KB, 220 KB, 280 KB

  2. Request 200 KB → allocate 400 KB (first fit). Remaining free: 150 KB, 550 KB, 220 KB, 280 KB.

  3. Request 350 KB → allocate 550 KB (first fit). Remaining free: 150 KB, 220 KB, 280 KB.

  4. Request 220 KB → allocate 220 KB. Remaining free: 150 KB, 280 KB.

  5. Request 180 KB → allocate 280 KB. Remaining free: 150 KB.

  6. Request 300 KB → cannot be allocated (only 150 KB remains). First-fit fails.

Conclusion: Because both common placement strategies (first-fit and best-fit) exhaust the partitions large enough to hold a 300 KB request before that request arrives, neither algorithm can satisfy all requests. Therefore the correct choice is none of them.

optionFeedback.html: This choice is incorrect. If you apply the best-fit rule step by step, the allocations are: 200 KB → 220 KB partition, 350 KB → 400 KB partition, 220 KB → 280 KB partition, 180 KB → 550 KB partition. After these allocations only the 150 KB partition remains, so the final 300 KB request cannot be satisfied.

This choice is incorrect. Neither first-fit nor best-fit can satisfy all requests in the given order. Both allocation strategies end up using the only partitions large enough for the final 300 KB request earlier in the sequence, leaving no partition ≥300 KB for the last request.

This choice is incorrect. Under first-fit the allocations are: 200 KB → 400 KB partition, 350 KB → 550 KB partition, 220 KB → 220 KB partition, 180 KB → 280 KB partition. Only a 150 KB partition remains, so the final 300 KB request cannot be served.
This choice is correct. A step-by-step check of both algorithms shows neither can satisfy the final 300 KB request given the allocation order, so none of the listed algorithms can serve all requests.

title: What type of memory allocation does the Fixed Size Partitioning
subject: Operating System

solution: Fixed-size partitioning is a contiguous memory-allocation method in which memory is divided into fixed-size partitions, and each process is loaded into one partition.

optionFeedback.html: This is correct. Fixed-size partitioning uses contiguous allocation because each process occupies one continuous partition.
This is not correct. Non-contiguous allocation is used by methods such as paging, not fixed-size partitioning.
This is not correct. Fixed-size partitioning is a contiguous allocation technique, not both contiguous and non-contiguous.
This is not correct. Contiguous allocation is the correct type used by fixed-size partitioning.

title: In the context of memory allocation strategies, what is the
subject: Operating System
text: In the context of memory allocation strategies, what is the key characteristic of the Best Fit algorithm?

options.html: Allocates the process to the smallest available block that is sufficient to hold it
Allocates memory by splitting existing blocks into equal parts
Allocates memory to the largest available partition regardless of process size
Allocates memory to the first partition large enough to hold the process

solution: The Best Fit algorithm searches the entire list of available free memory blocks to find the smallest possible block that is still large enough to hold the incoming process. By choosing a block whose size is closest to the process's required size, the algorithm minimizes the leftover, wasted space (known as internal fragmentation) created by that specific allocation.

optionFeedback.html: This option correctly identifies the Best Fit strategy's core mechanism. To verify, check if the algorithm scans all blocks to find the smallest fit rather than just the first available one.
Incorrect. This describes fixed-partitioning schemes or buddy-system allocation strategies, not the dynamic Best Fit algorithm.
Incorrect. This is the definition of the Worst Fit algorithm, which purposely chooses the largest block so that the leftover fragment remains large enough to be useful for future processes.
Incorrect. This is the definition of the First Fit algorithm, which stops scanning memory as soon as it finds any block that can fit the process, prioritizing speed over optimal placement.

title: Program is located in the smallest available hole in the
subject: Operating System
text: A program is located in the smallest available hole in the memory is
solution: Best fit memory allocation searches for the smallest available hole that can accommodate the program. This strategy minimizes external fragmentation by utilizing space more efficiently than first or worst fit approaches.

optionFeedback.html: Best fit allocation strategy searches through all available holes to find the smallest block that fits the program size. This minimizes wasted space compared to other methods like first fit or worst fit, which do not prioritize hole size.

First fit allocates the first available block regardless of size, not necessarily the smallest one. You should check if the definition matches searching for the minimal hole that fits the request size instead of just taking the first available space.

Worst-fit allocation specifically selects the largest available hole to minimize external fragmentation, not the smallest. You should check if you confused worst-fit with best-fit strategies when identifying memory allocation methods based on hole size requirements carefully.

Buddy systems split memory into fixed power-of-two blocks rather than searching for the smallest contiguous hole available in memory. Review how dynamic partitioning differs from buddy system allocation when locating suitable memory spaces for programs effectively.

title: What is the typical method of assigning processes to partitions
subject: Operating System
text: In fixed partitioning, what is the occupancy rule for each memory partition?
solution:
In contiguous memory allocation the operating system divides main memory into regions called partitions, and the partition is the unit of allocation: memory is handed out one whole partition at a time. Fixed (static) partitioning settles the number of partitions and their boundaries at system-generation time, before any process arrives, and those boundaries are never moved, split or merged while the system runs.

Applying that to the assignment step: because a boundary cannot move, a partition is either wholly free or wholly occupied. The loader places an admitted process into one partition, and that process owns the entire partition until it terminates or is swapped out.

  1. The partition table fixes k partitions of sizes S1, S2, …, Sk, decided before any process is admitted.

  2. A process of size p is admitted into a partition whose size Si is at least p, and it takes that partition as a unit.

  3. The unused Si − p bytes stay trapped inside that partition and cannot be given to a second process. That trapped space is internal fragmentation, the characteristic waste of the scheme.

  4. At most k processes can be resident at the same time, so the partition count bounds the degree of multiprogramming.

Cross-check against the other mechanisms named in this item; each governs a different decision:

Mechanism

Decision it governs

Round-robin

CPU scheduling: the order and time quantum with which ready processes use the processor

Dynamic allocation

Variable partitioning: region boundaries built at run time to the arriving process’s own request

Best-fit

Placement heuristic: which of the candidate free regions is chosen for a request

One process per partition

Occupancy rule of fixed partitioning: a partition is taken by a single process at a time

A placement heuristic such as best-fit may be layered on top of fixed partitioning to decide which partition to use, but it does not change how many processes a partition can accommodate. Therefore, the occupancy rule in fixed partitioning is one process per partition.

optionFeedback.html: Round-robin is a CPU-scheduling policy. Processes in the ready queue take the processor in turn, each for a fixed time quantum, after which the running process is pre-empted and returned to the back of the queue. It governs how processor time is shared among ready processes.
With one process per partition, unused bytes between the resident process’s size and the partition’s fixed size remain inside that partition. This unused portion is internal fragmentation.

Dynamic allocation builds region boundaries at run time, carving a region sized to the arriving process’s own request, so the number and sizes of regions change as processes enter and leave memory. It is the allocation discipline of variable (dynamic) partitioning.

Best-fit is a placement heuristic. Among the free regions large enough for a request it selects the region of smallest size, so the leftover hole is as small as possible. It ranks candidate regions; first-fit and worst-fit rank the same candidates by different criteria.

title: Which of the following is FALSE?
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following is FALSE?

options.html: DMA is a mechanism for allowing an I/O device to transfer data to and from memory without involving the CPU in the transfer.
An advantage of implementing threads in user space is that they don't incur the overhead of having the OS schedule their execution.
A TLB miss could occur even though the requested page was in memory.
A context switch from one process to another can be accomplished without executing OS code in kernel mode.

solution:
A context switch from one process to another can be accomplished without executing OS code in kernel mode.

Why this statement is false:

  • Changing the active address space: A process context switch normally requires loading a different page table base (or equivalent MMU state), which is a privileged operation that must be done in kernel mode.

  • Saving and restoring privileged state: The OS must save CPU registers and kernel-mode state for the outgoing process and restore them for the incoming process; this is handled by kernel code.

  • TLB and hardware updates: The MMU and TLB often require updates or flushes when switching address spaces, which involve privileged instructions or kernel-managed actions.

  • Kernel coordination: The OS scheduler decides which process runs and orchestrates the switch, including any bookkeeping and resource management, which executes in kernel mode.

  • Note: Switching between user-level threads within the same process can sometimes be done without kernel involvement, but that does not change the process address space and is not a process context switch.

Therefore, the statement is false: a context switch from one process to another requires executing OS code in kernel mode.

optionFeedback.html: This statement is correct. Direct Memory Access (DMA) lets an I/O device transfer data directly to or from main memory via a DMA controller, so the CPU does not have to copy the data. The CPU typically initiates the transfer and is interrupted or notified when the transfer completes.

This statement is correct as an advantage. Implementing threads in user space can avoid the overhead of kernel scheduling because switching between user-level threads does not require a kernel-mode context switch. However, note the trade-offs: blocking system calls can block the entire process, the kernel cannot schedule individual user threads on multiple CPUs, and some scheduling and preemption features are harder to implement in pure user-level threading.

This statement is correct. A Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is a cache of recent page table entries. A TLB miss can occur even when the requested page is resident in physical memory; the CPU must then consult the page table (possibly in memory) to get the mapping and load it into the TLB. A page fault only happens if the page is not present in physical memory.

This statement is false. A full context switch between processes requires kernel-mode involvement because the system must change the active address space (MMU/page table base), save and restore privileged CPU state, switch kernel stacks, and typically flush or update TLB entries. User-mode code cannot perform these privileged operations. (Switching between user-level threads within the same process can sometimes be done without kernel code, but that is not a process context switch.)

title: Let TLB hit ratio is and assume memory access time
subject: Operating System
text: Let TLB hit ratio is 80% and assume memory access time is 100 ns. One TLB miss requires extra memory access to the page table for the frame number. The Effective Access Time to read a virtual address is ______ % slowdown, compared to no-paging.
solution:
Answer: 20% slowdown.

Explanation and steps:

  1. Given hit ratio = 80% (0.8) and memory access time = 100 ns. A TLB miss requires one extra memory access to read the page table (so a miss causes two memory accesses total).

  2. Time on a TLB hit = 100 ns.

  3. Time on a TLB miss = 100 ns (page table access) + 100 ns (actual memory access) = 200 ns.

  4. Effective Access Time (EAT) = 0.8 * 100 ns + 0.2 * 200 ns = 80 ns + 40 ns = 120 ns.

  5. Slowdown compared to no-paging = (EAT - base) / base * 100% = (120 ns - 100 ns) / 100 ns * 100% = 20%.

Therefore the effective access time corresponds to a 20% slowdown compared to no paging.

title: Machine has 48-bit virtual addresses and 32-bit physical addresses. Pages
subject: Operating System
text: A machine has 48-bit virtual addresses and 32-bit physical addresses. Pages are 8K. How many entries are needed for an inverted page table?
solution:
Key idea: an inverted page table has one entry per physical frame, so the number of entries equals the number of physical frames (physical memory size divided by page size).

title: Consider movie player application that supports functions like play movies,
subject: Operating System
text: Consider a movie player application that supports functions like play movies, skip forward x data frames and skip backward x data frames. Suggest a memory management policy that will be best suited for this application.
solution:
Recommended policy: Use paging with prefetching (lookahead) and a sliding-window buffer of adjacent frames.

  • Why paging fits:

    Frames map naturally to fixed-size pages, allowing efficient disk-to-memory transfers and easy random access to any frame.

  • Prefetch / lookahead:

    Always load the next k pages ahead of the current frame and keep the previous k pages in memory. Prefetch asynchronously to hide I/O latency and choose k based on network/disk bandwidth and available memory.

  • Page replacement policy:

    Evict pages farthest from the current playback position (distance-based) or use LRU within the sliding window. This preserves nearby frames needed for forward/backward skips and leverages locality of reference.

  • Implementation notes:

    Maintain an indexed cache or circular buffer of page numbers, perform asynchronous reads for prefetch, and dynamically adjust the buffer size based on user behavior and system resources.

  • Why other approaches are less suitable:

    Overlays require manual partitioning and swapping logic, adding programmer overhead. Segmentation manages variable-sized regions and can cause fragmentation; it does not provide the simple fixed-block caching and prefetch benefits needed for frame-based playback.

optionFeedback.html: Paging is the best fit because movie frames map well to fixed-size pages that can be loaded on demand. Use prefetching (lookahead) to load upcoming pages before they are needed and keep a small buffer of recently used pages around the current frame. This supports fast forward/backward skips and exploits locality of reference with low programmer overhead.

Overlays require the programmer to manually manage which code/data regions are loaded into a fixed memory area. This adds complexity and is not well suited to automatically caching many sequential video frames or handling unpredictable skips.

Segmentation provides variable-sized logical regions and is useful when different logical objects need independent protection or sharing. Video frames are uniform blocks of data, so segmentation adds complexity and fragmentation without providing the caching and prefetch benefits that paging offers.

Rejecting all listed options is incorrect because paging directly supports the application's needs. A paging-based approach with prefetching and a buffer window is a practical, efficient solution for play/skip operations.

subject: Operating System
text: Suppose the time to service a page fault is on average 10 milliseconds, while a memory access takes 1 microsecond. Then a 99.99% hit ratio results in an average memory access time of
solution:
Effective (average) memory access time (EAT) combines a fast path — a hit serviced directly from memory — and a slow path — a miss that must first pay the full page-fault service time. In general, EAT = (Hit Ratio × Memory Access Time) + (Miss Rate × Page-Fault Service Time), where Miss Rate = 1 − Hit Ratio. Because page-fault service time is typically orders of magnitude larger than a single memory access, even a very small miss rate can dominate the result, so every term must be converted to one consistent time unit before combining them.

  1. Identify the given values: memory access time = 1 microsecond; page-fault service time = 10 milliseconds; hit ratio = 99.99% = 0.9999, so miss rate = 1 − 0.9999 = 0.0001 (0.01%).

  2. Convert every time to the same unit (microseconds): 10 milliseconds = 10,000 microseconds.

  3. Apply the EAT formula: EAT = (0.9999 × 1 microsecond) + (0.0001 × 10,000 microseconds).

  4. Compute each weighted term separately: 0.9999 × 1 microsecond = 0.9999 microseconds; 0.0001 × 10,000 microseconds = 1 microsecond.

  5. Sum the two weighted terms: 0.9999 microseconds + 1 microsecond = 1.9999 microseconds, which rounds to approximately 2 microseconds.

Cross-check: since the hit ratio is almost 1, the hit term alone contributes almost exactly 1 microsecond (0.9999 × 1 microsecond ≈ 1 microsecond), and the miss term also works out to exactly 1 microsecond (0.0001 × 10,000 microseconds = 1 microsecond); two terms each close to 1 microsecond must sum to close to 2 microseconds, confirming 1.9999 microseconds ≈ 2 microseconds independently of the step-by-step arithmetic above.

This shows how even a 0.01% miss rate can nearly double the effective access time when the page-fault penalty is four orders of magnitude larger than a single memory access.

This option calculates the virtual address space (entries × page size). Physical space depends on frame number bits available in each entry.
The page table entry size is 11 bits. Subtracting the valid/invalid bit leaves 10 frame number bits (2^10 frames). Multiply by page size 512 bytes (2^9) to get total physical address space of 2^19.
This value suggests using all 11 bits for the frame number. Remember to exclude the valid/invalid bit from the entry size when calculating frame bits.

title: Computer uses bit virtual address space, and GB physical address
subject: Operating System
text: A computer uses 40 bit virtual address space, and 2 GB physical address space with page size 128KB. The page table entry is of 2 bytes and if multilevel paging is implemented on virtual address then number of level of page table are: __________
solution:
Answer: 2 levels

Reasoning:

  1. Page size = 128 KB = 2^17 bytes, so the page offset requires 17 bits.

  2. Virtual address size = 40 bits, so the virtual page number (VPN) bits = 40 - 17 = 23 bits.

  3. Page table entry size = 2 bytes. Entries that fit in one page = page size / PTE size = 2^17 / 2 = 2^16 entries per page. Each page-table level can therefore index 16 bits of the VPN.

  4. Number of levels needed = ceil(VPN bits / bits indexed per level) = ceil(23 / 16) = 2.

  5. Sanity check: With two levels, the top-level needs ceil(2^23 / 2^16) = 2^7 = 128 entries, which fits in a single page (since one page can hold 2^16 entries).

title: Consider 32-bit machine where four-level paging scheme is used. If
subject: Operating System
text: Consider a 32-bit machine where a four-level paging scheme is used. If the hit ratio to TLB is 90%, and it takes 20 nanosecond to search the TLB and 100 nanoseconds to access the main memory, what is effective memory access time in nanoseconds?
solution:
Key idea: account for TLB search time on every access, and on a TLB miss include the memory accesses required to walk the four-level page table plus the final data memory access.

  • On a TLB hit (90%): TLB search (20 ns) + memory access (100 ns) = 120 ns.

  • On a TLB miss (10%): TLB search (20 ns) + four page-table memory accesses to walk the four-level page table (4 × 100 ns = 400 ns) + final data memory access (100 ns) = 20 + 400 + 100 = 520 ns.

EAT calculation:

EAT = 0.9 × 120 + 0.1 × 520 = 108 + 52 = 160 ns.

Final effective memory access time = 160 ns.

title: Consider 32-bit machine where four-level paging scheme is used. If
subject: Operating System
text: Consider a 32-bit machine where four-level paging scheme is used. If the hit ratio to TLB is 98%, and it takes 20 nanosecond to search the TLB and 100 nanoseconds to access the main memory what is effective memory access time in nanoseconds?
solution:
Let H = 0.98 (TLB hit ratio), T = 20 ns (TLB search time), and M = 100 ns (memory access time). Four-level paging means k = 4 memory accesses to walk the page table on a TLB miss.

On a TLB hit, the cost is T + M (TLB lookup plus one memory access for the data).

On a TLB miss, the cost is T + k*M + M (TLB lookup, k memory accesses to walk the page table, and one final memory access for the data).

Effective access time (EAT):

EAT = H*(T + M) + (1 - H)*(T + k*M + M)

Substitute values: k = 4

  1. Cost on hit = T + M = 20 + 100 = 120 ns

  2. Cost on miss = T + 4*M + M = 20 + 400 + 100 = 520 ns

  3. EAT = 0.98*120 + 0.02*520 = 117.6 + 10.4 = 128 ns

Final answer: 128 ns

title: Suppose you have 47-bit virtual address space with page size
subject: Operating System
text: Suppose you have a 47-bit virtual address space with a page size of 16KB and that page table entry takes 8 bytes. How many levels of page tables would be required to map the virtual address space if every page table is required to fit into a single page?
solution:
1. **Page Offset:** The page size is 16KB ($2^{14}$ bytes), so the offset requires 14 bits.

  2. **Entries per Page:** Each PTE is 8 bytes ($2^3$). A single page can hold $16KB / 8B = 2^{14} / 2^3 = 2^{11}$ entries. This means each level of the page table consumes 11 bits of the virtual address.

  3. **Index Bits:** The total virtual address is 47 bits. Subtracting the 14-bit offset leaves $47 - 14 = 33$ bits for page table indices.

  4. **Levels Required:** We need to cover 33 index bits using 11-bit chunks per level. $33 / 11 = 3$. Thus, exactly 3 levels are needed.

optionFeedback.html: Two levels only cover 22 index bits ($11 imes 2$), but you need to map 33 index bits (47 total - 14 offset).

With a 16KB page size ($2^{14}$), each table holds $2^{11}$ entries (8 bytes). A 47-bit address minus the 14-bit offset leaves 33 bits. Dividing these 33 bits by 11 bits per level results in exactly 3 levels.
This option is incorrect because it suggests an extra level. The calculation shows exactly 3 levels are needed to cover the remaining 33 bits of the address.
This option is incorrect because it suggests too many levels. The calculation shows exactly 3 levels are needed, not 5.

title: In Multilevel Paging, how many levels of page tables are

solution: Multilevel Paging uses multiple levels of page tables.. The number of levels in multilevel paging is variable because it depends entirely on the architecture of the CPU and the size of the virtual address space it needs to support.The goal is to ensure that each individual page table fits within a single page frame of memory.

optionFeedback.html: : Incorrect. This describes Single-level Paging. In this scheme, a single linear page table is used to map the entire virtual address space to physical memory. This becomes highly inefficient in terms of memory consumption when the address space is large (e.g., 64-bit systems), as the entire table must reside in contiguous memory.

Incorrect (Partially). While two-level paging is a common form of multilevel paging (often called "Hierarchical Paging"), it is just one specific instance. Defining multilevel paging as strictly "two levels" is too restrictive, as modern architectures often require more to manage massive address spaces effectively.

Incorrect. Similar to Option B, this is too specific. While many modern 64-bit systems use 3, 4, or even 5 levels of paging, "Multilevel Paging" as a concept does not mandate a minimum of three levels. It simply requires that there be more than one level.
Correct. The number of levels in multilevel paging is variable because it depends entirely on the architecture of the CPU and the size of the virtual address space it needs to support.

title: Computer with 32-bit address uses two-level page table. Virtual addresses
subject: Operating System
text: A computer with a 32-bit address uses two-level page table. Virtual addresses are split into a 9-bit top level page table field, an 11-bit second level page table field and an offset. How large are the pages ?
solution: The page offset is calculated by subtracting the page table fields from the total address bits: 32 - 9 - 11 = 12 bits. Page size equals 2 raised to the power of offset bits, so 2^12 bytes = 4096 bytes or 4 KB.

optionFeedback.html: This option is incorrect because the page offset determines size. Calculate offset as 32 minus top-level and second-level bits to find the correct page size.
Correct. Offset = 32 - 9 - 11 = 12 bits. Page size = 2^12 bytes = 4 KB.

This option suggests an offset of 13 bits since log2(8KB) equals 13. However, the total address is 32 bits with 9 plus 11 bits used for page table indices. Subtract these from 32 to find the actual offset size.
This page size is too large. The offset bits determine the page size, not the total address space. Recalculate the offset by subtracting both page table fields from 32 bits, then compute 2^offset.

title: Computer uses 46-bit virtual address, 32-bit physical address, and three-level
subject: Operating System
text:
A computer uses 46-bit virtual address, 32-bit physical address, and a three-level paged page table organization. The page table base register stores the base address of the first-level table (T1), which occupies exactly one page. Each entry of T1 stores the base address of a page of the second-level table (T2). Each entry of T2 stores the base address of a page of the third-level table (T3). Each entry of T3 stores a page table entry (PTE). The PTE is 32 bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a 1 MB 16-way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is 64 bytes.

What is the size of a page in KB in this computer?
solution:
Concept

In a hierarchical (multi-level) page table, the virtual address splits into a page offset plus one index field per level. If the page size is 2P bytes, the offset uses P bits. A table that "occupies exactly one page" must therefore fit in 2P bytes, so the number of entries it can hold is the page size divided by one entry's size. Since every entry stores a base address / PTE of 32 bits = 4 bytes, a one-page table holds 2P / 4 = 2P−2 entries, i.e. each level it feeds consumes (P − 2) index bits.

Application

  1. Let the page size be 2P bytes; the page offset is P bits.

  2. The virtual address is 46 bits, so the bits used for paging (the Virtual Page Number) are 46 − P, split across the three levels T1, T2, T3.

  3. T1 occupies one page and each entry is 4 bytes, so T1 has 2P / 4 = 2P−2 entries → the T1 index needs (P − 2) bits. T2 and T3 are each one page of the same 4-byte entries, so each of those levels is indexed by (P − 2) bits as well.

  4. Add the three index fields and set them equal to the VPN bits: (P − 2) + (P − 2) + (P − 2) = 46 − P, i.e. 3(P − 2) = 46 − P.

  5. Solve: 3P − 6 = 46 − P → 4P = 52 → P = 13.

  6. Page size = 213 bytes = 8192 bytes = 8 KB.

Cross-check

With P = 13, each level supplies P − 2 = 11 index bits, so three levels give 3 × 11 = 33 bits, plus the 13-bit offset = 46 bits = the full virtual address. The split is consistent, confirming the page size is 8 KB. (The cache details — 1 MB, 16-way, 64-byte blocks — belong to a companion part of this problem and are not needed to size the page.)

optionFeedback.html: 2 KB corresponds to P = 11. This results from assuming a one-page table holds 2P entries — i.e. ignoring that each entry is 4 bytes — so the per-level index is taken as P bits instead of (P − 2). Dropping the entry-size factor under-counts the offset and gives too small a page.

4 KB corresponds to P = 12. This typically comes from using a 16-bit (2-byte) entry, giving 2P−1 entries per page and a (P − 1)-bit index per level. The stem fixes the entry/PTE at 32 bits = 4 bytes, so the per-level index is (P − 2), not (P − 1).

8 KB is P = 13. With 4-byte entries each one-page level is indexed by (P − 2) = 11 bits, so three levels use 33 bits and the offset uses 13 bits, totalling exactly the 46-bit virtual address — the constraint balances precisely at this page size.

16 KB is P = 14. This appears when the VPN is taken from the 32-bit physical address, or when only the offset/physical-frame arithmetic is balanced rather than equating three full index fields to (46 − P). Sizing must use the 46-bit virtual address across all three levels.

title: Match the following:
subject: Operating System
text: Match the following:
solution:
Correct mapping and explanation:

  • 1. Inverted page table — One entry for each real page of memory. Inverted page tables index by physical frame, so there is one entry per real (physical) page.

  • 2. Page table — One entry for each logical page of the program. A standard page table maps each virtual/logical page to a frame.

  • 3. Segmentation — Supports user view of code (and data). Segmentation reflects logical divisions used by the programmer such as code, stack, and data segments.

  • 4. Hashed paging — Use of chaining. Hashed paging uses a hash structure to locate page table entries; collisions are commonly handled by chaining.

  • 5. External fragmentation — Contiguous memory allocation. External fragmentation arises when free memory is split into small noncontiguous holes under contiguous allocation schemes.

Therefore the correct mapping string is: 1-e,2-c,3-b,4-a,5-d.

optionFeedback.html: The mapping '1-e,2-c,3-a,4-b,5-d' is incorrect. Segmentation is not 'Use of chaining' and hashed paging is not 'Supports user view of code'. The correct relationships are: inverted page table → one entry for each real page of memory; page table → one entry for each logical page of the program; segmentation → supports the user view of memory/code; hashed paging → uses hashing with chaining to resolve collisions; external fragmentation → related to contiguous memory allocation.

The mapping '1-e,2-c,3-d,4-b,5-a' is incorrect. While inverted page table → one entry per real page (1-e) and page table → one entry per logical page (2-c) are correct, segmentation should be matched to supporting the user's view of code/segments (not contiguous allocation in this context), hashed paging is associated with hashing and collision handling (use of chaining), and external fragmentation corresponds to issues arising from contiguous memory allocation (not chaining).

The mapping '1-e,2-c,3-b,4-a,5-d' is correct. Reasoning: inverted page table has one entry per real (physical) page; a normal page table has one entry per logical page of the process; segmentation reflects the user’s view (segments like code, stack, data); hashed paging uses hashing techniques where chaining can resolve collisions; external fragmentation is a consequence of contiguous memory allocation.

The mapping '1-c,2-e,3-b,4-a,5-d' is incorrect because it swaps the meanings of inverted page table and regular page table. A regular page table has one entry per logical page (2-c), whereas an inverted page table has one entry per real page of memory (1-e). The rest (segmentation → supports user view, hashed paging → use of chaining, external fragmentation → contiguous allocation) are correctly described but the first two are reversed here.

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE? Inverted page tables
subject: Operating System
text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

I) Inverted page tables not contain one entry per physical frame as opposed to one for each virtual page as in the case of standard page tables.

II) Hashed page tables maintains a hash table of virtual to physical translations.
solution:
Inverted: contains one entry per physical frame as opposed to one for each virtual page as in the case of standard page tables. This makes it much smaller compared to standard page tables. However, the lookup time can be very high, because the whole table has to be linearly searched typically.

Hashed: maintains a hash-table of virtual-to-physical translations. Has the advantage of inverted tables (smaller size compared to standard tables) while the lookup is much faster compared to inverted tables.

optionFeedback.html: Statement I is incorrect because inverted page tables have one entry per physical frame, not per virtual page. This contradicts the claim in I.
Statement II is correct because hashed page tables use a hash table to map virtual addresses to physical ones, enabling efficient lookups.
This option claims both statements are true, but statement I is incorrect because inverted page tables have one entry per physical frame, not per virtual page. Therefore, this choice is incorrect.

This option says neither statement is true, but statement II is actually correct because hashed page tables do use a hash table for virtual-to-physical translations. Therefore, this choice is incorrect.

title: Which of the following is/are true:
subject: Operating System
text: Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: Using large blocks in fixed partitioning may increase internal fragmentation
Using variable partitioning may increase internal fragmentation
For a system to be in deadlock, the following conditions must be satisfied: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, circular wait, and no preemption
If each resource has exactly one instance and if resource allocation graph contains a cycle then the system may or may not be in deadlock

solution:
Concept — partitioning and fragmentation: In fixed (static) partitioning, memory is divided into partitions of pre-decided sizes and each process is loaded into one whole partition. If a partition is larger than the process it holds, the unused space left inside that partition is wasted — this waste is called internal fragmentation. In variable (dynamic) partitioning, each process instead gets a partition sized exactly to its need, so internal fragmentation is eliminated; but as processes are loaded and removed over time, memory breaks up into small unusable gaps lying between allocated blocks — this waste is called external fragmentation.

Concept — deadlock necessary conditions and the resource-allocation graph (RAG): A deadlock can occur only if all four Coffman conditions hold at the same time — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; if even one is absent, deadlock is impossible. Separately, the resource-allocation graph gives a cycle test: when every resource type in the system has exactly one instance, a cycle in the graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock (cycle present ⇔ the system is deadlocked). When some resource types instead have multiple instances, a cycle is still necessary but is no longer sufficient by itself — that is the only case where the system "may or may not" be deadlocked.

Applying this to each statement:

  • The statement about large blocks in fixed partitioning increasing internal fragmentation is true — this is exactly the fixed-partitioning waste described above.

  • The statement about variable partitioning increasing internal fragmentation is false — variable partitioning removes internal fragmentation by sizing each partition to the process; it trades that for external fragmentation instead.

  • The statement listing mutual exclusion, hold and wait, circular wait, and no preemption as the conditions for deadlock is true — these are precisely the four Coffman conditions that must all hold together for a deadlock.

  • The statement about a resource-allocation-graph cycle with single-instance resources being only a maybe-deadlock is false — in the single-instance case a cycle guarantees deadlock; the "may or may not" behaviour belongs only to the multiple-instance case, which this statement is not describing.

Cross-check: the two false statements each swap in the OTHER case of a true/false pair — variable partitioning is wrongly credited with fixed partitioning's internal-fragmentation problem, and the single-instance RAG rule is wrongly given the multiple-instance case's uncertainty. Recognising which member of each pair (fixed vs variable; single-instance vs multi-instance) a statement actually describes resolves all four in one pass.

Therefore, the true statements are the fixed-partitioning/internal-fragmentation one and the four-necessary-conditions one, so those two options are correct; the other two swap in the wrong case of their respective pair and are false.

optionFeedback.html: True. In fixed partitioning each process is placed in a fixed-size partition. If the partition is larger than the process needs, the unused space inside that partition is wasted — this is internal fragmentation.

False. Variable partitioning allocates memory sized exactly to the process, so internal fragmentation is minimized. It can, however, cause external fragmentation — unused small gaps between allocated regions — which may prevent allocation of a larger request later.

True. The four Coffman conditions — mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait — are necessary for deadlock: whenever a system is deadlocked, all four conditions hold together. If even one of these conditions is absent, deadlock cannot occur.

False. When every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph is sufficient on its own to guarantee a deadlock — it is not merely possible. The "may or may not" phrasing only applies when some resource types have multiple instances.

title: Assume that both logical and physical addresses are of the
subject: Operating System
text: Assume that both logical and physical addresses are of the same size, 32 bits. Memory is byte addressable, and the logical address space is divided into 32 equal-sized segments. What must be the page size such that the page table of the segment fits exactly in one page of the memory by taking the entry size as 8 Bytes?

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are False? Compaction technique is
subject: Operating System
text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are False?

P: Compaction technique is to avoid external fragmentation

Q: Paging is a memory management scheme that permits the physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous

R: Segmentation is a memory management scheme that supports the user's view of memory

S: Both segmentation and paging will avoid internal fragmentation.
solution:
Concept

Main memory is handed out in allocation units, and the size rule for those units decides which kind of waste can appear. Internal fragmentation is space wasted inside a unit that was allocated to a process but not fully used, so it can arise only when the units are fixed-size. External fragmentation is free space that does exist but lies in scattered holes, none individually large enough to satisfy a request, and it arises when the units are variable-sized and are allocated and released over time. Compaction is a separate remedy rather than an allocation scheme: it relocates already-allocated blocks so that the scattered holes merge into one larger contiguous hole.

Application to the four statements

  1. P — "Compaction technique is to avoid external fragmentation." Compaction slides allocated blocks together so that separate small holes become one contiguous hole, which is exactly the condition external fragmentation describes. Compaction therefore targets external fragmentation, and the statement holds.

  2. Q — "Paging permits the physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous." Paging splits the logical address space into fixed-size pages and maps each page to any free physical frame, so the frames holding one process need not be adjacent in physical memory. The statement holds.

  3. R — "Segmentation supports the user's view of memory." Segmentation divides a program into logical units such as code, data, stack and heap, which is how a programmer already pictures the program, and each segment is addressed as <segment number, offset>. The statement holds.

  4. S — "Both segmentation and paging will avoid internal fragmentation." Paging allocates whole fixed-size frames, so the last frame of a process is usually only partly filled and that unused tail is internal fragmentation. Paging therefore does not avoid internal fragmentation, so the combined claim about both schemes cannot hold. The statement fails.

Cross-check

Scheme

Allocation unit

Fragmentation it can suffer

Paging

Fixed-size pages and frames

Internal (unused tail of the last frame)

Segmentation

Variable-size segments

External (scattered holes between segments)

The table shows the trade-off directly: a fixed-size unit buys freedom from external fragmentation at the cost of internal fragmentation, while a variable-size unit does the reverse. No single scheme in this pair escapes both, which is why a claim that both schemes avoid internal fragmentation cannot survive.

Result

Statements P, Q and R all hold, and S fails. The set of false statements is exactly {S}.

optionFeedback.html: This selection treats two of the four statements as false: that compaction's purpose is to avoid external fragmentation, and that segmentation and paging both avoid internal fragmentation. Compaction is a relocation of already-allocated blocks rather than an allocation policy, while paging allocates in whole fixed-size frames and segmentation allocates in variable-size segments.

This selection treats one of the four statements as false: that paging permits a process's physical address space to be non-contiguous. Paging maps fixed-size logical pages onto physical frames through a page table.

This selection treats one of the four statements as false: that segmentation and paging both avoid internal fragmentation. Paging allocates in whole fixed-size frames and segmentation allocates in variable-size segments, the two schemes named in that claim.

This selection treats two of the four statements as false: that paging permits a process's physical address space to be non-contiguous, and that segmentation and paging both avoid internal fragmentation. Paging maps fixed-size logical pages onto physical frames through a page table, allocating in whole fixed-size frames, while segmentation allocates in variable-size segments.

title: Which of the following heap memory allocation strategies is likely

text: Which of the following heap memory E allocation strategies is likely to exploit spatial locality of memory accesses in a program, the most?
solution: Next Fit is the strategy that best exploits spatial locality. It continues searching from the last allocated position, clustering new memory blocks near previous ones in the heap. This reduces the distance between related data objects compared to First Fit or Best Fit, which may scatter allocations.
